research.dossier:
DOSSIER R01 — Fleet & network (documentation half; measurements belong to spike S-01). Date verified: 2026-08-22. Sources: Tailscale KB pages (cited by "Last validated" date since the KB is unversioned), Tailscale client source at tag v1.102.3, llama.cpp at tag b10581 (commit 2115b73d8ebdbd659075cce66c609506863bc826, the newest release on 2026-08-22), NVIDIA CUDA release notes and GPU tables.

1. TAILSCALE CONNECTION MODEL (what the plan can assume). Tailscale offers three connection types — direct (UDP peer-to-peer), DERP-relayed, and Peer-Relay (another tailnet device relays) — all end-to-end WireGuard-encrypted; "the primary difference between them is performance, not security" (F1). Every connection STARTS relayed via DERP and is upgraded to direct if NAT traversal succeeds; otherwise it tries a peer relay, otherwise stays on DERP and periodically re-checks (F2). DERP servers have "limited QoS", are "generally slower than direct connections and may offer lower maximum throughput", and being relayed when direct was possible "is one of the most common causes of performance issues" (F3). DERP cannot read traffic (F4). Clients pick the lowest-latency DERP region; the US has 10 regions (F5).

2. WHEN HOME NETWORKS GET RELAYED. Tailscale's official connectivity matrix (KB 1411): No-NAT+anything → Direct; Easy+Easy → Direct; Easy+Hard → Relayed; Hard+Hard → Relayed (F6). Easy NAT = full-cone NAT / UPnP, NAT-PMP or PCP available / hairpinning / consistent port mapping. Hard NAT = per-destination port mapping with unpredictable external ports. NOTE: KB 1257 says only "Tailscale can't establish a direct connection if both devices are behind a hard NAT", and the 2020 NAT-traversal blog says the birthday-paradox trick gets through ONE hard NAT — the KB pages are not fully consistent; plan conservatively per the 1411 matrix and measure (open question). Tailscale's own 2020 blog: "home routers tend to be easy NATs"; under CGNAT, port-mapping protocols don't help across the carrier box, and two peers behind the same CGNAT need the ISP box to hairpin — "If both hairpinning and port mapping protocols fail, you're stuck with relaying" (F14). Tailscale IPs themselves come from the CGNAT range 100.64.0.0/10 (F13).

3. HOW TO IMPROVE ODDS OF DIRECT (what to put in the member setup guide). Enable NAT-PMP or UPnP on the home router; or open/forward UDP 41641 on the public IP ("ensures a direct connection from any peer device, where possible"); port changeable via tailscaled --port (F7). Firewall egress needed: TCP *:443 (control + DERP data), UDP from :41641 to *:*, UDP *:3478 (STUN), optional TCP *:80 (F8). Peer Relays (Tailscale ≥1.86, any OS except iOS/tvOS/Android, needs one reachable UDP port, `tailscale set --relay-server-port=N` + a `tailscale.com/cap/relay` grant) are "usually faster than DERP" but still slower than direct (F11).

4. WHAT `tailscale netcheck` / `status` / `ping` FIELDS MEAN (S-01 must record these per node). netcheck: UDP (false ⇒ will rely on DERP), IPv4/IPv6 public endpoints, MappingVariesByDestIP ("the most important field" — true ⇒ hard NAT), HairPinning, PortMapping (UPnP/NAT-PMP/PCP; false ⇒ "device likely cannot use direct connections"), Nearest DERP + per-region DERP latency (F9). status column 5: "active; direct <ip:port>" vs 'active; relay "<city>"' vs "peer-relay <ip:port>:vni:<id>"; JSON: `tailscale status --json | jq '.Peer[].Relay'`. ping: lines read "via DERP(nyc) in 130ms" until a direct path appears as "via <ip:port> in 35ms"; `--until-direct` defaults true; otherwise ends "direct connection not established" (F10).

5. USERSPACE-NETWORKING MODE ON THE HUB — A TOPOLOGY PROBLEM. KB 1112: with `--tun=userspace-networking` there is no TUN interface; tailscaled "functions as a SOCKS5 or HTTP proxy which other processes ... can connect through"; apps must be pointed at ALL_PROXY/HTTP_PROXY; the mode is "primarily for serverless environments" (F12). Tailscale source (v1.102.3 netstack.go) shows inbound TCP to the node's Tailscale IP on port P is dialed to 127.0.0.1:P on the host (F12b). Meanwhile llama.cpp's RPC client dials workers with a plain TCP connect() and has no proxy support (F20). Consequence: on solarplexus as currently configured, llama-server `--rpc 100.x.y.z:50052` CANNOT reach workers (outbound 100.x traffic has no route without TUN), but an rpc-server on solarplexus bound to its default 127.0.0.1:50052 IS reachable from peers (inbound gets forwarded to loopback). CLAUDE.md §3.2 assigns llama-server to solarplexus — that assignment needs either TUN mode on the hub or role inversion. This is the single most important finding for the topology ADR.

6. WHAT THE llama.cpp RPC README SAYS ABOUT LATENCY/BANDWIDTH: NOTHING QUANTITATIVE (F19). At b10581 the README (a) names the binary `ggml-rpc-server` (CLAUDE.md still says `rpc-server`), (b) warns it is "proof-of-concept ... fragile and insecure. Never run the RPC server on an open network", (c) defaults to 127.0.0.1:50052 and prints "Never expose the RPC server to an open network!" whenever --host ≠ 127.0.0.1, (d) splits weights + KV cache across local+remote devices in proportion to available memory (`--tensor-split` overrides), (e) offers `-c` local cache to avoid re-streaming weights at load, (f) uses TCP with TCP_NODELAY, RDMA/RoCEv2 optional on Linux. Per-token cost must be reasoned from source + maintainer statements: SET_TENSOR and GRAPH_COMPUTE/GRAPH_RECOMPUTE are fire-and-forget on the wire; GET_TENSOR (and SET_TENSOR_HASH for >10 MiB payloads) block for a reply (F21). The RPC author wrote in PR #12943 that SET_TENSOR was sent "4 times per token" and that the gain from not awaiting its reply "depends on the network latency" (F22). Graph re-send is avoided via GRAPH_RECOMPUTE when the graph uid is unchanged (F23). Derived (UNVERIFIED, F24): decode is RTT-bound, not bandwidth-bound — per token the payload crossing a split boundary is roughly n_embd × 4 bytes (≈16 KiB at n_embd 4096), so the floor is (blocking round trips per token) × RTT; prefill payload scales with batch tokens; model LOAD does stream gigabytes unless `-c` cache is warm (≈13–14 min for 10 GB at 100 Mbit/s). Client and servers must share RPC protocol 5.x (HELLO rejects major mismatch or newer minor) — build every node from the same tag (F25).

7. WI-FI VS WIRED: no primary source (Tailscale KB or llama.cpp README) addresses it (F26, unverified). Because RPC decode cost is RTT/jitter-bound (F21–F24), Wi-Fi's extra and variable latency matters more than its bandwidth; S-01 must measure `tailscale ping` RTT distribution and tokens/s wired vs Wi-Fi on the same pair.

8. FLEET CUDA REALITY. CUDA 13.0 removed offline compilation and library support for Maxwell/Pascal/Volta; 12.x toolkits still target them (F27). CUDA 13.x needs driver ≥580; 12.x needs ≥525 (F28). GTX 970 = compute capability 5.2 (Maxwell); RTX 3050 = 8.6; RTX 2070 listed under 7.5 (SUPER variant not listed separately) (F29). So: the hub on driver 535 can run only CUDA 12.x builds, and a CUDA-13.1 ggml-rpc-server built on the RTX 3050 node cannot run on the GTX 970 — one shared binary is impossible across this fleet; plan per-node builds from one pinned tag, or a CUDA 12.x build for all (F30: llama.cpp build docs show `-DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES="..."`). Tailscale Personal plan verified: $0, up to 6 users, unlimited user devices (F15) — matches CLAUDE.md §3.1.

Raw sources saved under /tmp/claude-1000/-home-piratejohn-projects-corvid/98295c4f-5e2f-4bfa-a894-5509959d4ba7/scratchpad (kb_*.txt, rpc_readme_b10581.md, llama.cpp/ sparse checkout at b10581, ts_netstack.go at v1.102.3, cuda130_rn.txt).

facts.statement: Tailscale connects tailnet devices using three connection types — direct (UDP peer-to-peer), DERP-relayed, and Tailscale Peer Relay — and 'All three options are end-to-end encrypted with WireGuard. The primary difference between them is performance, not security. Direct connections usually provide the lowest latency and highest throughput, while relayed connections are a fallback when direct connectivity isn't possible.'

'All connections start as relayed through a DERP server, and Tailscale then tries to upgrade them to a direct connection. If that fails, Tailscale tries to connect them using a peer relay. If that fails, the connection remains relayed through the DERP server.' Tailscale 'periodically re-checks if it can establish a direct connection or a peer relay connection.'

'DERP servers are reliable but have limited quality of service (QoS) characteristics, so they are generally slower than direct connections and may offer lower maximum throughput. Because of this, using a relayed connection when a direct connection would be possible is one of the most common causes of performance issues.' Peer relay connections 'are usually faster than DERP connections ... However, they still introduce more latency than a fully direct connection'.

'Tailscale encrypts all data sent between devices using a DERP relayed connection using WireGuard. Because Tailscale private keys never leave the local device that generated them, it's impossible for a DERP server to decrypt your traffic. A DERP server blindly forwards already-encrypted traffic from one device to another.' DERP servers are dual-stack (IPv4 and IPv6).

Each client 'selects a home DERP server based on latency information and reports its selection to the coordination server'; 'Tailscale clients automatically select the nearest relay for low latency.' US DERP locations: Ashburn, Chicago, Dallas, Denver, Honolulu, Los Angeles, Miami, New York City, San Francisco, Seattle. `tailscale netcheck` lists the DERP servers applicable to a device; the full DERP map with RegionIDs is at https://controlplane.tailscale.com/derpmap/default (e.g. New York = RegionID 1).

Official connectivity matrix: No NAT + No NAT → Direct; No NAT + Easy NAT → Direct; No NAT + Hard NAT → Direct; Easy NAT + Easy NAT → Direct; Easy NAT + Hard NAT → Relayed; Hard NAT + Hard NAT → Relayed. 'Tailscale uses a relayed connection if one of the following is true: Both devices have a hard NAT configuration. One device has a hard NAT configuration and the other has an easy NAT configuration.' Easy NAT examples: 'full cone NAT, support for port mapping protocols (such as UPnP, PCP, or NAT-PMP), support for hair pinning, and consistent port mapping.' Devices with IPv6 'are considered easy NAT because they create direct connections in almost every situation.' (Note: KB 1257 states only 'Tailscale can't establish a direct connection if both devices are behind a hard NAT' and defines hard NAT as 'each outbound connection gets its own port mapping that only accepts replies from that specific destination, and each connection uses a different external port that outside devices cannot predict' — the two pages differ on the Easy+Hard case.)
facts.version: KB page 'Last validated: Jan 7, 2026' (KB 1257 'Last validated: Jun 1, 2026')

facts.statement: Home/small-office guidance: 'you can enable NAT-PMP or UPnP port mapping on your router to give Tailscale more predictable, reachable ports.' 'By default, opening UDP port 41641 on a device's public IP address ensures a direct connection from any peer device, where possible. You can change this port number by passing --port=<number> to tailscaled. On Linux, you can set this in /etc/defaults/tailscaled.' Prevent relays caused by blocked UDP by allowing 'outbound and return UDP traffic.'

Firewall egress Tailscale recommends when devices are on difficult networks: 'Let your internal devices start TCP connections to *:443' (coordination server and 'data connections to the DERP relays use HTTPS on port 443'); 'Let your internal devices start UDP from :41641 to *:*' ('Direct WireGuard tunnels use UDP with a source port that defaults to 41641'); 'Let your internal devices start UDP to *:3478' (STUN, which 'lets tailscaled to determine if it is behind "easy NAT" (source port maps to the same external port for all destinations) or "hard NAT" (port number varies per destination)'); optionally TCP *:80. On Ubuntu: `sudo ufw allow 41641/udp`. Windows: PORT=N in tailscaled-env.txt.

`tailscale netcheck` fields: 'UDP shows whether UDP traffic is enabled on the current network. If this is false, it's unlikely Tailscale will be able to make point-to-point connections, and will instead rely on our encrypted TCP relays (DERP)'; 'IPv4 and IPv6 show your network public IP addresses and support for both protocols'; 'MappingVariesByDestIP describes whether your device is behind a difficult NAT that varies the device's IP address depending on the destination' (KB 1411: 'the most important field to determine why a device isn't using direct connections'; True ⇒ hard NAT, likely relayed); 'HairPinning describes whether your router can route connections from endpoints on your LAN back to your LAN using those endpoints' globally-mapped IPv4 addresses/ports'; 'PortMapping describes a list of which three port-mapping services exist on your router. Possible values are "UPnP", "NAT-PMP", and "PCP"' (KB 1411: if false 'The device likely cannot use direct connections'; if any present the device 'might be able to use direct connections, even if ... MappingVariesByDestIP is true'); 'DERP latency and Nearest DERP describe latency from our encrypted TCP relays (DERP). The lowest latency ("nearest") server is used for traffic.' Blank fields mean the property could not be measured. Flags: --every, --format=json, --verbose.
facts.version: KB CLI reference (netcheck section) and KB 1411 'Last validated: Jan 7, 2026'

facts.statement: `tailscale status` column 5: 'active' includes the connection type — 'If the connection is direct, it includes peer device's IP address'; 'If the connection is relay, it includes the DERP server's city code (nyc, fra, tok, syd)'; 'If the connection is peer-relay, it includes the Tailscale IP address of the peer relay and the VNI'; 'idle' = no current traffic; '-' = never any traffic; tx/rx byte counts shown. Example direct line: '100.113.160.82 device-a tagged-devices linux active; offers exit node; direct 140.82.13.138:41641'; example relayed: '100.104.93.78 localhost-0 user@ android active; relay "tor"'. Machine-readable: `tailscale status --json | jq -r '.Peer[].Relay | select(.!="")'`. `tailscale ping <host>` prints e.g. 'pong from another-device (100.113.160.82) via DERP(nyc) in 130ms' while negotiating, then 'via 140.82.13.138:41641 in 35ms' once direct; `--until-direct` 'Stop once a direct path is established. Defaults to true'; if never direct it ends with 'direct connection not established'.
facts.version: KB CLI reference (status, ping sections); examples from KB 1257 'Last validated: Jun 1, 2026'

facts.statement: Tailscale Peer Relays let a tailnet device relay for others when direct fails. Requirements: peer relay device runs Tailscale 1.86 or later on any OS other than iOS, Apple TV, or Android, with 'At least one configurable UDP port ... accessible from other devices in the tailnet'; clients also need 1.86+. Enable with `tailscale set --relay-server-port=40000` (disable with `--relay-server-port=""`) plus a grant with app capability 'tailscale.com/cap/relay' in the tailnet policy. Tailscale tries direct, then peer relay, then DERP. Status shows 'peer-relay <ip>:<udp-port>:vni:<id>'.

Userspace networking mode (`tailscaled --tun=userspace-networking`, or FLAGS="--tun=userspace-networking" in /etc/default/tailscaled) is for systems without /dev/net/tun: 'tailscaled functions as a SOCKS5 or HTTP proxy which other processes in the container can connect through' (SOCKS5 since v1.8, HTTP proxy since v1.16); applications must be configured e.g. 'ALL_PROXY=socks5://localhost:1055/ HTTP_PROXY=http://localhost:1055/'; 'Userspace networking mode is primarily for serverless environments.' The KB page says nothing about inbound connections or performance. In the client source (v1.102.3, wgengine/netstack/netstack.go, acceptTCP: `case isTailscaleIP: dialIP = ipv4Loopback` then forwardTCP to 127.0.0.1:<same port>), an inbound TCP connection to the node's Tailscale IP on port P is forwarded to 127.0.0.1:P on the host; `ProcessLocalIPs is whether netstack should handle incoming traffic directed at the Node.Addresses (local IPs)`.
facts.version: KB page 'Last validated: Nov 12, 2025'; source at https://github.com/tailscale/tailscale/blob/v1.102.3/wgengine/netstack/netstack.go

facts.statement: Tailscale IP addresses come from the RFC 6598 Carrier-Grade NAT range 100.64.0.0/10 (100.64.0.0–100.127.255.255); 'conflicts might occur when using Tailscale with other VPNs that use the same address space.' A device's Tailscale IP stays constant across network changes (e.g. Wi-Fi to cellular).

Tailscale's NAT-traversal write-up (David Anderson, Aug 21 2020): 'home routers tend to be easy NATs, and hard NATs tend to be office routers or cloud NAT gateways'; port-mapping protocols (UPnP IGD, NAT-PMP, PCP) when available make 'one NAT vanish from the data path', but 'many devices come with a single "UPnP" checkbox that actually toggles UPnP, NAT-PMP and PCP all at once'; under CGNAT 'Aside from the port mapping protocols, everything from our current bag of tricks works fine', two peers behind the same CGNAT need the carrier box to hairpin, and 'If both hairpinning and port mapping protocols fail, you're stuck with relaying.'

Tailscale Personal plan: '$0 Free forever', 'Unlimited user devices', 'Up to 6 users'; tailnets created with public-domain accounts (Gmail, Apple, personal GitHub) are auto-enrolled in Personal; non-commercial use only.

Tailscale performance KB: 'Direct connections nearly always result in lower latency and higher throughput'; to raise the odds, expose a public IP, open a firewall port, or set up Peer Relays; Linux kernel 6.2+ with Tailscale 1.54+ enables UDP transport-layer offloads (ethtool rx-udp-gro-forwarding on, rx-gro-list off) for exit nodes/subnet routers; 'higher CPU clock speed is more important than more cores.' The KB contains no Wi-Fi-specific guidance.

llama.cpp RPC README at tag b10581: the server binary is `ggml-rpc-server` (not `rpc-server`); '> [!IMPORTANT] This example and the RPC backend are currently in a proof-of-concept development stage. As such, the functionality is fragile and insecure. **Never run the RPC server on an open network or in a sensitive environment!**' The RPC backend 'communicates with one or several instances of ggml-rpc-server and offloads computations to them'; the main host runs `llama-cli`/`llama-server ... --rpc 192.168.88.10:50052,192.168.88.11:50052`; build with `-DGGML_RPC=ON` (e.g. `cmake .. -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DGGML_RPC=ON`). Example output shows 'Starting RPC server v3.0.0 / endpoint : 127.0.0.1:50052'.

ggml-rpc-server defaults and flags (tools/rpc/rpc-server.cpp, b10581): host default "127.0.0.1", port default 50052, threads default hardware_concurrency/2; flags `-t, --threads N`, `-d, --device <dev1,dev2,...>`, `-H, --host HOST`, `-p, --port PORT`, `-c, --cache`. If host != "127.0.0.1" it prints: 'WARNING: Host ('%s') is != '127.0.0.1'' / 'Never expose the RPC server to an open network!'. Exposed devices are controllable via `--device CUDA0` or CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES; with no accelerator it exposes a single CPU device.

The RPC README at b10581 contains NO quantitative statement of latency or bandwidth required per token, and no explicit 'RPC is for fitting models, not speed' sentence. Its only performance statements are: the local cache 'can speed up model loading significantly, especially when using large models' by avoiding transferring large tensors over the network, and RDMA 'for lower latency and higher throughput' on RoCEv2 NICs (Linux, libibverbs, auto-negotiated). Per-token network cost therefore has to be inferred from source/maintainer statements (F21–F24).

RPC transport at b10581 is plain TCP (README diagram labels every link 'TCP'); the client sets TCP_NODELAY ('set TCP_NODELAY to disable Nagle's algorithm', transport.cpp) and connects with a bare `::connect()` on a socket — no SOCKS5/HTTP-proxy code exists in ggml/src/ggml-rpc/transport.cpp or ggml-rpc.cpp (grep for 'socks'/'proxy' returns nothing). RDMA is an optional alternative transport on Linux only.

RPC wire semantics at b10581 (ggml/src/ggml-rpc/ggml-rpc.cpp): request = '| rpc_cmd (1 byte) | request_size (8 bytes) | request_data |'; two send paths — one with 'No response' (fire-and-forget) and one that blocks reading '| response_size (8 bytes) | response_data |'. RPC_CMD_SET_TENSOR, RPC_CMD_GRAPH_COMPUTE and RPC_CMD_GRAPH_RECOMPUTE use the no-response path; RPC_CMD_GET_TENSOR, RPC_CMD_SET_TENSOR_HASH (tried first when a tensor payload exceeds HASH_THRESHOLD = 10 MiB), ALLOC_BUFFER, GET_DEVICE_MEMORY, HELLO etc. block for a reply. `ggml_backend_rpc_synchronize` is a no-op ('we don't have any async operations'). Hence each decode step's network floor is set by the number of blocking (reply-awaiting) calls, chiefly GET_TENSOR, times RTT.

RPC author Radoslav Gerganov (rgerganov), PR #12943 'rpc : do not wait for response when sending RPC_CMD_SET_TENSOR' (merged 2025-04-25): 'RPC_CMD_SET_TENSOR always returns an empty response and we send this 4 times per token. We can improve TG speed if we don't wait for this empty response. The performance impact of this change depends on the network latency.' (Maintainer statement that per-token RPC cost is latency-bound; the '4 per token' figure is as of April 2025.)
facts.version: PR merged 2025-04-25; behaviour confirmed present at b10581 (F21)

facts.statement: At b10581 `ggml_backend_rpc_graph_compute` re-sends the serialized graph only when `cgraph->uid` changes; otherwise it sends the small RPC_CMD_GRAPH_RECOMPUTE request ('reuse' path), so per-token graph serialization traffic is avoided in steady-state decode. Tensor copies between two RPC servers are only done server-side (RPC_CMD_COPY_TENSOR) when src and dst are on the same socket; otherwise (`src_ctx->sock != dst_ctx->sock`) cpy_tensor returns false and the scheduler falls back to get_tensor + set_tensor through the main host. Original design (PR #6829, merged 2024-05-14): 'allow distributed LLM inference using multiple hosts running on different kinds of hardware'; at that time 'Pipeline parallelism is not currently supported'.

DERIVED ESTIMATE (not stated in any primary source): for layer-split decode, the activation crossing each device boundary per generated token is ≈ n_embd × sizeof(float) bytes (≈16 KiB at n_embd 4096; ≈32 KiB at 8192), so decode bandwidth is negligible on any home link and the per-token floor ≈ (blocking round trips per token, ≥1 per remote-boundary exit) × RTT — e.g. ≥2 RTT/token with two remote servers, i.e. ≥40 ms/token at 20 ms RTT before any compute. Prefill payload scales with batch tokens (2048 tokens × 16 KiB ≈ 32 MiB per boundary). Model LOAD streams the remote shard's weights over the network unless the `-c` cache is warm (10 GB at 100 Mbit/s ≈ 13–14 min). Must be measured in S-01 (count GET_TENSOR per token with GGML_RPC_DEBUG=1).
facts.version: reasoning over llama.cpp tag b10581 source; numbers are arithmetic, not measurements

facts.statement: RPC protocol version at b10581 is 5.1.0 (RPC_PROTO_MAJOR_VERSION 5, MINOR 1, PATCH 0 in ggml/include/ggml-rpc.h; server banner 'RPC server v3.0.0' is the server program version). The client HELLO handshake rejects a server if `response.major != RPC_PROTO_MAJOR_VERSION || response.minor > RPC_PROTO_MINOR_VERSION` ('RPC server version mismatch'), so all nodes must be built from compatible (ideally identical) llama.cpp tags. Split policy: 'By default, llama.cpp distributes model weights and the KV cache across all available devices -- both local and remote -- in proportion to each device's available memory'; override with `--tensor-split`. Local cache: `-c` stores tensors under $HOME/.cache/llama.cpp/rpc (LLAMA_CACHE overrides). Debug: GGML_RPC_DEBUG=1.

No primary source consulted (Tailscale KB 1257/1232/1411/1320/1080/1082/1112, the llama.cpp RPC README and source at b10581) makes any statement about Wi-Fi versus wired links for RPC or for Tailscale performance; Tailscale KB mentions Wi-Fi only in passing (guest Wi-Fi as an unpredictable network; TUN 'like Ethernet or Wi-Fi'). Any claim that Wi-Fi hurts per-token latency rests on F21–F24 (RTT-bound protocol) plus general Wi-Fi behaviour (shared half-duplex medium, higher and more variable RTT) and must be measured in S-01, not cited.
facts.version: negative finding across the sources listed

facts.statement: CUDA Toolkit 13.0 release notes §2.6.2: 'Architecture support for Maxwell, Pascal, and Volta is considered feature-complete. Offline compilation and library support for these architectures have been removed in CUDA Toolkit 13.0 major version release. The use of CUDA Toolkits through the 12.x series to build applications for these architectures will continue to be supported, but newer toolkits will be unable to target these architectures.'

CUDA driver compatibility table (CUDA 13.3 Update 1 release notes, §2.2): CUDA 13.x requires driver >= 580; CUDA 12.x requires driver >= 525 (and < 580 for the 'max' column); 11.x >= 450. Therefore the hub on driver 535 can only run CUDA 12.x binaries (its CUDA 12.2 runtime fits), while a node on CUDA 13.1 needs driver 580+.

NVIDIA compute-capability tables: GeForce GTX 970 is listed under compute capability 5.2 (Maxwell) on the legacy-GPUs page; GeForce RTX 3050 is listed under 8.6 (Ampere) on the CUDA GPUs page; GeForce RTX 2070 is listed in the 7.5 (Turing) group — the 'RTX 2070 SUPER' variant is not listed separately, so its 7.5 classification is inferred, not read.

llama.cpp build docs (docs/build.md, b10581): CUDA builds default to '-arch=native' detection ('nvcc warning : Cannot find valid GPU for '-arch=native', default arch is used' when none found); explicit targets via `cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES="86;89"` after looking up each device's Compute Capability. Combined with F27–F29: one CUDA binary cannot serve both the GTX 970 (needs 12.x toolkit, CC 5.2) and a CUDA-13.1-built RTX 3050 node; a CUDA 12.x build with architectures '52;75;86' would cover the current Linux fleet.

`tailscale nc <hostname-or-IP> <port>` — 'Connect to a port on a host, connected to stdin/stdout' — exists in the CLI and is a possible (untested) shim for dialing tailnet TCP ports from a userspace-networking node without SOCKS support in the client application.

recommendations: TOPOLOGY ADR (reserved 0006): resolve the userspace-mode conflict on solarplexus before Phase 1. Facts F12+F20 mean llama-server on the hub cannot dial `--rpc 100.x:50052` workers today. Options to weigh in the ADR: (a) switch solarplexus tailscaled to kernel TUN mode (preferred if /dev/net/tun is available — then it can bind services to its 100.x IP and be a candidate peer relay); (b) invert roles: run llama-server (the RPC client) on a TUN-mode node (e.g. the RTX 2070 Super laptop) and run ggml-rpc-server on solarplexus at its default 127.0.0.1:50052, which peers reach via netstack's inbound→loopback forwarding; (c) bridge with `tailscale nc`/socat per worker (fragile, last resort).

Binding rule for §5.6: ggml-rpc-server binds to the node's Tailscale IP (100.x) on TUN-mode nodes, never 0.0.0.0; on userspace-mode nodes leave the default 127.0.0.1 (inbound arrives via tailscaled). Keep upstream's own warning text ('Never expose the RPC server to an open network!') in the runbook; add a CI/agent check that rejects `-H 0.0.0.0`.

Spike S-01 protocol must record per node pair: `tailscale netcheck --format=json` (UDP, MappingVariesByDestIP, PortMapping, Nearest DERP + latency table), `tailscale ping --until-direct` outcome and steady RTT, `tailscale status --json` `.Peer[].Relay`/`CurAddr`; then ggml-rpc-server decode tokens/s and ms/token for: same-LAN wired, same-LAN Wi-Fi, cross-house direct, and (if obtainable) cross-house DERP-relayed. Count blocking round trips per token with GGML_RPC_DEBUG=1 to calibrate F24.

Set Phase 1 expectations in the spec as RTT-bound: decode floor ≈ (blocking RPC round trips per token) × RTT; bandwidth only matters for prefill and model load. verdicts.reason: Fetched https://tailscale.com/kb/1257/connection-types directly (curl, raw HTML) and via WebFetch. The page is Tailscale's own KB (primary source) and shows "Last validated: Jun 1, 2026", matching the stated version. It opens: "Tailscale connects devices within a Tailscale network (known as a tailnet) using three connection types: Direct connections: Devices send packets directly to each other using UDP. DERP relayed connections: Devices send packets through DERP servers. Tailscale Peer Relay connections: Devices send packets through another device in the same tailnet acting as a relay." Immediately followed by the verbatim sentences: "All three options are end-to-end encrypted with WireGuard. The primary difference between them is performance, not security. Direct connections usually provide the lowest latency and highest throughput, while relayed connections are a fallback when direct connectivity isn't possible." The claim's gloss "direct (UDP peer-to-peer)" is also supported: the page says direct connections use UDP and later describes "a direct (peer-to-peer) connection" established via NAT traversal. Every element of the claim matches the source verbatim or in substance; nothing is outdated for the stated version.

Fetched https://tailscale.com/kb/1257/connection-types directly (raw HTML via curl, 260 KB, and via WebFetch). The page header reads "Connection types — Last validated: Jun 1, 2026", matching the stated version. The page contains, verbatim and contiguously: "All connections start as relayed through a DERP server, and Tailscale then tries to upgrade them to a direct connection. If that fails, Tailscale tries to connect them using a peer relay. If that fails, the connection remains relayed through the DERP server." and, in the Peer Relay section: "Tailscale periodically re-checks if it can establish a direct connection or a peer relay connection." Both quotes match the claim exactly. The source is Tailscale's own KB (first-party primary documentation). No discrepancy, omission, or outdating found.

verdicts.corrected_statement: Tailscale performance KB (Last validated Dec 4, 2025): "Direct connections nearly always result in lower latency and higher throughput"; to increase the likelihood of a direct connection, expose a public IP address or open a firewall port when necessary; additionally, Tailscale Peer Relay servers in your own infrastructure are used when a direct connection isn't possible and are "usually faster than DERP relay servers". Tailscale 1.54+ with Linux kernel 6.2+ enables UDP transport-layer offloads; for exit nodes/subnet routers run `ethtool -K $NETDEV rx-udp-gro-forwarding on rx-gro-list off` (non-persistent; networkd-dispatcher script shown). "In general, higher CPU clock speed is more important than more cores." The KB contains no Wi-Fi-specific guidance.

The CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES claim is not in rpc-server.cpp itself but is stated verbatim in tools/rpc/README.md at the same tag (line 68: "You can control the set of exposed CUDA devices with the CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES environment variable or the --device command line option", with `--device CUDA0` example), which also states "If there are no accelerators, it exposes a single CPU device." Only nit: the threads default is strictly max(1, hardware_concurrency/2), not bare hardware_concurrency/2 — a floor-of-1 edge case, not a substantive error. Claim stands.
verdicts.corrected_statement: (No correction needed; optional precision: threads default is max(1, hardware_concurrency()/2), and the CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES statement is sourced from tools/rpc/README.md at b10581 rather than rpc-server.cpp.)

verdicts.reason: Fetched https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/b10581/tools/rpc/README.md (HTTP 200, 4100 bytes; tag b10581 confirmed via GitHub API -> commit 2115b73d). Full-text read plus grep for ms/latency/bandwidth/Gbps/Mbps/token/speed/throughput/fit confirms: no quantitative latency or bandwidth figure, no per-token network cost, and no sentence stating RPC is for fitting models rather than speed. The only performance statements are (1) "Local cache": "The RPC server can use a local cache to store large tensors and avoid transferring them over the network. This can speed up model loading significantly, especially when using large models." and (2) "RDMA transport": "On Linux systems with RoCEv2-capable NICs (e.g. Mellanox ConnectX), the RPC backend can use RDMA instead of TCP for lower latency and higher throughput. The transport is negotiated automatically ... RDMA is enabled by default when libibverbs is found at build time." Both match the claim's characterization exactly (Linux, libibverbs, auto-negotiated, RoCEv2). Other README content (proof-of-concept/insecure warning, memory-proportional weight+KV split, --tensor-split, CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES/--device, GGML_RPC_DEBUG) contains no performance claims. Source is the primary upstream file at the stated version; claim supported as stated.

Verified against the primary source at the stated tag. Fetched raw ggml/src/ggml-rpc/transport.cpp at b10581 (HTTP 200, 683 lines): set_no_delay() carries the exact comment "// set TCP_NODELAY to disable Nagle's algorithm" (line 577) and socket_t::connect() creates an AF_INET SOCK_STREAM socket, applies set_no_delay, resolves with gethostbyname, and calls a bare `::connect(sockfd, ...)` (line 645) with no proxy handshake. Case-insensitive grep for "socks" and "proxy" in transport.cpp and ggml-rpc.cpp (2065 lines, also fetched at b10581) returns nothing; the directory at b10581 contains only CMakeLists.txt, ggml-rpc.cpp, transport.cpp, transport.h. RDMA: transport.cpp gates all RDMA code behind #ifdef GGML_RPC_RDMA; tools/rpc/README.md at b10581 says "On Linux systems with RoCEv2-capable NICs ... the RPC backend can use RDMA instead of TCP ... negotiated automatically" and ggml/src/ggml-rpc/CMakeLists.txt comments "RDMA auto-detection (Linux only, requires libibverbs)" with the option forced OFF on WIN32/APPLE. README mermaid diagram: the three RPC-backend<->ggml-rpc-server edges are all labeled |TCP|. Minor precision notes (not enough to refute): (a) "every link" is slightly overstated — intra-host edges in the diagram (llama-cli<->RPC backend, server<->CUDA/Metal devices) carry no label, but those are not network links; only the three network edges are labeled and all say TCP; (b) RDMA is "optional" in the sense of a CMake option auto-enabled ON when libibverbs is found and negotiated at runtime with TCP fallback, not opt-in; the CMake gate is literally NOT WIN32 AND NOT APPLE, described by upstream as "Linux only". Also note connect() is IPv4-only (AF_INET + gethostbyname).

research.dossier:
DOSSIER R02 — Tailscale: membership, ACLs, DNS, identity (verified 2026-08-22 against tailscale.com KB pages, the pricing page, and tailscale/tailscale at tag v1.102.3, released 2026-08-20).

1. MEMBERSHIP AND PLAN LIMITS. The current free Personal plan is "$0 Free forever", "Up to 6 users", "Unlimited user devices", "Up to 3 ACL groups", "Up to 50 tagged resources to start" (F1, F5). Tailnets created with a public-domain login (Gmail, Apple, personal GitHub) are auto-enrolled in Personal; the plan is non-commercial only (F2). Seats are counted per user, not device; an invited user only occupies a seat on first admin-console login or first device authentication (F4). The old 3-user Personal and 6-user Personal Plus plans are legacy; new Personal = 6 (F3). Two ways to bring a friend in: (a) a one-time URL "Invite any user" (the mechanism for shared-domain/personal tailnets; friends sign in with any IdP or passkey; invites expire in 30 days; available on all plans) — the friend becomes a full tailnet member and is covered by autogroup:member (F6, F7, F8); (b) node sharing — share a specific machine (e.g. solarplexus) with a user on another tailnet; the recipient gets "access to only the shared machine in your tailnet, and nothing else" (F9). Sharing is quarantined/one-directional by default: the shared machine can receive connections from the recipient but cannot initiate them; mutual sharing is possible by sharing in both directions (F10). The sharer learns the recipient's email and avatar, can write ACL rules against the recipient's email or autogroup:shared, tags/groups/subnets are stripped, only users (not tags) can accept, and the recipient must be Owner/Admin/IT admin of a tailnet (every fresh personal login creates one) (F11). Shared machines must be addressed by FQDN hostname.tailnet-name.ts.net, never the short name (F12). Crucially for zero-login, Serve identity headers ARE populated for external users who accepted a share (F13). Shared users are NOT autogroup:member (F8). Practical reading for CORVID: up to 6 full members (founder + 5) get short names, SSH, tags, full ACLs; everyone beyond that can be a *consumer* via a shared solarplexus with identity headers, but cannot easily be a *contributor* without mutual sharing, because the hub cannot open connections to them (F10).

2. ACLs, TAGS, SSH POLICY. A new tailnet's policy allows all; once an "acls"/"grants" section exists the model is deny-by-default, directional, enforced on each device; grants are the recommended syntax (F14). Tags are service-account identities: applying a tag removes user identity, a tagged device must keep at least one tag, tag ownership is declared in tagOwners, and tagged devices can only SSH into other tagged devices; all plans include 50 tagged devices (F15). The SSH policy section has action "accept" | "check", src, dst, users, checkPeriod, acceptEnv; checkPeriod default 12h (1 min–168 h or "always"); check mode itself is on all plans but a NON-default checkPeriod and localpart:*@domain user mapping require Premium/Enterprise (F16, F19). The default SSH rule is check-mode, autogroup:member → autogroup:self, users [autogroup:nonroot, root]; a destination host must still opt in with `tailscale set --ssh`; editing the ssh section overrides the default (F17). Allowed SSH shapes: user→own devices, user→tagged device, user→shared tagged device, tagged→tagged (never check mode). Server side only on Linux and the open-source macOS tailscaled; it claims port 22 only on the Tailscale IP, leaving sshd untouched (F18).

3. DNS. MagicDNS is on by default for tailnets created on/after 2022-10-20, needs no nameserver on v1.20+, gives machine-name.tailnet-name.ts.net and auto-adds the tailnet search domain; per-device opt-out is `tailscale set --accept-dns=false` (F20). By default devices keep their local DNS settings and only use tailnet nameservers when needed; "Override DNS servers" forces the global nameservers; a restricted nameserver (split DNS) answers only its domain; resolver order is not guaranteed, so a LAN resolver with different answers should be added as split DNS for its domain, not as a global nameserver (F21). On Linux, Tailscale tries to cooperate with whatever DNS system exists; with NetworkManager + systemd-resolved, /etc/resolv.conf must symlink to /run/systemd/resolve/stub-resolv.conf; without a DNS manager tailscaled and dhclient fight over resolv.conf; Tailscale's own resolver is 100.100.100.100 (F22). `--accept-dns` defaults to true; `--hostname` changes the MagicDNS name (F23).

4. KEY EXPIRY. Default 180 days, configurable 1–180, per-device "Disable Key Expiry" in the admin console; first-time tagged devices get expiry disabled by default; `tailscale up --force-reauth` renews; admins can "Temporarily extend key" for 30 minutes on an expired device (F24, F15).

5. IDENTITY: SERVE HEADERS VS WHOIS. `tailscale serve` proxies tailnet traffic to a local service, requires HTTPS certs enabled, honours ACLs, and injects exactly three headers — Tailscale-User-Login, Tailscale-User-Name, Tailscale-User-Profile-Pic — after stripping any incoming copies; not for Funnel traffic and not populated for traffic from tagged devices; values may be RFC2047 Q-encoded; Tailscale's stated best practice is that the backend listens on localhost only so nobody can reach it bypassing Serve (F25). v1.92+ can also forward Tailscale-App-Capabilities via --accept-app-caps (F25). Serve CLI: `tailscale serve [--bg] [--http|--https|--tcp|--tls-terminated-tcp=<port>] [--set-path] [--yes] <target>`, `serve status`, `serve reset`, `... off` (F26). HTTPS prerequisites: MagicDNS on, "Enable HTTPS" acknowledged (machine names + tailnet DNS name go to public CT logs), `tailscale cert` obtains Let's Encrypt 90-day certs that YOU must renew when delivered as files; tailnet name cannot be changed later except default↔random (F27). `tailscale whois ip[:port]` returns Machine {Name, ID, Addresses, AllowedIPs}, User {Name = owner email, ID}, Capabilities (grants); tagged peers show Tags instead of User; `--json` must precede the IP; `--proto tcp|udp` (F28). Whois is the right primitive for non-HTTP services (llama.cpp RPC, the agent) and for a backend that wants to double-check a Serve header; headers are the right primitive for web apps behind Serve. Whois on a share recipient's connection is undocumented (F38, unverified).

6. OPERATOR. `tailscale set --operator=<user>` / `tailscale up --operator=<user>` / `tailscale login --operator`: "A Unix username other than root to operate tailscaled". `tailscale set` changes only the flags given; `tailscale up` flags are not persisted and must all be repeated (or `--reset`) (F29).

7. USERSPACE NETWORKING (the hub today). `tailscaled --tun=userspace-networking` runs without /dev/net/tun; outbound traffic from local apps must go through tailscaled's SOCKS5 (v1.8+) or HTTP (v1.16+) proxy (`--socks5-server`, `--outbound-http-proxy-listen`, ALL_PROXY/HTTP_PROXY); Tailscale positions it "primarily for serverless environments" (F30). It is netstack-based: TCP and UDP only, ping reconstructed, other IP protocols unsupported, performance "acceptable" vs kernel "best" (F31). From the v1.102.3 source: in this mode netstack handles incoming traffic to the node's Tailscale IPs and, for a port not served by Serve/SSH, dials 127.0.0.1:<same port> on the host — so a hub service must listen on 127.0.0.1 (there is no tailscale0 interface to bind to), and anything listening on loopback is reachable tailnet-wide on that port unless ACLs restrict it (F32). Client-side `tailscale ssh` exists precisely for userspace nodes that cannot dial directly; `tailscale wait` only waits for the Running state there (F33). Whether the Tailscale SSH *server* and Serve work on a userspace-mode host is not stated in the docs (F39, F40, unverified) — spike it on solarplexus.

8. FUNNEL. Funnel is on all plans and the Serve page says it is enabled by default at the tailnet level; CORVID's "zero public exposure" rule therefore needs an explicit check that no node has a funnel configured (F41).

9. LICENSING. tailscaled/CLI/Linux client: BSD-3-Clause at v1.102.3; Windows/macOS GUIs and the coordination server are proprietary; DERP is open; Headscale v0.29.3 is BSD-3-Clause by Juan Font (F34, F35).

Bottom line for the spec: Tailscale Personal covers a 6-member core with everything CORVID needs (MagicDNS, ACLs/grants, tags, SSH check mode at the default period, Serve identity headers, node sharing, HTTPS). The hub's userspace mode contradicts CLAUDE.md §3.2's "bind to the Tailscale interface only" — either move solarplexus to kernel/TUN mode or restate the rule as "listen on 127.0.0.1, expose via Serve/ACL".

facts.statement: Tailscale's Personal plan is "$0 Free forever" with "Unlimited user devices", "Up to 6 users", "Up to 3 ACL groups", "Up to 50 tagged resources to start", and 1,000 ephemeral-resource minutes per month; paid plans are Standard ($8/user/month) and Premium ($18/user/month).

"If you create a tailnet with a public domain, such as Gmail, Apple, or a personal GitHub account, it's treated as personal use. These tailnets are automatically enrolled in the free Personal plan." The Personal plan "is only suitable for non-commercial use of Tailscale".

"The new Personal plan now allows 6 users, an increase from the former plan's 3 users. This is also equivalent to the former Personal Plus plan, which had a maximum of 6 users as well." Legacy Personal/Personal Plus accounts may stay as-is; moving to a new plan is one-way.

Seat semantics: "A user device is simply anything that is not tagged as a resource! User devices are free and unlimited." "A tagged resource is a device that is owned by a tag rather than a user identity." 50 tagged resources included, $1/month each beyond. "a user who is invited does not occupy a seat until they first log in to the admin console or when they first authenticate a device." Tailscale states it is "currently not enforcing the hard limits or overages of ACL groups, multiple tailnets, tagged resources, and ephemeral resources".
"The Personal plan permits 6 free users in a single Tailscale network, known as a tailnet. You can also share devices with other users with node sharing."

Invite any user: "You can send a one-time use invitation to any user you want to join a Tailscale network (tailnet) in the form of a generated URL. You might want to use one-time user invites to add users such as friends, family, or contractors to a personal tailnet". Available for all plans; "Unused invites expire after 30 days"; Owner/Admin/IT admin sends (email or copy-link) and chooses the role; invitee signs in with any identity provider or passkey then installs the client; if user approval is enabled the admin must approve; on the invitee's own tailnet, "By default, tailnets only allow Admin users to accept an invitation to join external tailnets."

Email 'team invites' require a custom-domain tailnet: "Your tailnet must use a custom domain. If your tailnet uses shared domains (such as example@gmail.com) you can send invites using a URL link instead." "GitHub user accounts don't have email addresses, so you cannot send an invite to GitHub accounts." Unused team invites expire after 90 days.

autogroup:member = "any user who is a direct member (including all invited users) of the tailnet. Does not include users from shared devices." autogroup:shared = "any user who accepted a sharing invitation to your network". autogroup:self "only applies to user-owned devices. It does not apply to tagged devices." autogroup:tagged = any tagged device. Legacy autogroup:members still works but cannot be mixed with autogroup:member.

Node sharing: "You can share access to specific machines with people outside your Tailscale network (known as a tailnet) without exposing them to the public internet. Sharing gives the recipient access to only the shared machine in your tailnet, and nothing else." "Sharing is available for all plans"; still labelled beta; requires Tailscale v1.4+. "A recipient needs to be an Owner, Admin, or IT admin of a tailnet to accept a shared machine invitation." "Sharing respects the access control policies and MagicDNS settings of both your tailnet and the recipient's tailnet."

Sharing is one-directional by default (quarantine): "Tailscale quarantines shared machines by default. A shared machine can receive incoming connections (from the other user's tailnet) but cannot start connections." "it's possible to 'mutually share' machines, allowing the machines to make outbound connections to each other" by each side sharing to the other's user.

What sharing exposes and how it can be policed: "Accepting an invite exposes: The email and avatar of the recipient (required to help confirm invites); Physical machine IPs of machines from your tailnet". After acceptance the sharer sees the recipient's "profile picture and email address in the Share dialog". ACL rules can target the recipient's email or autogroup:shared. "Sharing strips tags, groups, and subnet information from the recipient tailnet." "A machine cannot be shared with a tag or accessed by tagged machines on another tailnet, as only users can accept machine shares." Invite links are single-use or reusable (up to 1,000 uses); unused links expire in 30 days. "shared machines appear in the other tailnet as the sharer, not the owner of the machine." Deleting the sharing user deletes the shares they manage.

"Shared machines can only be reached by using their fully qualified domain name, which looks like <hostname>.<tailnet-name>.ts.net" — the short machine name does not work for shared machines (MagicDNS for shared machines needs Tailscale v1.4+).

Serve identity headers are populated for share recipients: "Although identity headers are only populated for tailnet traffic, this includes traffic from external users who have accepted a share of your device. For example, if you share a device with a friend and have it configured with a Serve proxy, Tailscale populates the identity headers when your friend visits the Serve URL."

"When you first create your tailnet, the default tailnet policy file enables communication between all devices within the tailnet." "ACLs are deny-by-default, directional, locally enforced, and don't affect local network traffic." "in the absence of an acls section in the tailnet policy file, Tailscale applies the default allow all policy"; "To deny all traffic, use an empty object for the acls section". Tailscale recommends grants for all new policy; ACLs keep working indefinitely; ACLs available on all plans.

Tags: "Applying a tag to a device removes any user-based authentication." "You cannot remove all tags from a device. A device with a tag-based identity must have at least one tag." "Devices with a tag-based identity can only SSH into other tagged devices; they cannot SSH into devices with a user-based identity." "When you apply a tag to a device for the first time and authenticate it, the tagged device's key expiry is disabled by default." Apply via `sudo tailscale login --advertise-tags=tag:server` (tags cannot be removed via --advertise-tags if the device used an auth key); Owner/Admin/Network admin can apply any tag; "All plans include 50 tagged devices."

SSH policy rule fields: action ("accept" accepts already-authenticated tailnet users; "check" requires periodic re-authentication), src (user, group, tag, user:*@domain, autogroup; never bare *), dst (user, tag, or autogroup; only port 22; never bare *), users (host usernames; autogroup:nonroot; localpart:*@<domain>), checkPeriod ("minimum of one minute and a maximum of 168 hours (one week)", "If not specified, the default is 12 hours", or "always"), acceptEnv (host v1.76.0+). Policy-syntax page marks checkPeriod as "available for only on the Premium and Enterprise plans".
facts.version: KB last validated Jan 5, 2026 (policy-syntax KB last validated Apr 8, 2026)

facts.statement: Default SSH rule when the policy is unmodified: {"action":"check","src":["autogroup:member"],"dst":["autogroup:self"],"users":["autogroup:nonroot","root"]}. "You still need to opt in a destination device." "Modifying the access control policy for SSH overrides this default configuration, and removing it disables Tailscale SSH in your tailnet." Evaluation order: check policies before accept policies (most restrictive wins).

Tailscale SSH: server component "is only available on: Linux; macOS open source tailscale + tailscaled CLI devices" (v1.24+); clients can be any platform. Enable with `tailscale set --ssh` (generates host key, intercepts port 22 on the Tailscale IP only; /etc/ssh/sshd_config and authorized_keys untouched). Only allowed connection kinds: user→own devices, user→tagged device, user→shared tagged device, tagged→tagged ("An SSH access rule from a tagged device cannot be in check mode"). "You can also connect over SSH to a node that is tagged and has been shared with you". Both a network rule (port 22) and an ssh rule are required. `tailscale set --shields-up` blocks all incoming tailnet connections incl. SSH; `tailscale set --ssh=false` disables.

Pricing: "Tailscale SSH is available on all plans"; "Check mode itself is available for all plans, including the Personal plan. To change the check mode length from the default value, a Premium or Enterprise plan is required." Advanced Tailscale SSH = "non-default check mode length and localpart username matching" (Premium+). In the compare table the 'Basic Tailscale SSH' row shows a check mark in the Personal column and the text "Up to 5 hosts" in the Standard column. Personal tailnets get basic user roles Owner, Admin, Member.

MagicDNS: "Tailnets created on or after October 20, 2022 have MagicDNS enabled by default." "MagicDNS does not require a DNS nameserver if running Tailscale v1.20 or later." FQDN = <machine name>.<tailnet DNS name> e.g. monitoring.yak-bebop.ts.net; Tailscale auto-adds the tailnet search domain so the bare machine name works for your own tailnet's devices; "accessing devices shared with you requires using the full domain name". Per-device opt-out on Linux: `tailscale set --accept-dns=false`. Some macOS CLI tools (host, nslookup) bypass system DNS and won't resolve MagicDNS names.

Tailnet DNS: "By default, your tailnet's devices use their local DNS settings for all queries. To force clients to always use the nameservers you define, you can enable the Override DNS servers toggle." "A restricted nameserver only applies to DNS queries matching a specific search domain. Using a restricted nameserver is also known as split DNS." "When MagicDNS is enabled, it is always the first domain in the Search Domains list." Resolver ordering is not guaranteed: "Tailscale either proxies all DNS requests (in which case Tailscale queries all nameservers in parallel and uses the quickest response) or defers to the operating system"; for a private resolver with different answers "you're probably better off using the split DNS feature". Public global nameservers are queried over DoH automatically. Search domains need v1.34+. MagicDNS cannot hold arbitrary records.

Linux DNS: "Tailscale attempts to interoperate with any Linux DNS configuration it finds already present." With NetworkManager + systemd-resolved, /etc/resolv.conf must be a symlink to /run/systemd/resolve/stub-resolv.conf (`sudo ln -sf /run/systemd/resolve/stub-resolv.conf /etc/resolv.conf`, then restart systemd-resolved, NetworkManager, tailscaled). "Without any DNS management system installed, DHCP clients like dhclient and programs like tailscaled have no other options than rewriting the /etc/resolv.conf file themselves, which results in them sometimes fighting with each other." Tailscale's own DNS server address is 100.100.100.100.

`tailscale up` flags: "--accept-dns Accept DNS configuration from the admin console. Defaults to accepting DNS settings."; "--hostname=<name> Provide a hostname to use for the device instead of the one provided by the OS. Note that this will change the machine name used in MagicDNS."; "--operator=<user> Provide a Unix username other than root to operate tailscaled."; "--ssh Run a Tailscale SSH server ... Defaults to false."; "--reset Reset unspecified settings to default values." "Flags are not persisted between runs; you must specify all flags each time."

Key expiry: "By default, new domains are set with an expiry period of 180 days." Custom period selectable "from 1 to 180 days" (applies to devices that log in after the change). Disable per device via Machines page > Disable Key Expiry ("available for all plans"). Expired device: `tailscale up --force-reauth` renews; admins can "Temporarily extend key" for 30 minutes. "When you apply a tag to a device for the first time and authenticate it, the tagged device will have key expiry disabled by default."

Tailscale Serve: "lets you route traffic from other devices on your Tailscale network (known as a tailnet) to a local service running on your device"; "requires you to enable HTTPS certificates in your tailnet"; ACL rules apply; CLI changed in v1.52; `tailscale serve 3000` proxies to http://127.0.0.1:3000 at https://<machine>.<tailnet>.ts.net. Identity headers added to proxied requests (and stripped from incoming requests to prevent spoofing): "Tailscale-User-Login" (e.g. alice@example.com), "Tailscale-User-Name" (display name), "Tailscale-User-Profile-Pic" (URL); non-ASCII may be RFC2047 "Q" encoded; "Funnel traffic ... does not include identity headers"; "These identity headers are not populated for traffic originating from tagged devices." Best practice: "only have the service listen on localhost" because anyone who can reach the service directly could forge the headers. v1.92+: `--accept-app-caps` forwards "Tailscale-App-Capabilities" (JSON). Limitations: names restricted to device-name.tailnet-name.ts.net; the same port cannot be both Serve and Funnel; macOS file serving only in the open-source client.

`tailscale serve` CLI: `tailscale serve [flags] <target>` with --bg (run in background), --http=<port>, --https=<port> (default), --tcp=<port>, --tls-terminated-tcp=<port>, --set-path=<path>, --yes; targets may be a port, host:port, or URL (e.g. tcp://localhost:3000, https+insecure://localhost:3000); `tailscale serve status [--json]`, `tailscale serve reset`; turn one off by re-running the original command with `off` appended (all original flags required).

Enabling HTTPS: requires MagicDNS enabled, then "Enable HTTPS" on the DNS page and acknowledging "that your machine names and your tailnet DNS name will be published on a public ledger" (Certificate Transparency). Certificates come from Let's Encrypt via `tailscale cert`, are issued on the tailnet name (changeable only between default and randomly generated names), have a 90-day expiry, and "for any certificates that you create using tailscale cert, you are responsible for renewing the certificate." "You cannot obtain an HTTPS URL to go to a bare hostname, such as https://machine-name." Private keys never leave the machine.

`tailscale whois ip[:port]` — "Get the machine and user associated with a Tailscale IP." For user devices it returns Machine {Name, ID, Addresses, AllowedIPs}, User {Name = "the email address for the owner of the device", ID}, Capabilities ("the grants for the device"); for tagged devices Machine includes Tags and there is no User block. `--json` (must come before the ip[:port] argument) and `--proto=tcp|udp`. `tailscale whoami [--json]` is whois on the local node.

`tailscale set --operator=<user>`: "A Unix username other than root to operate tailscaled." `tailscale set` "does not require the complete set of desired settings. It only updates the settings you explicitly set." The same --operator flag exists on `tailscale up` and `tailscale login`. `tailscale get [--set-flags]` prints current preferences.

Userspace networking mode: "lets you run Tailscale where you don't have access to create a VPN tunnel device"; start with `tailscaled --tun=userspace-networking --socks5-server=localhost:1055 --outbound-http-proxy-listen=localhost:1055` (SOCKS5 v1.8+, HTTP proxy v1.16+), or FLAGS="--tun=userspace-networking" in /etc/default/tailscaled; local applications must be pointed at the proxy (ALL_PROXY / HTTP_PROXY) to reach the tailnet. "Userspace networking mode is primarily for serverless environments. We recommend using it with ephemeral nodes and auth keys".

Userspace ("netstack") mode is used when tailscaled runs with --tun=userspace-networking ("used when running as a regular, non-root user") or on non-Linux OSes; it uses gVisor netstack; "Tailscale terminates TCP and UDP connections from the origin Tailscale peer and makes new outbound connections"; ICMP: only ping, reconstructed; "any IP protocol other than TCP or UDP (such as SCTP) is not supported in userspace mode"; summary table: performance kernel "best" vs userspace "acceptable", maturity "stable" vs "new (in Tailscale)".

Source-level behaviour of inbound traffic on a userspace-networking node: cmd/tailscaled/netstack.go sets `ns.ProcessLocalIPs = onlyNetstack` (line 41), where ProcessLocalIPs "is whether netstack should handle incoming traffic directed at the Node.Addresses (local IPs)" (wgengine/netstack/netstack.go line ~198); in netstack's TCP forwarder, after Serve/SSH handlers (TCPHandlerForDst) get first refusal, a connection to the node's own Tailscale IP falls to `case isTailscaleIP: dialIP = ipv4Loopback` and is forwarded to 127.0.0.1:<same port> on the host (netstack.go lines ~1691-1733; comments describe "rewriting the dial target to 127.0.0.1:<port> and forwardTCP'ing the connection onto whatever ... service happens to be listening on the host's loopback at that port"). Consequence: on the hub there is no tailscale0 interface to bind to; services must listen on 127.0.0.1 and become reachable from the tailnet on that port subject to ACLs.
facts.version: tailscale/tailscale v1.102.3 (also wgengine/netstack/netstack.go at the same tag)

facts.statement: `tailscale ssh`: "when your local node is in userspace-networking mode and can't make a direct connection, use tailscale ssh. This sets up an SSH ProxyCommand to connect through the local tailscaled daemon." `tailscale wait`: "If running in userspace-networking mode, this command only waits for tailscaled and the Running state, as no physical network interface exists."

facts.statement: Tailscale SSH and ACL mechanics on sharing: "Granting access to autogroup:member also grants access to external invited users if the destination node is shared with them, even if they have no nodes in your tailnet." (so autogroup:member in an ssh src can reach share recipients on a shared tagged node).

What `tailscale whois` returns for a connection that arrives from a node-share recipient (whether User.Name is the recipient's login as exposed by the share) is not documented on the CLI or sharing pages; the sharing page only confirms the sharer learns the recipient's email/avatar and Serve populates identity headers for them.

Whether the Tailscale SSH *server* works on a host whose tailscaled runs in --tun=userspace-networking mode is not stated in the Tailscale SSH or userspace-networking KB pages (the SSH page only says it uses "netstack port interception").

Whether `tailscale serve` works on a userspace-networking node is not stated on the Serve or userspace-networking KB pages; the v1.102.3 netstack source consults Serve/SSH handlers (TCPHandlerForDst) before loopback forwarding, which suggests it does, but this was not confirmed end-to-end.
facts.version: KB last validated Nov 12, 2025; source tailscale v1.102.3

recommendations: Membership tiers (feed ADR 0002): the founder's Personal tailnet holds at most 6 users (F1). Use URL 'Invite any user' (F6) for the founder + up to 5 contributing friends — they become autogroup:member (F8), get short MagicDNS names, Tailscale SSH, tags and full ACL targeting. Everyone beyond that is a *consumer* reached via node-sharing of solarplexus only (F9); they must use the FQDN (F12), appear as autogroup:shared (F8), still get Serve identity headers for zero-login (F13), but the hub cannot open connections to their machines (F10), so a share-only friend cannot be a compute contributor without mutual sharing. Decide explicitly who is a member vs a sharee.

Zero-login design: put every member-facing web app behind `tailscale serve` on solarplexus (F25, F26), have backends listen on 127.0.0.1 only, and trust exactly the three headers Tailscale-User-Login / Tailscale-User-Name / Tailscale-User-Profile-Pic (F25). For non-HTTP services (llama.cpp RPC, the agent's API) and for defence in depth, resolve the peer IP with `tailscale whois --json` (F28). Treat header values as possibly RFC2047 Q-encoded (F25).

Hub networking contradiction: solarplexus runs tailscaled in userspace mode, so there is no Tailscale interface to bind to and inbound tailnet TCP is forwarded to 127.0.0.1:<port> (F32); the CLAUDE.md §3.2 rule 'rpc-server binds to the Tailscale interface only' cannot be implemented there, and anything on loopback is tailnet-reachable. Either (a) move solarplexus to kernel/TUN mode (root tailscaled; better performance, F31) and keep the bind-to-tailscale-IP rule, or (b) restate the rule for userspace nodes as 'listen on 127.0.0.1, never 0.0.0.0, and gate ports with grants'. Write this into the topology ADR.

Spike before Phase 1 (F39, F40): on solarplexus verify `tailscale serve`, the Tailscale SSH server, and rpc-server reachability all work in userspace mode; record results in docs/runs/. If any fail, that decides (a) above.

Tags for infrastructure only: tag solarplexus and always-on workers (e.g. tag:corvid-hub, tag:corvid-worker) via tagOwners; their key expiry is disabled by default (F15, F24), which is what an unattended hub needs. Never tag friends' laptops (tagging removes user identity and tagged devices cannot SSH into user devices; identity headers are not populated for tagged sources) (F15, F25).

Key expiry policy: user devices expire every 180 days by default (F24); tell members they will re-authenticate roughly twice a year; disable expiry only on tagged infrastructure; document the admin 'Temporarily extend key' 30-minute rescue for an expired remote box.

SSH policy on Personal: keep check mode at the default 12 h (changing checkPeriod needs Premium, F16/F19); add an accept or check rule src founder → dst tag:corvid-* users [root, autogroup:nonroot] plus the matching grants port-22 rule (F17, F18); tagged→tagged SSH cannot be check mode (F18). Server side is Linux and open-source macOS tailscaled only (F18), so Windows friends are SSH clients, never servers.

DNS: keep MagicDNS on (default, F20) and do NOT enable 'Override DNS servers' (F21). If a LAN resolver (Pi-hole, router) must answer a local domain, add it as a restricted (split-DNS) nameserver for that domain rather than a global one (F21). On Linux build nodes ensure /etc/resolv.conf -> /run/systemd/resolve/stub-resolv.conf when systemd-resolved + NetworkManager are present (F22); debug with `tailscale dns status`.

HTTPS/Serve prerequisites: before enabling HTTPS, choose final machine names and a randomised tailnet DNS name (both are published to CT logs and the tailnet name cannot be changed later except default<->random) (F27). Serve auto-provisions its own certs; anything issued with `tailscale cert` you must renew yourself every 90 days (F27).

Zero-public-exposure CI check: Funnel is enabled by default at the tailnet level (F36); add `tailscale funnel status` (must be empty) and `tailscale serve status` review to the no-0.0.0.0 check, and consider removing the `funnel` nodeAttr from the policy file.

Operator: run `tailscale set --operator=<user>` on founder/member Linux boxes so the CORVID agent and CLI can call tailscaled without sudo (F29); `tailscale set` is idempotent per flag, unlike `tailscale up` which needs every flag repeated (F23, F29).

Pin client v1.102.3 (released 2026-08-20, F35) as the reference version for CLI syntax (Serve CLI changed at 1.52; app-caps header at 1.92; acceptEnv at 1.76) and record it in the §4 credit row; Headscale v0.29.3 (BSD-3) stays the documented escape hatch (F34).
Member-facing copy: sharees see the shared machine listed as owned by the sharer and must type the full name host.tailnet.ts.net (F11, F12) — put that exact FQDN on the onboarding index card.
open_questions: What does `tailscale whois` report (User.Name/ID) for a connection from a node-share recipient on another tailnet — their login email, or nothing? (F38) Test once the first friend is shared in.
Do `tailscale serve` and the Tailscale SSH server function on solarplexus while tailscaled is in --tun=userspace-networking mode? (F39, F40) Decides whether the hub must move to TUN/kernel mode.

Can a share-only friend contribute compute at all, i.e. does mutual sharing (friend shares their rpc-server box back to the founder) work in practice, and is it acceptable UX for a non-technical friend who is Owner of their own auto-created tailnet? (F10, F11)
How many of the ~20 friends in §10 need to be full members (≤6 incl. founder) versus sharees? The 6-user cap forces a tiering decision before Phase 0 invites go out. (F1)

Does the pricing table's 'Basic Tailscale SSH' cell for Personal (check mark, vs 'Up to 5 hosts' on Standard) really mean unlimited SSH hosts on Personal? The Personal highlights say 'Try SSH and Kubernetes features'. Verify in the admin console. (F19)
Is any LAN resolver in use on the build nodes today (Pi-hole/router DNS) that would need a split-DNS restricted nameserver, or is MagicDNS alone sufficient? (F21, F22)
Tailscale says it is currently not enforcing ACL-group/tagged-resource limits (F4); what is the date when enforcement begins, and will 3 ACL groups suffice for CORVID's policy design?
Before enabling HTTPS: which machine names and which tailnet DNS name are acceptable to publish in Certificate Transparency logs? (F27)
