verdicts.reason: Fetched https://tailscale.com/pricing directly (HTTP 200, 2026-08-22) and verified every quoted string in the raw HTML: Personal plan "$0" / "Free forever" / "Unlimited user devices" / "Up to 6 users" / "Up to 3 ACL groups" / "Up to 50 tagged resources to start" / "1,000 mins per month for ephemeral resources"; Standard "$8 Per user, per month"; Premium "$18 Per user, per month". The page is the vendor's own pricing page (primary). Minor caveats that do not contradict the claim: (1) a fourth, custom-priced Enterprise tier also exists, so "paid plans are Standard and Premium" is the list of fixed-price paid tiers, not an exhaustive list; (2) the FAQ states Tailscale is "currently not enforcing the hard limits or overages of ACL groups, multiple tailnets, tagged resources, and ephemeral resources"; (3) paid-plan billing is monthly seat-based (no separate annual price shown). The comparison table additionally reads "$0 for up to 6 users" and "50 tagged resources included; add more for $1/month each."

Cited source is primary (Tailscale's own pricing page) and was fetched live on 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200, both via WebFetch and raw curl of the served HTML). Under the FAQ heading "What is the difference between business and personal use? What determines who gets access to trials and who stays on the Personal plan?" the page reads verbatim: "Our Personal plan is for individuals who want to use Tailscale at home. This is a free plan and is only suitable for non-commercial use of Tailscale. ... If you create a tailnet with a public domain, such as Gmail, Apple, or a personal GitHub account, it's treated as personal use. These tailnets are automatically enrolled in the free Personal plan. If you create a tailnet with a custom domain, it's considered business use, and you'll be automatically enrolled in a free trial." Both quoted fragments in the claim match the served text word-for-word (only difference: the page uses a typographic apostrophe in "it's"). A second FAQ entry on the same page reinforces it: "the Personal plan is not intended for commercial use." The page also confirms the Personal plan is "$0 Free forever", "Up to 6 users", "Unlimited user devices". Claim stands as stated for the stated version.

Fetched https://tailscale.com/pricing directly (curl, 2026-08-22; 519 KB HTML) and extracted the FAQ text. The "Legacy plans" FAQ contains the quoted sentence verbatim (only difference is a typographic apostrophe: "former plan’s 3 users"): "Has the maximum number of users changed for the free Personal plan? The new Personal plan now allows 6 users, an increase from the former plan’s 3 users. This is also equivalent to the former Personal Plus plan, which had a maximum of 6 users as well." The paraphrased second part is also supported by the adjacent FAQ: "Current Personal Plus users will be able to keep their plans as is or switch to the free Personal Plan ... If you prefer to stay on the former Personal and Personal Plus plans, you can continue using them as legacy accounts for the foreseeable future ... However, moving to a new plan is a one-way change, and you won’t be able to move back to your previous legacy plan." The pricing tier table on the same page corroborates: Personal = "$0 for up to 6 users", "Unlimited user devices". Source is Tailscale's own pricing page (primary) and the served version matches the stated date. Minor nuance only, not a refutation: the page qualifies legacy retention with "for the foreseeable future", so "may stay as-is" should be read with that caveat.

Fetched https://tailscale.com/pricing live on 2026-08-22 (raw HTML via curl, 519 KB, plus WebFetch). Every quoted string in the claim appears verbatim in the page's FAQ: "A user device is simply anything that is not tagged as a resource! User devices are free and unlimited." and "A tagged resource is a device that is owned by a tag rather than a user identity." (FAQ "What are user devices, tagged resources, and ephemeral resources?"); the comparison table row "Tagged resources" reads "50 tagged resources included; add more for $1/month each." and the Personal plan highlights say "Up to 50 tagged resources to start"; the FAQ "What about users who have not accepted an invite or are pending approval?" contains exactly "a user who is invited does not occupy a seat until they first log in to the admin console or when they first authenticate a device."; and the FAQ "How will we know when an account approaches its plan limits?" contains exactly "we are currently not enforcing the hard limits or overages of ACL groups, multiple tailnets, tagged resources, and ephemeral resources." The source is Tailscale's own first-party pricing page (primary), the version (as served 2026-08-22) matches, and the claim does not overstate it. Minor note, not a refutation: the $1/month overage line sits in a table cell under the plan comparison rather than in a Personal-plan-only sentence, and the page adds that enforcement of those limits is planned "over the next few months", so the non-enforcement statement is explicitly temporary.

Fetched the cited KB page raw (curl, 215 KB HTML) and it contains the claimed text verbatim under the "Personal plan" heading: "The Personal plan permits 6 free users in a single Tailscale network, known as a tailnet. You can also share devices with other users with node sharing." The page header reads "Last validated: Apr 8, 2026", matching the stated version, so the claim is not outdated. The source is primary (Tailscale's own knowledge base). Cross-checked against a second primary source, https://tailscale.com/pricing (fetched 2026-08-22), which corroborates: Personal plan "Users: $0 for up to 6 users", "User Devices: Unlimited", and FAQ "The new Personal plan now allows 6 users, an increase from the former plan's 3 users." No discrepancy found; claim stands as stated.

Fetched the cited primary source (Tailscale's own docs page, header "Last validated: Jan 5, 2026" — matches stated version). Every component of the claim is present verbatim: (1) "You can send a one-time use invitation to any user you want to join a Tailscale network (tailnet) in the form of a generated URL. You might want to use one-time user invites to add users such as friends, family, or contractors to a personal tailnet or an organization tailnet for authentication." (2) "Inviting any user to a tailnet is available for all plans." (3) "Unused invites expire after 30 days." (4) "You need to be an Owner, Admin, or IT admin to send an invitation by using email" / "...to send an invitation link", with "Select the user role you want to automatically assign..." (email) and "Select the user role you want to assign to the invite link" (link). (5) Accept an invite: "Sign in to Tailscale with your identity provider or passkey. Download the Tailscale client." (6) "If your tailnet has user approval enabled, you must approve invited users before they can join the tailnet." (7) "By default, tailnets only allow Admin users to accept an invitation to join external tailnets." Minor notes, not contradictions: the claim's first quote truncates the sentence after "personal tailnet" (source continues "or an organization tailnet for authentication"); only one role can be assigned per email-invite batch; and the page adds a billing caveat the claim omits — "Tailscale bills for every active user on every tailnet" and invited users who join count toward the inviting tailnet's billing (relevant to the free Personal plan's user cap, but not asserted otherwise by the claim).

Fetched https://tailscale.com/kb/1064/invite-team-members (Tailscale's own KB, primary source; page header reads "Last validated: Jan 5, 2026", matching the stated version). All three quoted passages appear verbatim: Prerequisites section: "Your tailnet must use a custom domain. If your tailnet uses shared domains (such as example@gmail.com) you can send invites using a URL link instead."; Limitations section: "You can only invite users in the same domain. GitHub user accounts don't have email addresses, so you cannot send an invite to GitHub accounts."; intro: "Unused invites expire 90 days after the last welcome invite was sent." The page opens with "If your Tailscale network (tailnet) uses a custom domain, you can send a team invite to one or more email addresses simultaneously," confirming the email-invite/custom-domain framing. Only a minor precision nuance, not a refutation: the 90-day clock runs from the last welcome invite sent (resending resets it), and the "same domain" limitation also applies (invited addresses must match the tailnet's custom domain). Claim stands for the stated version.

Fetched https://tailscale.com/kb/1337/policy-syntax (raw HTML, 2026-08-22); page header reads "Last validated: Apr 8, 2026", matching the stated version. Every sub-claim is present verbatim on the page: autogroup:member — "Use to allow access for any user who is a direct member (including all invited users) of the tailnet. Does not include users from shared devices."; autogroup:shared — "Use to allow access for any user who accepted a sharing invitation to your network."; autogroup:self — "autogroup:self only applies to user-owned devices. It does not apply to tagged devices." (page also adds "You cannot use autogroup:self with autogroup:tagged"); autogroup:tagged — "Use to allow access for any user who is a device that is tagged" (claim's "any tagged device" is a faithful paraphrase); legacy — "The legacy autogroup autogroup:members will continue to work, but it's best practice to use autogroup:member instead. You cannot use both autogroup:member and autogroup:members in the same tailnet policy file." Source is Tailscale's own KB (primary). Minor nuance not contradicting the claim: the page also notes that granting access to autogroup:member "also grants access to external invited users if the destination device is shared with them, even if they have no devices in your tailnet."

Fetched https://tailscale.com/kb/1084/sharing (primary: Tailscale's own KB; page shows "Last validated: Jan 5, 2026", matching the stated version). Every element of the claim appears verbatim or is directly supported: (a) "You can share access to specific machines with people outside your Tailscale network (known as a tailnet) without exposing them to the public internet. Sharing gives the recipient access to only the shared machine in your tailnet, and nothing else." (b) "Sharing is available for all plans." (c) "Sharing is currently in beta." (d) "To try it, follow the steps below to enable it for your network using Tailscale v1.4 or later." (supports "requires v1.4+"). (e) "A recipient needs to be an Owner, Admin, or IT admin of a tailnet to accept a shared machine invitation." (f) "Sharing respects the access control policies and MagicDNS settings of both your tailnet and the recipient's tailnet." No discrepancy found; claim stands as written. Minor optional enrichment (not a refutation): the page also notes sharing strips tags, groups, and subnet information from the recipient tailnet; shared machines are quarantined by default (can receive but not initiate connections); invite links expire after 30 days; shared machines are reachable only via FQDN <hostname>.<tailnet-name>.ts.net.

Fetched https://tailscale.com/kb/1084/sharing (primary source, Tailscale's own KB; page shows "Last validated: Jan 5, 2026", matching the stated version). The page states verbatim: "Tailscale quarantines shared machines by default. Claim stands as stated.

Fetched the cited primary source (Tailscale KB 1068 "Group devices with tags", page header reads "Last validated: Dec 4, 2025" — matches the stated version) and verified every component verbatim in the raw HTML: (1) "Applying a tag to a device removes any user-based authentication." (2) Limitations: "You cannot remove all tags from a device. A device with a tag-based identity must have at least one tag." (3) "Devices with a tag-based identity can only SSH into other tagged devices; they cannot SSH into devices with a user-based identity." (4) Key expiry: "When you apply a tag to a device for the first time and authenticate it, the tagged device's key expiry is disabled by default." (5) CLI: "run tailscale login command with the --advertise-tags=tag:<tag-name> flag" with example `sudo tailscale login --advertise-tags=tag:server`; and "You cannot remove tags using the --advertise-tags flag if the device uses an auth key. Instead, generate a new auth key with the latest set of tags." (6) Requirements: "Owner, Admin, or Network admin can apply any tag, even if they don't own the tag." (7) Top of page: "Tags are available for all plans. All plans include 50 tagged devices. If you need more than 50 tagged devices, contact our Sales team." Source is Tailscale's own documentation (primary). No discrepancy found; claim stands as stated.

Fetched the cited primary source (tailscale.com/kb/1193/tailscale-ssh, page header "Last validated: Jan 5, 2026") and the policy-syntax page (tailscale.com/kb/1337/policy-syntax, "Last validated: Apr 8, 2026"); both dates match the claim's stated version. Every element of the claim is supported verbatim by the SSH KB: action — "accept accepts connections from users already authenticated in the tailnet. check requires users to periodically reauthenticate according to the checkPeriod"; src — "This can be a user, group, tag, user:*@<domain>, or autogroup. This cannot be a bare wildcard *"; dst — "This can be a user, tag, or autogroup. Unlike ACLs, a port cannot be specified. Only port 22 is allowed ... This cannot be a bare wildcard *"; users — "The set of allowed usernames on the host ... Specify autogroup:nonroot ... Specify localpart:*@<domain>"; checkPeriod — "with a minimum of one minute and a maximum of 168 hours (one week). If not specified, the default is 12 hours. You may also specify always to require check mode on every connection"; acceptEnv — "The host must be running Tailscale v1.76.0 or later to use acceptEnv". The policy-syntax page's checkPeriod entry reads exactly "This policy is available for only on the Premium and Enterprise plans." (same grammatical oddity the claim quotes). Only non-contradicting nuances found: the policy-syntax page describes SSH dst more narrowly (tag, autogroup:self if src is only users/groups, or a single named user if src is that same user) and flags localpart:*@<domain> as Premium/Enterprise-only; neither contradicts the claim as stated against its cited source.

Fetched https://tailscale.com/kb/1193/tailscale-ssh (primary Tailscale KB, page shows "Last validated: Jan 5, 2026", matching the stated version). The page's "SSH access rules in default access control policy" section shows verbatim: "ssh": [{ "action": "check", "src": ["autogroup:member"], "dst": ["autogroup:self"], "users": ["autogroup:nonroot", "root"] }], described as the default policy for new tailnets or tailnets that have not modified their ACLs. Immediately after it states verbatim "You still need to opt in a destination device." and "Modifying the access control policy for SSH overrides this default configuration, and removing it disables Tailscale SSH in your tailnet." The "Order of evaluation" section states "SSH access rules are evaluated considering the most restrictive policies first: Check policies, Accept policies" with the alice@example.com / group:devops example where the check rule applies. Every element of the claim is supported verbatim; nothing is outdated or contradicted.

Fetched https://tailscale.com/kb/1193/tailscale-ssh (primary: Tailscale's own KB; page header reads "Last validated: Jan 5, 2026", matching the stated version). Every element of the claim is supported verbatim or near-verbatim: (a) "Tailscale SSH's server component is only available on: Linux / macOS open source tailscale + tailscaled CLI devices" and "You can connect from any device running Tailscale, regardless of platform" and "requires Tailscale v1.24 or later"; (b) "tailscale set --ssh ... generates a host key pair, shares its public half with the Tailscale control plane ... and configures tailscaled to intercept all traffic from your tailnet that is routed to port 22 on the Tailscale IP address"; "Your SSH configuration (/etc/ssh/sshd_config) and keys (~/.ssh/authorized_keys) files will not be modified, which means that other SSH connections to the same host, not made over Tailscale, will still work" (supports the "Tailscale IP only" reading); (c) "The only kinds of connections that are allowed are: From a user to their own devices... From a user to a tagged device... From a user to a shared tagged device... From a tagged device to another tagged device, for any tags. An SSH access rule from a tagged device cannot be in check mode."; (d) "You can also connect over SSH to a node that is tagged and has been shared with you, as long as the destination host has Tailscale configured with SSH and the destination's access control policy lets you connect over SSH"; (e) "For a connection to be permitted, the tailnet policy file must contain rules permitting both network access and SSH access" plus the prerequisite "Ensure an access control policy exists that grants the source with access to the destination on port 22" (the page notes the default policy already grants this); (f) "To block incoming connections from the tailnet to your device, including Tailscale SSH connections: tailscale set --shields-up" and "Run tailscale set on the device with --ssh=false to disable Tailscale SSH". No discrepancy found; the only paraphrase ("on the Tailscale IP only") is a fair reading of the source text.

Fetched https://tailscale.com/pricing on 2026-08-22 (HTTP Date: Sat, 22 Aug 2026 13:38:54 GMT; primary source, Tailscale's own site). Raw HTML confirms every element of the claim verbatim: FAQ text "Tailscale SSH is available on all plans as a powerful feature..."; "Advanced Tailscale SSH further enables functionality like non-default check mode length and localpart username matching."; "Check mode itself is available for all plans, including the Personal plan. To change the check mode length from the default value, a Premium or Enterprise plan is required." (link to policy-file#checkperiod); "Personal tailnets get access to the basic user roles of Owner, Admin, and Member." Compare-table column order is Personal | Standard | Premium | Enterprise; the underlying row data is {"Basic Tailscale SSH": personal "Y", standard "Up to 5 hosts", premium "Y", enterprise "Y"} and the rendered <tr> cells are [checkmark, "Up to 5 hosts", checkmark, checkmark] -- i.e. check mark in Personal, "Up to 5 hosts" in Standard, exactly as claimed. "Advanced Tailscale SSH" row is N, N, Y, Y (Premium+), supporting the claim. Only nit: the source phrases Advanced SSH as "functionality like ..." (examples), whereas the claim uses "=" as if exhaustive; the quoted fragment itself is verbatim, so this does not rise to refutation. Note: a summarizing fetch initially transposed the Personal/Standard cells; the raw page markup and embedded JSON were checked directly and support the claim as stated.

Fetched https://tailscale.com/kb/1081/magicdns (Tailscale's own KB, primary source; page header reads "Last validated: Jan 5, 2026", matching the stated version). Every element of the claim appears verbatim or near-verbatim in the page: (1) "Tailnets created on or after October 20, 2022 have MagicDNS enabled by default." (2) "MagicDNS does not require a DNS nameserver if running Tailscale v1.20 or later. Otherwise, your network must have at least one DNS nameserver set in the DNS page of the admin console." (3) FQDN table: machine name "monitoring" + tailnet name "yak-bebop.ts.net" = "monitoring.yak-bebop.ts.net". (4) "when you enable MagicDNS, Tailscale automatically adds search domains to your network. With these search domains you only need to type the machine name to access a device" and "accessing devices shared with you requires using the full domain name" (also: "You must also use the shared device's full domain name. For example, ping webserver.example2.ts.net"). (5) "On Linux, stop accepting DNS with: tailscale set --accept-dns=false" (confirmed in raw HTML code block; macOS = uncheck "Use Tailscale DNS settings", Windows = deselect "Use Tailscale DNS"). (6) "Some CLI tools on macOS such as host or nslookup circumvent system DNS resolution, and will not work with MagicDNS." No contradiction found; only minor omitted nuance is that shared devices are reachable via MagicDNS only on Tailscale v1.4 or later, which does not alter the claim.

missing: ACL authoring syntax is absent (F14–F17 give defaults/semantics only) and ADR-0002's baseline cannot be written from this dossier: give one exact `acls` rule and one exact `grants` rule (src/dst with `host:port`, port lists/ranges, `*`), the `tagOwners` block for `tag:hub` (who may apply it; a tag must be declared in tagOwners before a device can carry it), and confirm grants (and `app` capabilities) are available on the Personal plan. Also state whether adding any custom `acls` section silently replaces the default allow-all (so an incomplete rule set locks out the founder's own devices), and that ACLs do not affect LAN traffic (F14) — on the one-LAN build fleet member↔member denial can only be verified over tailnet IPs/MagicDNS names.

Can `autogroup:member` and/or `autogroup:self` appear in an `acls`/`grants` **dst** with a port list (e.g. `autogroup:member:7070`)? ADR-0002's amendment (member devices never tagged; hub→member agent/rpc ports expressed via users/autogroup:member) depends on this and the policy-syntax page is not cited for dst autogroups.

Does the bare `*` source of the default allow-all policy (F14) include node-share recipients (autogroup:shared), i.e. can Zach's shared-in access today reach every port on the shared machine, and once a custom `acls` section exists must `autogroup:shared` be named explicitly for the share to keep working? F9 says sharing respects ACLs but never says whether `*` covers shared users.

F38 can be closed from the package without new research: Serve identity headers are computed from `b.WhoIs` (R07-F22) and are populated for share recipients (F13) ⇒ whois returns the recipient's UserProfile/LoginName for traffic from a shared-in node. State that inference (status: inferred, pending the Zach test) so the Caddy forward_auth/whois path (ADR-0003) is known to work for sharees.

Exact `Tailscale-User-Login` / whois `UserProfile.LoginName` format per identity provider: Google = email, GitHub = `user@github`?, Apple Hide-My-Email relay address?, Microsoft, passkey-only accounts? The coordinator keys members on this string (ADR-0001 partition), and F7 already shows GitHub accounts have no email — but the resulting login string is not recorded.

One tailnet per device at a time: can a device be logged into two tailnets simultaneously, or does accepting the founder's invite move Zach's machine out of his own tailnet (new node, new 100.x IP, new MagicDNS name; old share to be removed), using `tailscale switch` / the GUI account switcher to flip? And does accepting an 'Invite any user' link with a fresh Gmail identity also auto-create the friend's own tailnet (which tailnet does their client land in after install)? Needed for ADR-0002 decision 5 (Zach) and the onboarding index card.

Seat accounting for sharing: does a user who only accepts node shares (never invited) count toward the 6-user Personal cap? F5 implies not but never states it. Is there a cap on recipients per shared machine (F11 gives only the 1,000-use invite link), and does a friend who is both an invited member and the Owner of their own Gmail tailnet fall under the unenforced 'multiple tailnets' limit (F4)? Decides whether '6 members + shares' is a viable consumer tier for the 7th+ friend (ADR-0002 revisit).

Tagging ahnoway: ADR-0002 decision 3 lists 'ahnoway-as-builder' under `tag:hub`, but F15/F25 mean a tagged node carries no user identity — the founder would lose zero-login (no Serve headers, whois returns tags) from his own laptop. The dossier should say explicitly that only solarplexus and optiplex may be tagged, and that key expiry on ahnoway is handled via the per-device 'Disable Key Expiry' (F24), not tagging.

Funnel hardening (§5.6): F36 says Funnel is 'enabled by default' and 'can be turned off' but not how. Record the exact switch — the `funnel` attr in the policy file's `nodeAttrs` (is it present in a fresh default policy, targeting autogroup:member?), removal vs admin-console toggle — and the verification command (`tailscale funnel status` must be empty) for the no-public-exposure CI check.

Serve operational facts for S-05 / ADR-0003: does `tailscale serve --bg` config persist in tailscaled state across tailscaled restart and reboot (or must a systemd unit re-apply it)? Does Serve auto-provision and auto-renew its Let's Encrypt cert (F27 only covers `tailscale cert`, which is operator-renewed; R07-F19 repeats that)? Does `--http=<port>` work with tailnet HTTPS certificates disabled (F25 says Serve 'requires HTTPS'; R07-F23 shows the flag exists; unverified)? Are identity headers and X-Forwarded-For added on `--http` and not on `--tcp` listeners (R07-F22 says the Rewrite hook runs for every web handler — cite it)?

What `--operator` unlocks (F29 defines the flag only): state that on Linux every local client gets LocalAPI read (status/whois/ping) while write (`up`/`set`/`serve`/`funnel`) needs root or the operator (R07-F25), and whether cert fetching (`tailscale cert`, Caddy *.ts.net certs) needs operator or the separate `TS_PERMIT_CERT_UID` (R07-F18). The Phase 0 plan issues `sudo tailscale set --operator=$USER` on ahnoway on this basis.

CLI commands the Phase 0 plan already relies on are not in the dossier (kb/1080 was a seed): `tailscale dns status` output lines, `tailscale ip -4`, `tailscale status --self --json` fields (Self.Online, Self.DNSName, Self.TailscaleIPs, Self.ID/StableID, Self.Tags, Self.UserID), `tailscale switch`, `tailscale ping`. Also the roster-key question (R06 open question): which identifier is stable across rename/re-auth/expiry (StableID vs Name vs node key), plus the MagicDNS name collision rule (two members both named 'desktop' → `desktop-1`?) and whether an admin-console rename survives an OS hostname change.

Conditional fallback if Phase 0 Task 2 (hub to kernel mode; R00-F2/F3/D10 explain why it is userspace) rolls back: the dossier should state in one place that on a userspace hub (a) outbound dials from non-proxy-aware processes (llama-server `--rpc`, psql, agent callbacks) need the SOCKS5/HTTP proxy (F30), `tailscale nc` (R01-F31) or tsnet, (b) MagicDNS resolution for host processes and name resolution inside the SOCKS proxy are untested, (c) F39/F40 (SSH server, `tailscale serve`) remain unverified. Otherwise mark F30–F33/F39/F40 as moot once kernel mode lands.

Member-role visibility and join controls for the §5.7 privacy note: what can a Personal-tailnet 'Member' (F19) see in the admin console — all machines, other members' login emails, the policy file? Is device approval available on Personal, and does 'user approval' (F6) apply to invite-link joins? Needed to tell friends honestly what other friends can see.

Membership lifecycle: what happens to a removed/suspended member's devices (and any tagged device they enrolled), can a member leave the tailnet themselves, and does removing them revoke in-flight Tailscale SSH/Serve sessions? F11 covers only deletion of shares they manage.

Per-platform coverage for the mixed fleet (F18 settles only the SSH server): which of `tailscale set --accept-dns`, `--operator`, `serve`, `whois`, `dns status` exist on the macOS App Store vs standalone vs open-source variants and on Windows, where the CLI binary lives on macOS/Windows (for the agent and the per-OS guides), how MagicDNS is toggled in the GUIs, and what the GUI shows/asks when a member's 180-day key expires (F24 gives only the Linux `--force-reauth` path).

Headscale parity for the 7th-member escape hatch (F34/F35 give licence and version only): does Headscale v0.29.3 support node sharing, grants, Tailscale SSH policy, Serve/HTTPS certs with identity headers, and ts.net-style MagicDNS names? Either answer it or explicitly defer it to the ADR that ADR-0002 decision 2 promises.

research.dossier:
DOSSIER R03 — llama.cpp RPC on the CORVID build fleet (verified 2026-08-22 against primary sources; repo cloned at tags b10581 and b10566/v0.2.0 and key files diffed).

1. Release/version landscape. llama.cpp now has two tag lines: vX.Y.Z "stable" tags (v0.2.0 published 2026-08-21, commit bb4caa75 = nightly b10566; its only asset is nightly-tag.txt containing "b10566", binaries live on the b10566 release) and b[NUM] nightly prereleases on almost every master commit (b10581 at 10:13Z today, 26 assets). Every file this dossier cites (tools/rpc/README.md, rpc-server.cpp, ggml-rpc.h, ggml-cuda CMakeLists, common/arg.cpp, server README, docker files, release.yml CMAKE_ARGS) is byte-identical between b10566 and b10581, so "pin v0.2.0 (=b10566)" is safe and everything below applies.

2. Binaries. The Linux release tarballs (ubuntu-x64, ubuntu-vulkan-x64, also macos-arm64 and win-cpu/win-cuda zips) DO ship ggml-rpc-server (the tool was renamed from rpc-server; the executable is ggml-rpc-server / ggml-rpc-server.exe) plus libggml-rpc, because release.yml sets CMAKE_ARGS "-DGGML_RPC=ON" for all jobs and tars the whole build/bin. But there is NO Linux CUDA release asset at all: Linux assets are CPU (GGML_BACKEND_DL with ~15 CPU variant .so files), Vulkan, SYCL, OpenVINO. Linux + CUDA + RPC therefore means building from source (or an in-house container). The official Docker images are CUDA 12.8.1 (tags *-cuda) and 13.3.0 (*-cuda13), built WITHOUT GGML_RPC (cuda.Dockerfile's cmake line has no -DGGML_RPC=ON; GGML_RPC defaults OFF) and light/server targets copy only llama/llama-cli/llama-completion or llama/llama-server — so no official image provides ggml-rpc-server, and llama-server inside them cannot use --rpc ("failed to find RPC backend").

3. Building. tools/rpc/README.md (the only RPC build doc — docs/build.md has no RPC section): cmake -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DGGML_RPC=ON on each worker; the main host must ALSO be built with -DGGML_RPC=ON plus its own local backends. docs/build.md: cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON builds for the attached GPU (GGML_NATIVE -> CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=native when CUDA>=11.6 and CMake>=3.24); -DGGML_NATIVE=OFF for a cover-all build; -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES="86;89" to pin; -DCMAKE_CUDA_COMPILER=/opt/cuda-X/bin/nvcc (+rpath) to pick a toolkit. ggml-cuda CMake needs CMake>=3.18 and fails hard if no CUDA toolkit. No explicit minimum toolkit version is enforced; code has CUDART_VERSION>=11070/11080/12000 feature gates.

4. GTX 970 (Maxwell, cc 5.2) on driver 535 / CUDA 12.2. (a) llama.cpp's non-native default arch list includes 50-virtual (PTX only) ONLY when the toolkit is <13 (comment: "50 == Maxwell, lowest CUDA 12 standard"); CUDA 13 builds cannot target it at all. (b) NVIDIA: CUDA 12.x "will continue to support building applications for these architectures"; CUDA 13.0 "Offline compilation and library support for these architectures have been removed". (c) Driver math: CUDA 12.2 GA's bundled driver is 535.54.03; minor-version compatibility lets any 12.x toolkit run on >=525.60.13 (<580) EXCEPT "Applications that compile device code to PTX will not work on older drivers" and it "requires passing the target architecture argument to NVCC (-arch=sm_xx)". Consequence: on the hub, either build with the 12.2 toolkit that matches driver 535, or with any 12.x toolkit but pass -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=52-real (SASS, not PTX). Forward-compat packages are Data-Center/NGC-RTX/Jetson only, so CUDA 13 on a GTX 970 with driver 535 is not an option; CUDA 13.x needs driver >=580 (13.1 GA >=590.44.01). (d) Performance: Maxwell is below GGML_CUDA_CC_DP4A (610) so MMQ int8 kernels are unavailable and below PASCAL so mul_mat_vec fusion is disabled — it works via the slower generic/cuBLAS paths. The RTX 3050 (cc 8.6, CUDA 13.1) and RTX 2070 Super (cc 7.5) are in every default list.

5. rpc-server at this tag: flags are -h, -t/--threads N (default hardware_concurrency/2), -d/--device <list>, -H/--host (default 127.0.0.1), -p/--port (default 50052), -c/--cache; there is NO --mem flag any more. Binding to anything but 127.0.0.1 prints the upstream banner "Never expose the RPC server to an open network! This is an experimental feature and is not secure!"; README says "Never run the RPC server on an open network or in a sensitive environment!". Transport is raw IPv4 TCP (AF_INET), no TLS/auth/proxy; server -H must be a dotted IPv4 literal (inet_addr); client --rpc host:port resolves via gethostbyname (MagicDNS names OK). Protocol is 5.1.0; client refuses a server with a different major or a higher minor — run the same build everywhere. Cache (-c) lives at $LLAMA_CACHE or $XDG_CACHE_HOME/llama.cpp or ~/.cache/llama.cpp + rpc/.

6. llama-server/--rpc semantics: --rpc SERVERS (env LLAMA_ARG_RPC) registers each endpoint's devices as RPC<n>[host:port]; --list-devices shows them; -dev selects; -ngl default "auto" with --fit on; -sm layer default. Default split: weights and KV across all local+remote devices "in proportion to each device's available memory" (llama-model.cpp: "default split, by free memory" via ggml_backend_dev_memory), override with -ts. llama-server defaults --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 (LLAMA_ARG_HOST/PORT). Logging: default -lv 3 (info) does not log request bodies; bodies/prompt tokens are SRV_DBG/SLT_DBG (level 5), so never run with -v; --log-disable mutes everything; --log-prompts-dir writes prompts to disk (keep off); --slots is on by default (no prompt text in it), --props/--metrics off, --slot-save-path off. llama-bench has "-rpc, --rpc <rpc_servers> register RPC devices (comma separated)".

7. Service plumbing. systemd 261 docs: loginctl enable-linger makes "a user manager ... spawned for the user at boot and kept around after logouts", units go in ~/.config/systemd/user (or /etc/systemd/user for admin-created user units). NVIDIA 535 README: /dev/nvidia* default to UID 0, GID 0, mode 0666 (created by the driver or setuid nvidia-modprobe), tunable with NVreg_DeviceFileUID/GID/Mode (e.g. GID=44 video, 0660); CUDA guide: "no CUDA-capable devices" usually means /dev/nvidia* missing or wrong permissions. So a non-root service user works out of the box unless a distro/udev rule tightened the mode.

8. The hub's Tailscale userspace mode is a real blocker for the plan as written: in that mode tailscaled is a SOCKS5/HTTP proxy with no tun interface; llama-server's --rpc and ggml-rpc-server speak plain TCP with no proxy support, and --host needs a local IPv4 — so the hub can neither reach workers' tailnet IPs as an RPC client nor bind the OpenAI endpoint to a tailnet IP. Either switch the hub to kernel/tun mode or move the llama-server role to a tun-mode node.

.devops/cuda.Dockerfile: ARG CUDA_VERSION=12.8.1, UBUNTU_VERSION=24.04, base docker.io/nvidia/cuda:${CUDA_VERSION}-{devel,runtime}-ubuntu${UBUNTU_VERSION}; build line is 'cmake -B build -DGGML_NATIVE=OFF -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DGGML_BACKEND_DL=ON -DGGML_CPU_ALL_VARIANTS=ON -DLLAMA_BUILD_TESTS=OFF ${CMAKE_ARGS} -DCMAKE_EXE_LINKER_FLAGS=-Wl,--allow-shlib-undefined .' where CMAKE_ARGS is only set to -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES when CUDA_DOCKER_ARCH != default — i.e. GGML_RPC is never enabled (ggml/CMakeLists.txt: option(GGML_RPC 'ggml: use RPC' OFF). 'light' copies llama, llama-cli, llama-completion; 'server' copies llama, llama-server; 'full' copies build/bin/*. Hence no official image ships ggml-rpc-server or the RPC backend (inferred from the Dockerfile; image contents not pulled).

tools/rpc/README.md: 'This example and the RPC backend are currently in a proof-of-concept development stage. As such, the functionality is fragile and insecure. Never run the RPC server on an open network or in a sensitive environment!' Build: 'On each remote host, build the backends for each accelerator by adding -DGGML_RPC=ON' e.g. 'cmake .. -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DGGML_RPC=ON'; 'On the main host build llama.cpp with the backends for the local devices and add -DGGML_RPC=ON'; usage 'llama-cli -hf ggml-org/gemma-3-1b-it-GGUF -ngl 99 --rpc 192.168.88.10:50052,192.168.88.11:50052'. 'By default, ggml-rpc-server exposes all available accelerator devices on the host. If there are no accelerators, it exposes a single CPU device.' Device selection via CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES or --device. Cache: '-c' ... 'stored in the $HOME/.cache/llama.cpp/rpc directory and can be controlled via the LLAMA_CACHE environment variable'. Debug: GGML_RPC_DEBUG=1. RDMA auto-negotiated when libibverbs found at build time. The executable target is ggml-rpc-server (tools/rpc/CMakeLists.txt set(TARGET ggml-rpc-server)). docs/build.md contains no RPC section.

tools/rpc/rpc-server.cpp usage at this tag: '-h, --help', '-t, --threads N  number of threads for the CPU device (default: hardware_concurrency()/2, min 1)', '-d, --device <dev1,dev2,...>  comma-separated list of devices', '-H, --host HOST  host to bind to (default: 127.0.0.1)', '-p, --port PORT  port to bind to (default: 50052)', '-c, --cache  enable local file cache'. There is no -m/--mem option. If host != 127.0.0.1 it prints: 'WARNING: Host ('%s') is != '127.0.0.1' / Never expose the RPC server to an open network! / This is an experimental feature and is not secure!'. With -c the cache dir is fs_get_cache_directory()+'rpc/' where the base is $LLAMA_CACHE, else $XDG_CACHE_HOME/llama.cpp or $HOME/.cache/llama.cpp (Linux), ~/Library/Caches/llama.cpp (macOS), %LOCALAPPDATA%/llama.cpp (Windows). Startup prints each device as '<name>: <description> (<total> MiB, <free> MiB free)'.

ggml/src/ggml-rpc/transport.cpp: the server socket is AF_INET with SO_REUSEADDR, binds to inet_addr(host) and rejects non-dotted-quad hosts ('Invalid host address'); the client resolves the --rpc host with gethostbyname() and connects with plain TCP (TCP_NODELAY). No TLS, authentication, or proxy support exists in the transport. ggml/include/ggml-rpc.h defines RPC_PROTO_MAJOR_VERSION 5, MINOR 1, PATCH 0 and GGML_RPC_MAX_SERVERS 16; ggml-rpc.cpp rejects a server when 'response.major != RPC_PROTO_MAJOR_VERSION || response.minor > RPC_PROTO_MINOR_VERSION' with 'RPC server version mismatch'. Client-side devices are named 'RPC<idx>[<endpoint>]'.

common/arg.cpp: '--rpc SERVERS  comma-separated list of RPC servers (host:port)' (env LLAMA_ARG_RPC); add_rpc_devices() calls ggml_backend_load_all(), looks up backend 'RPC' (throws 'failed to find RPC backend' if the build lacks GGML_RPC), and calls ggml_backend_rpc_add_server(endpoint) + ggml_backend_register for each endpoint. '-ngl N  max. number of layers to store in VRAM, either an exact number, auto, or all (default: auto)'; common.h n_gpu_layers=-1 (auto) and fit_params=true ('whether to fit unset model/context parameters to free device memory'). '-sm {none,layer,row,tensor}' with 'layer (default): split layers and KV across GPUs (pipelined)'; '-ts N0,N1,...  fraction of the model to offload to each GPU, comma-separated list of proportions, e.g. 3,1'; '-dev <dev1,dev2,..>  comma-separated list of devices to use for offloading (none = don't offload)'; '--list-devices  print list of available devices and exit'; '-mg INDEX'.

Layer split semantics: tools/rpc/README.md: 'By default, llama.cpp distributes model weights and the KV cache across all available devices -- both local and remote -- in proportion to each device's available memory. You can override this behavior with the --tensor-split option'. src/llama-model.cpp implements this: when tensor_split is all zeros, '// default split, by free memory' — splits[i] = free bytes from ggml_backend_dev_memory(dev,&free,&total) (falling back to host memory if a device reports 0/0); layers are then assigned by upper_bound over the normalised cumulative splits, and the input layer is always kept on the CPU.

tools/server/README.md option table: '--rpc SERVERS  comma-separated list of RPC servers (host:port) (env: LLAMA_ARG_RPC)'; '--log-disable  Log disable'; '--log-file FNAME  Log to file (env: LLAMA_ARG_LOG_FILE)'; '-v, --verbose, --log-verbose  Set verbosity level to infinity'; '-lv, --verbosity, --log-verbosity N  ... 0: generic output, 1: error, 2: warning, 3: info, 4: trace, 5: debug (default: 3) (env: LLAMA_ARG_LOG_VERBOSITY)'; '--metrics ... (default: disabled)'; '--props  enable changing global properties via POST /props (default: disabled)'; '--slots, --no-slots  expose slots monitoring endpoint (default: enabled)'; '--slot-save-path PATH  path to save slot kv cache (default: disabled)'. llama-server defaults --host 127.0.0.1, --port 8080 (common.h hostname/port; env LLAMA_ARG_HOST/LLAMA_ARG_PORT).

Prompt/request logging in llama-server is debug-level only: tools/server/server-http.cpp logs SRV_DBG("request:  %s", req.body) and SRV_DBG("response: %s", res.body); per-token prompt dumps are SLT_DBG. SRV_DBG/SLT_DBG map to LOG_DBG = LOG_LEVEL_DEBUG (5) in common/log.h, above the default threshold 3, so at default verbosity request bodies are not logged; -v (INT_MAX) logs them. common/arg.cpp also has '--log-prompts-dir PATH  Log prompts to directory (auto-created if not present; only used for debugging, default: disabled)' for SERVER and CLI, and '--log-disable' pauses the main log entirely. '--verbose-prompt' exists but is not registered for the server example.

tools/llama-bench/README.md usage lists '-rpc, --rpc <rpc_servers>  register RPC devices (comma separated)', alongside '-ngl, --n-gpu-layers <n> (default: -1)', '-sm, --split-mode <none|layer|row|tensor> (default: layer)', '-mg, --main-gpu <i> (default: 0)', '-ts, --tensor-split <ts0/ts1/..> (default: 0)', '-dev, --device <dev0/dev1/...> (default: auto)'.

docs/build.md CUDA section: 'cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON; cmake --build build --config Release'; 'By default llama.cpp will be built for the hardware that is connected to the system at that time. facts.statement: ggml/src/ggml-cuda/CMakeLists.txt: cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.18) 'for CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES'; find_package(CUDAToolkit) with message(FATAL_ERROR "CUDA Toolkit not found") otherwise. If CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES is unset: GGML_NATIVE with CUDA>=11.6 and CMake>=3.24 => 'native'; else list = [50-virtual 61-virtual 70-virtual only if CUDAToolkit_VERSION < 13] + 75-virtual 80-virtual 86-real + [89-real 90-virtual if >=11.8] + [120a-real if >=12.8] + [121a-real if >=12.9]. Comment: '50 == Maxwell, lowest CUDA 12 standard ... XX-virtual == compile CUDA code as PTX, do JIT compilation to binary code on first run; XX-real == compile CUDA code as device code for this specific architecture'. No minimum CUDA toolkit version is enforced; common.cuh gates features on CUDART_VERSION >= 11070 / 11080 / 12000 / 12030.

Maxwell (cc 5.2) code-path limits in llama.cpp CUDA: common.cuh defines GGML_CUDA_CC_PASCAL 600, GGML_CUDA_CC_DP4A 610 '// minimum compute capability for __dp4a, an intrinsic for byte-wise dot products', VOLTA 700, TURING 750, AMPERE 800; mmq.cu returns false (MMQ not used) when ggml_cuda_highest_compiled_arch(cc) < GGML_CUDA_CC_DP4A; ggml-cuda.cu disables mul_mat_vec fusion when cc <= GGML_CUDA_CC_PASCAL ('fusion is not universally faster on Pascal'). No code path refuses cc 5.x outright; a GTX 970 runs through the generic/cuBLAS paths.

CUDA 12.9 release notes, 1.5.2 Deprecated Architectures: 'Maxwell, Pascal, and Volta architectures are now feature-complete with no further enhancements planned. While CUDA Toolkit 12.x series will continue to support building applications for these architectures, offline compilation and library support will be removed in the next major CUDA Toolkit version release.' CUDA 12.9 GA toolkit driver >=575.51.03; 12.9 Update 1 >=575.57.08.

CUDA 13.0 release notes, 2.6.2 Deprecated Architectures: 'Architecture support for Maxwell, Pascal, and Volta is considered feature-complete. Offline compilation and library support for these architectures have been removed in CUDA Toolkit 13.0 major version release. The use of CUDA Toolkits through the 12.x series to build applications for these architectures will continue to be supported, but newer toolkits will be unable to target these architectures.' cuFFT: 'Removed support for Maxwell, Pascal, and Volta GPUs, corresponding to compute capabilities earlier than Turing.' CUDA 13.0 GA Linux driver >=580.65.06; '13.x series are ABI-compatible with drivers ... r580 and newer'.

CUDA 12.2 release notes: Table 3 'CUDA 12.2 GA — Linux x86_64 Driver Version >=535.54.03'; Table 2 minimum driver for CUDA minor version compatibility: CUDA 12.2.x/12.1.x/12.0.x >=525.60.13. (Driver 535 on the hub is the 12.2 GA toolkit driver.)

CUDA Compatibility guide, Minor Version Compatibility caveats: 'Applications using PTX will see runtime issues — Applications that compile device code to PTX will not work on older drivers. If the application requires PTX then administrators have to upgrade the installed driver.' and 'Requires target architecture argument to NVCC — Minor Compatibility requires passing the target architecture argument to NVCC, for example nvcc -arch=sm_xx.' Also 'features introduced in a newer version of the toolkit and driver may return ... cudaErrorCallRequiresNewerDriver'. Forward Compatibility page: 'Forward Compatibility is applicable only for systems with: NVIDIA Data Center GPUs. Select NGC Server Ready SKUs of RTX cards. Jetson boards.'

Derived constraint for the hub (GTX 970, cc 5.2, driver 535 = CUDA 12.2 GA driver): llama.cpp's default Maxwell target is '50-virtual' (PTX, JIT at runtime) and NVIDIA says PTX built with a newer 12.x toolkit will not run on an older driver under minor-version compatibility; therefore on the hub either build with the CUDA 12.2 toolkit, or build with any 12.x toolkit and pass -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=52-real (SASS for sm_52, which minor-version compatibility does support on driver >=525.60.13). CUDA 13.x cannot target cc 5.2 and needs driver >=580 anyway. This combination of F17+F21+F23 is an inference; the 'build with 12.2 on driver 535' path has not yet been executed on the hub.

NVIDIA driver 535 README FAQ 'How and when are the NVIDIA device files created?': device files are created by the user-space driver component or, lacking root, by 'the setuid root nvidia-modprobe utility'; 'it will default to creating the device files with the following attributes: UID: 0 - root, GID: 0 - root, Mode: 0666 - rw-rw-rw-. Existing device files are changed if their attributes don't match these defaults.' Different attributes can be set with kernel module parameters NVreg_DeviceFileUID, NVreg_DeviceFileGID, NVreg_DeviceFileMode (example: UID=0, GID=44 (video), Mode=0660); 'The NVreg_ModifyDeviceFiles NVIDIA kernel module parameter will disable dynamic device file management, if set to 0.' 'When possible, it is recommended to use your Linux distribution's native mechanisms for managing kernel module loading and device file creation.'
facts.version: NVIDIA Linux driver 535.261.03 README (identical text in 535.247.01 and 535.230.02)

facts.statement: CUDA Installation Guide for Linux (13.3), 11.2.2.1: 'If a CUDA-capable device is installed but deviceQuery reports that no CUDA-capable devices are present, this likely means that the /dev/nvidia* files are missing or have the wrong permissions.' systemd loginctl(1): 'enable-linger [USER…], disable-linger [USER…] — Enable/disable user lingering for one or more users. If enabled for a specific user, a user manager is spawned for the user at boot and kept around after logouts. This allows users who are not logged in to run long-running services. Takes one or more user names or numeric UIDs as argument. If no argument is specified, enables/disables lingering for the user of the session of the caller. See also KillUserProcesses= setting in logind.conf(5). Added in version 233.'
facts.version: systemd 261.2 (same text in local man page, systemd 261)

facts.statement: systemd.unit(5) 'Load path when running in user mode (--user)': '$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/systemd/user or $HOME/.config/systemd/user — User configuration ($XDG_CONFIG_HOME is used if set, ~/.config otherwise)'; '/etc/systemd/user — User units created by the administrator'; '$XDG_DATA_HOME/systemd/user or $HOME/.local/share/systemd/user — Units of packages that have been installed in the home directory'; '/usr/lib/systemd/user — User units installed by the distribution package manager'.

Tailscale KB 'Userspace networking mode (for containers)' (last validated Nov 12, 2025): 'Tailscale works on Linux systems using a device driver called /dev/net/tun ... For those environments [without it], userspace networking mode offers a different way of running, where tailscaled functions as a SOCKS5 or HTTP proxy which other processes in the container can connect through.' Enabled with 'tailscaled --tun=userspace-networking --socks5-server=localhost:1055 --outbound-http-proxy-listen=localhost:1055' or FLAGS="--tun=userspace-networking" in /etc/default/tailscaled; 'After Tailscale is authenticated, your application can connect using a SOCKS5 or HTTP proxy or both ... generally by setting the ALL_PROXY and HTTP_PROXY environment variables'; 'Userspace networking mode is primarily for serverless environments.' The page does not describe how inbound connections reach local services in this mode.

Derived: because ggml-rpc/llama-server use direct TCP connect()/bind() with no proxy support (F10) and Tailscale userspace mode only exposes tailnet connectivity through a local SOCKS5/HTTP proxy (F29), the hub as currently configured cannot act as the --rpc client to workers' tailnet IPs nor bind llama-server/ggml-rpc-server to a tailnet IPv4 address. Whether 'tailscale serve' could front an inbound TCP port in userspace mode was not verified from Tailscale docs in this dossier.

llama.cpp LICENSE: 'MIT License — Copyright (c) 2023-2026 The ggml authors'. Version metadata at v0.2.0/b10581: CMakeLists LLAMA_VERSION 0.2.0, ggml 0.21.0 (shipped as libllama.so.0.2.0 and libggml-base.so.0.21.0). The RPC backend was added by PR #6829 'ggml : add RPC backend' by rgerganov (Radoslav Gerganov), merged 2024-05-14; CODEOWNERS assigns /ggml/src/ggml-rpc/ and /tools/rpc/ to @ggml-org/ggml-rpc ('ggml-org/ggml-rpc : rgerganov').

recommendations: Pin llama.cpp to a single tag for the whole fleet and record it in the spec as 'v0.2.0 (= b10566)'; RPC protocol 5.1.0 mismatch across builds is a hard failure, so every node's ggml-rpc-server and the hub's llama-server must come from the same tag (F1, F10).

Linux CUDA nodes must build from source: cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DGGML_RPC=ON (add -DGGML_NATIVE=OFF or an explicit CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES when building on one box for another). Do not plan on the official Docker images or the ubuntu release tarballs for GPU RPC workers — the tarballs are CPU/Vulkan only and the images lack the RPC backend (F3, F4, F7). The CPU/Vulkan tarballs are still useful for a quick no-GPU smoke test (they do contain ggml-rpc-server).

Hub (GTX 970, driver 535): build with the CUDA 12.2 toolkit that matches driver 535, or with any 12.x toolkit plus -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=52-real so Maxwell gets SASS rather than PTX (F17, F21, F23, F24). Never install CUDA 13 on that box for this purpose (needs driver >=580 and cannot target cc 5.2). Treat the 970 as a 'fits, but slow' device (no MMQ/dp4a, F18) — primarily extra VRAM for the split, and consider the Vulkan backend as a fallback experiment if the CUDA 12.2 build fights the host toolchain.

RTX 3050 node on CUDA 13.1: default arch list covers 86-real; requires driver >=590.44.01 (F22). RTX 2070 Super (cc 7.5) is covered by every default list. Keep per-node builds native (GGML_NATIVE on) since each node compiles its own ggml-rpc-server.

Write the rpc-server unit as: ExecStart=.../ggml-rpc-server -H <node's Tailscale IPv4> -p 50052 [-c] [-d CUDA0]; -H must be a dotted IPv4 literal (F10) and the upstream 'not secure' banner will print and is expected (F9). Add the spec sentence that the RPC server is unauthenticated raw TCP and the tailnet is the only boundary; combine with Tailscale ACLs limiting port 50052 to the hub.

Resolve the hub's Tailscale userspace-mode problem before Phase 1 (F29, F30): either switch solarplexus to kernel/tun mode, or run llama-server on a tun-mode node and keep the hub as a worker only after confirming it can accept inbound tailnet TCP. This is an ADR-worthy decision (topology ADR 0006 is reserved).

llama-server on the hub: --host <tailnet IPv4> --port 8080 --rpc <worker1>:50052,<worker2>:50052 -ngl auto (default) and let the default free-memory split do the work; only add -ts if the split is bad. Use --list-devices first to confirm RPC<n>[host:port] devices appear (F11, F12). Keep logging at default -lv 3 and never use -v or --log-prompts-dir in service units (F14); consider --no-slots and leave --metrics/--props off unless needed; optionally --log-file to a member-readable location for the thank-you board.
Benchmark the split with llama-bench --rpc <servers> -ngl 99 before committing to a model, since RPC exists to fit, not to speed up (F15).

Service user: run ggml-rpc-server as a dedicated non-root user under a user manager with loginctl enable-linger and the unit in ~/.config/systemd/user (F27, F28); verify ls -l /dev/nvidia* shows 0666 (F25) and, if a distro has tightened it, add the user to the group named by the device GID rather than changing module parameters. Set LLAMA_CACHE (or let it default to ~/.cache/llama.cpp/rpc) to a disk with room for the cached tensors when using -c.
Credit rows: llama.cpp row already exists; add the release/tag convention and the RPC maintainer handle (rgerganov) to docs, and add Tailscale userspace-mode note to the hub's page.
open_questions: Does the hub really need Tailscale in userspace mode (no /dev/net/tun)? If the reason is historical, moving to tun mode removes the blocker in F30; if it is a hard constraint, does 'tailscale serve --tcp' accept inbound RPC and can the hub reach workers at all as an RPC client? Not verified from Tailscale docs here.

Can the CUDA 12.2 toolkit be installed alongside the hub's current OS toolchain (gcc/glibc compatibility), or is the simpler route -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=52-real with a newer 12.x toolkit? Needs a spike on solarplexus (F24 is an inference until executed).
Is the GTX 970's 4 GB worth the RPC round-trips for the chosen Phase 1 model, or should the hub be the llama-server host with the 2070 Super and 3050 as RPC workers? llama-bench numbers needed.

What exactly is in the CUDA 12.4 Windows release zip beyond ggml-cuda.dll (we observed ggml-rpc-server.exe and CPU dlls in it), and is the cudart zip required on a friend's Windows PC that lacks a CUDA toolkit? Needs a Windows test before the Windows onboarding card is written.
Does the macOS release tarball's ggml-rpc-server work unsigned on a friend's Mac (Gatekeeper), or must Macs build from source / use brew? Not researched in this dossier.
Will the v0.x stable cadence be slow enough to pin for a whole phase, or should the spec pin the b-number directly (v0.2.0 = b10566)?
Distro-specific /dev/nvidia* permissions on Ubuntu Server (hub) and Arch/EndeavourOS (laptops): confirm with ls -l on each node; the NVIDIA default is 0666 but udev rules can differ.

verdicts.reason: Verified against the cited primary source and the GitHub REST API on 2026-08-22. (1) GET /repos/ggml-org/llama.cpp/releases/latest returns tag_name=v0.2.0, prerelease=false, published_at=2026-08-21T18:32:48Z — exact match; the newer b10567..b10582 releases are all prerelease=true. (2) refs/tags/v0.2.0 is an annotated tag object (8a35040e...) whose object is commit bb4caa7540188872173c44d161602d9271386413; refs/tags/b10566 is a lightweight tag pointing directly to bb4caa7540188872173c44d161602d9271386413 — so 'resolves to' and 'also tag b10566' both hold (note: the release's target_commitish field is 5a32f7b66..., but that is GitHub's branch/commit-at-creation metadata, not what the tag resolves to). (3) Release body contains verbatim: '- tag `vX.Y.Z` - stable, slower release cadence, recommended for downstream distribution and casual users' and '- tag `b[NUM]` - bleeding edge, faster release cadence, recommended for developers and technical users'. The claim's second quote is truncated (drops 'recommended for developers and technical users') and omits the backticks, but is not misquoted. (4) The release has exactly one API asset: nightly-tag.txt (7 bytes); downloaded content is 'b10566\n'. The GitHub web UI shows '3 assets' only because it counts the auto-generated source zip/tar.gz. (5) The b10566 release (prerelease=true, published 2026-08-21T18:25:36Z, target bb4caa75...) carries 26 binary assets (llama-b10566-bin-macos-arm64.tar.gz, llama-b10566-bin-win-cuda-*.zip, llama-b10566-bin-ubuntu-*.tar.gz, etc.), and the v0.2.0 body links to it as 'Nightly build: b10566'. Claim stands as stated for version v0.2.0; only cosmetic nit is the abbreviated quote.

missing: Argument-order sensitivity of --list-devices / -dev / -mmdev relative to --rpc: at b10581 `--list-devices` prints and exit(0)s inside its parse handler (common/arg.cpp ~L2727) and `-dev` resolves names at parse time, so `llama-cli --list-devices --rpc H:P` (S-03's command) and `-dev RPC0` placed before `--rpc` cannot see RPC devices. The dossier's rec 7 and spec acceptance #1 assume the opposite. Missing: a verified fact that `--rpc <servers>` must precede `--list-devices`/`-dev`, the exact -dev names (RPC0, RPC1 ... global counter per F10), and the corrected acceptance command.

Silent local fallback, precisely: ggml_backend_rpc_get_device_count() logs `Failed to connect to <endpoint>` and returns 0, so add_rpc_devices registers a zero-device RPC registry and llama-server/llama-bench proceed locally with no error and no flag to make a missing endpoint fatal. Missing: that greppable log line, confirmation that no `--rpc-required`-style option exists, and a recommended ExecStartPre/TCP-probe gate for the host unit (needed for the reboot case where llama-server starts before the workers).

Mid-run worker loss: every RPC send/recv failure hits RPC_STATUS_ASSERT -> GGML_ABORT("Remote RPC server crashed or returned malformed response") so llama-server dies with SIGABRT (Restart=on-failure fires), but transport.cpp sets only TCP_NODELAY/SO_REUSEADDR (no SO_KEEPALIVE, SO_RCVTIMEO) so a worker that vanishes without FIN/RST (laptop lid closed, Wi-Fi drop) hangs llama-server indefinitely; and get_socket() caches one socket per endpoint for the process lifetime, so a restarted worker is never re-dialled without restarting llama-server. The spec's 'worker drops mid-run' row is still UNVERIFIED; a watchdog/health-timer design and StartLimitIntervalSec/StartLimitBurst values for the crash-restart loop are missing.

ggml-rpc-server concurrency model: the serve loop is serial (accept -> rpc_serve_client -> next accept; listen backlog 1) and the client holds its socket for its lifetime, so each worker serves exactly one llama-server/llama-bench at a time and a second client blocks in the accept queue; all buffers a client allocated are freed on its disconnect (~rpc_server). Missing from the facts; it is why 'stop the host unit before llama-bench' is required and it constrains Phase 2 (no two models/servers can share a worker).

supports_op on the RPC device returns true unconditionally (ggml-rpc.cpp ~L1913, TODO), so the scheduler never falls back to the hub CPU for an op the remote Vulkan backend lacks; the worker aborts instead and the hub sees 'Remote RPC server crashed'. Missing: whether ggml-vulkan at b10581 implements every op of the Phase 1 model (Qwen3.8-27B hybrid linear-attention/gated-delta ops) and the backups, and how `-fa auto` resolves over RPC -- this is the concrete form of the spec's 'if hybrid layers misbehave over RPC' risk and decides the smoke-test order.

Device ordering for -ts/-mg with RPC: src/llama.cpp ~L274 inserts RPC servers at the FRONT of the device list ('to minimize network transfers'), so index 0 = first --rpc endpoint, the hub's local Vulkan0 is last, and default -mg 0 = remote RPC0 (ahnoway). Missing: this ordering, its -mg consequence, and a worked mapping from the spec's per-node VRAM caps (7/5/3.5 GB) to -ts proportions given that F12's split is by layer COUNT (hybrid layers differ in size) plus per-device compute/KV buffers; also that the default free-memory split is recomputed at every start, so GB-per-node is nondeterministic unless -ts is set.

The --fit family is absent: `-fit/--fit on|off` (default on), `-fitt/--fit-target MiB0,MiB1,...` per device, `-fitc/--fit-ctx N`, `-fitp/--fit-print` (common/arg.cpp ~L2843-2900; common_fit_params in common.cpp). Missing: whether fit accounts for RPC device memory, that it only adjusts UNSET args (the spec sets -ngl 99 and -c 8192 explicitly, so nothing is fitted), and the exact failure/exit when weights+KV exceed the devices.

Where the overflow goes: Q8_0 (27.3 GiB) vs 18 GB pooled VRAM -- workers export only accelerator devices by default (F8), so their RAM (19 GB on optiplex) is NOT in the split; only the hub's ~12 GB free RAM backs non-offloaded layers. Missing: can a worker export `-d Vulkan0,CPU` (CPU device name, threads via -t, how an RPC CPU device reports free memory), and the resulting corrected 'pool' arithmetic (the spec's ~81 GB figure is unsupported by the dossier).

Complete list of prompt-exposing knobs: /slots includes `prompt` and `generated` text only when env LLAMA_SERVER_SLOTS_DEBUG != 0 (server-context.cpp ~L1300, L2464) -- the dossier's 'no prompt text in /slots' is right at default but the env gate is undocumented; and `-v` logs `launching slot : {...}` via slot.to_json() with prompt text (~L1731), which F14's corrected text omits. A single fact row enumerating LLAMA_SERVER_SLOTS_DEBUG, -v, --log-prompts-dir, --slot-save-path is needed for the unit's Environment= and the acceptance grep.

Worker -c cache facts (spec S6.1 asked for 'cache dir/size'): what is persisted (weights via SET_TENSOR_HASH only, or any KV/activation data -- matters for ADR-0001), size relative to the worker's share (two quants ~47 GB total), no eviction/how to clear, whether cache reads are charged to the cgroup (MemoryMax) as page cache, and the host RSS of ggml-rpc-server per GB of VRAM served (staging buffers) so MemoryMax=1.6G/3.2G defaults don't OOM-kill the worker on the first 27 GB load.

User-unit boot ordering: a --user manager cannot order After= system units, so `After=network-online.target tailscaled.service` in the plan's template is a no-op; with linger the unit starts before tailscale0 has its IPv4 and `-H <tailnet-ip>` bind fails. Missing: what ggml-rpc-server prints/returns on bind failure ('Failed to create server socket', exit code), a tested ExecStartPre wait (e.g. loop on `tailscale ip -4`), and the same for llama-server --host <tailnet-ip>.

Linger state per node + executor (spec S6.1 explicit key question): a table ahnoway=?, optiplex=yes (S-03), solarplexus=no; whether a non-root user can `loginctl enable-linger` for itself over ssh (polkit set-self-linger) or it is a root/founder step per node; and the XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS requirement for `systemctl --user` over non-login ssh that S-03 hit.

Device-node access for the CHOSEN backend (Vulkan) and the unattended service user: /dev/dri/renderD* group (render/video) and /dev/nvidia* as actually set on each node (`ls -l`), plus Vulkan ICD visibility (/usr/share/vulkan/icd.d/nvidia_icd.json, libvulkan1) for a non-login account; F25/F26 cover only the generic NVIDIA/CUDA default and the per-node check is still an open question although all three nodes are reachable.

Hub CUDA optimisation path (rec 3) is not executable from the dossier: (a) which 12.x toolkit is installable on Ubuntu 24.04 without touching driver 535 (noble's nvidia-cuda-toolkit = 12.0; NVIDIA ubuntu2404 repo starts later than 12.2) and the supported host gcc for it vs noble's gcc 13 (CUDA 12.2 supports <= gcc 12 -> gcc-12 + CMAKE_CUDA_HOST_COMPILER); (b) whether a native build on the hub (GGML_NATIVE=ON, CMake >= 3.24) already emits sm_52 SASS, making 52-real advice redundant, and which CUDART_VERSION >= 12030 code paths could raise cudaErrorCallRequiresNewerDriver on a 12.2 driver; (c) the last NVIDIA driver branch supporting Maxwell (R580?) as the 'upgrade the driver instead' alternative; (d) container route: cuda.Dockerfile's CMAKE_ARGS is not a build-arg (must patch for -DGGML_RPC=ON) and docker builds use GGML_NATIVE=OFF -> 50-virtual PTX -> needs CUDA_DOCKER_ARCH=52 on driver 535; (e) ahnoway's driver version and Arch `cuda` package version for the 2070S build are nowhere in R03.

llama-server flags the Caddy /chat route depends on: `--api-prefix PREFIX` (LLAMA_ARG_API_PREFIX), `--webui/--no-webui`, `--webui-config`, `-a/--alias` exist at b10581 but are not in F13; missing whether the built-in UI works under a reverse-proxied sub-path (the plan hedges between handle and handle_path) and what model name /v1/models returns for the curl test.

Pin hygiene: sha256 of llama-b10581-bin-ubuntu-vulkan-x64.tar.gz (the dossier downloaded it but recorded no digest); confirmation that the ubuntu-vulkan job is a GGML_BACKEND_DL build and where libggml-rpc.so/libggml-vulkan.so are searched (executable dir / GGML_BACKEND_PATH) so relocating or symlinking binaries doesn't silently drop the RPC backend; and the rec 1 'pin v0.2.0 (=b10566)' vs spec 'b10581' inconsistency resolved in the dossier.

Hub-as-worker in userspace Tailscale: F30 says the hub cannot bind or accept on a tailnet IPv4, but S-03 showed inbound tailnet TCP is forwarded to 127.0.0.1 (worker bound to loopback works); the Facts table is not reconciled and the forwarding behaviour is undocumented in KB 1112. If Phase 0 step 2 (kernel mode) slips, the fallback topology rests on an unverified mechanism; also `tailscale nc`/`tailscale serve --tcp` for outbound/inbound were not checked.

S-04 numbers are absent (spec S6.1: 'measured tok/s at 10% and under exception'): no pp/tg for any model > tiny, so acceptance test 3's 'within 20% of S-04' has no reference and the hub-as-bottleneck decision (ADR-0006 trigger) cannot be pre-judged.

Member-platform worker facts for ADR-0004(ii) remain open (already listed in Open questions but unresearched): whether the win-cuda zip needs the cudart zip on a PC without a CUDA toolkit, Windows Firewall/`-H <tailscale ipv4>` behaviour, and whether the macOS tarball's ggml-rpc-server runs unsigned under Gatekeeper.

Verification debt a plan writer must not read as settled: F24 (hub CUDA 12.x build) is an inference never executed; F21-F31 were never refuted (beyond cap); F7 (no ggml-rpc-server in official images) is inferred from the Dockerfile, not from a pulled image (one `docker run ... ls /app` closes it).

# DOSSIER R04 — Model selection for Phase 1 (CORVID)
Date verified: 2026-08-22. Fleet assumption (from task): largest single node = 6 GB VRAM + ~19 GB free RAM ≈ 25 GB; pool ≈ 18 GB VRAM (8+4+6) + ≈63 GB RAM ≈ 81 GB. llama.cpp pinned reference: stable tag v0.2.0 (2026-08-21) / nightly b10581 (2026-08-22).

## 1. Ranking basis (named, dated)
- **Primary basis: Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.1.1** (9 evals: GDPval-AA v2, tau3-Banking, Terminal-Bench v2.1, SciCode, AA-LCR, AA-Omniscience, HLE, GPQA Diamond, CritPt), open-weights table and per-model pages as displayed 2026-08-22 (R04-F1..F10). Scores are only comparable within this index version; they are NOT comparable to 2025-era AA numbers.
- **Cross-check: Arena (ex-LMArena) text leaderboard, snapshot "Last updated Aug 21, 2026", 7.9M votes / 394 models** (R04-F11): every open-weight entry in the top 50 is frontier-scale (GLM-5.x, Kimi K2.6, DeepSeek V4 Pro, MiMo-V2.5-Pro) — nothing that fits an 81 GB pool. So Arena tells us the ceiling, AA tells us the best-per-GB.
- **Demand signal: Hugging Face GGUF trending (2026-08-22)** is dominated by Qwen3.8-27B quants (unsloth repo 6.32M downloads) plus Muse-Glimmer-30B and Ornith-1.5-35B-A3B (R04-F12).
- Not used: HF Open LLM Leaderboard (no usable 2026 table surfaced; see open questions).

## 2. KV-cache arithmetic method (llama.cpp)
Per llama.cpp `llama-hparams.cpp` (R04-F45): per layer, K row width = n_embd_head_k × n_head_kv and V row width = n_embd_head_v × n_head_kv; the server's K/V cache types default to f16 = 2 bytes (R04-F44). So **KV bytes/token = Σ_layers 2 × n_head_kv × head_dim × 2 B** over full-attention layers; sliding-window layers are capped at the window length; linear-attention (Gated DeltaNet) layers hold a constant per-sequence recurrent state instead of a growing KV. All KV numbers below are DERIVED from primary config.json values (marked unverified = computed, not measured). **Critical:** `-c/--ctx-size` defaults to 0 = "loaded from model" (R04-F44), i.e. 262,144 for Qwen3.8-27B and 131,072 for Llama 3.3 70B — always pass `-c 4096`/`-c 8192` explicitly or KV balloons (16 GiB / 40 GiB).

## 3. Candidates that are IMPOSSIBLE on one node (> ~25 GB) yet FIT the pool (< ~81 GB)

## 5. Recommendation (headline)
**Phase-1 demo model: Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B at Q8_0 from ggml-org/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF (28.60 GB, 26.6 GiB), `-c 8192`.** It is the highest-scoring open-weight model in its size class on the named basis (AA v4.1.1 = 52, #1/137), Apache-2.0, ungated, the most-downloaded GGUF on HF this week, and its Q8_0 is the smallest quant that clears the 25 GB line with comfortable margin (≈29.3 GB incl. KV) while needing only ~11 GB of CPU RAM beyond the pool's 18 GB VRAM. Its tiny KV (64 KiB/token, hybrid linear attention) means context size barely moves the arithmetic. Same-class backups: Muse-Glimmer-30B Q8_0 (29.6 GB, AA 35) and Gemma 4 31B Q8_0 (32.6 GB, AA 30), both Apache-2.0. Keep Llama 3.3 70B / DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B as the "classic 70B" fallback only if Qwen3.8's hybrid architecture misbehaves over RPC — they are plain-attention and known-good but gated/heavier (≥27.5 GB at IQ3_XXS, 320 KiB/token KV). Avoid gpt-oss-120b (no headroom) and gated Gemma 3 for v1.

## 6. llama.cpp facts that gate the plan
- RPC README (master, 2026-08-22): "By default, llama.cpp distributes model weights and the KV cache across all available devices -- both local and remote -- in proportion to each device's available memory"; override with `--tensor-split`; build `-DGGML_RPC=ON`; the server binary is now shown as `bin/ggml-rpc-server -p 50052` with `--device CUDA0` and `-c` (local cache); warning: "Never run the RPC server on an open network or in a sensitive environment!" (R04-F42).
- Top-level README now shows `llama cli -hf …` / `llama serve -hf …`, while tools/server/README still shows `./llama-server` (R04-F46/F47) → confirm binary names at the pinned tag before writing setup docs.
- CUDA CMake defaults: compute-capability 50/61/70 targets are added only when CUDA < 13 ("Maxwell, lowest CUDA 12 standard") (R04-F48) → the GTX 970 (sm_52) hub must build with its CUDA 12.2; the RTX 3050 node on CUDA 13.1 cannot produce a 970-capable binary (irrelevant since each node builds its own).
- Server defaults: `--host 127.0.0.1`, `-ctk/-ctv f16`, `-ngl auto`, `-np -1 (auto)`, `--kv-unified` on when slots auto, `-c 0 = loaded from model` (R04-F44).

Same-class backups, in order: Muse-Glimmer-30B Q8_0 (unsloth, 29.61 GB, Apache-2.0, AA 35) and Gemma 4 31B-it Q8_0 (ggml-org, 32.64 GB, Apache-2.0, AA 30). Always pass -c explicitly (4096 or 8192). The server default -c 0 loads the model's max context: 262,144 for Qwen3.8-27B (16 GiB KV) and 131,072 for Llama 3.3 70B (40 GiB KV). Keep -ctk/-ctv at the f16 default for Phase 1; revisit q8_0 KV only if measurements require it.
