research.dossier:
DOSSIER R06 — Coordinator & schema (CORVID). Verified 2026-08-22 against primary sources only (docs.docker.com / compose-spec repo / docker/compose v5.5.0 source, postgresql.org docs for PG 18, docker-library postgres README + official-images tag list, tailscale.com KB + tailscale/tailscale source at main commit 86e5d38, kubernetes.io source, kernel cgroup-v2 doc, Hadoop Fair Scheduler doc, the DRF NSDI'11 paper PDF, llama.cpp server README at master e85caa8). Hub context assumed: Ubuntu hub (solarplexus) running Docker, Tailscale in userspace mode; coordinator = Python + Postgres.

1) POSTGRES AS ITS OWN COMPOSE PROJECT
- Isolation: Compose isolates environments by project name; precedence is -p flag > COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME > top-level `name:` > directory name (F6). So `name: corvid-db` in its own directory is a first-class separate project; the obsolete `version:` key should be omitted (F6).
- Resource caps: both styles are honored by `docker compose` v5.5.0 — service-level `cpus`/`mem_limit`/`mem_reservation`/`cpu_shares`/`pids_limit` AND `deploy.resources.limits.{cpus,memory,pids}` / `reservations.{memory,devices}` are mapped onto the container HostConfig in pkg/compose/create.go (F1–F3). Code comment: "Cpu reservation is a swarm option and PIDs is only a limit" — i.e. `reservations.cpus` is ignored outside Swarm (F2). Spec requires `cpus` and `deploy.cpus` to agree if both set (F3). Docker resource docs: `--memory` minimum 6m; `--cpu-shares` default 1024 is a soft weight only enforced under contention (F14).
- Data dir: for the postgres image 18+, PGDATA is /var/lib/postgresql/18/docker and the declared VOLUME moved to /var/lib/postgresql — mount there; for ≤17 mount /var/lib/postgresql/data (mounting /var/lib/postgresql on ≤17 WILL NOT persist) (F7). Bind-mount long syntax: type: bind, source, target, read_only, bind.create_host_path (default true); relative host paths resolve from the Compose file's directory (F5). Arbitrary --user works if PGDATA owner matches; initdb needs the UID in /etc/passwd (bind-mount /etc/passwd:ro) (F13).
- Shared memory: container /dev/shm defaults to 64MB; image README's own compose example sets `shm_size: 128mb` and suggests --shm-size=256MB (F8).
- Healthcheck: compose fields test/interval/timeout/retries/start_period/start_interval; `depends_on: {db: {condition: service_healthy}}` is guaranteed healthy-before-start (F4). pg_isready exit 0 = accepting, 1 = rejecting (startup), 2 = no response, 3 = bad params; wrong creds still work but log a failed attempt — so pass the real -U/-d (F12).
- Init: /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d scripts run only on an EMPTY data dir, as the postgres user; a failed script + orchestrator restart will NOT re-run them (F9). POSTGRES_PASSWORD is mandatory (F7).
- Version pin: current official tags include 18.6, 18.6-trixie, 18.6-alpine, 17.11 (F10); PG 18 supported until 2030-11-14, PG 17 until 2029-11-08 (F11). PostgreSQL License is BSD/MIT-like (F39); the image's Dockerfiles are MIT (F40).

2) QUEUE PATTERN (SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)
- PG 18 docs: "With SKIP LOCKED, any selected rows that cannot be immediately locked are skipped… can be used to avoid lock contention with multiple consumers accessing a queue-like table" (F15); with LIMIT, locking stops once enough rows are returned, but OFFSET-skipped rows DO get locked (F16). Feature since 9.5 (Thomas Munro) (F17).
- Companion primitives: LISTEN/NOTIFY payload <8000 bytes, delivered only on commit; docs recommend putting data in a table and sending only the key, ideally from a statement trigger (F18) — this is exactly "poll + wake-up" for a job table. Advisory locks exist (session vs transaction level; pg_try_advisory_xact_lock non-blocking) but are NOT needed for the claim query and are dangerous with LIMIT (F19). Partial index `WHERE state='queued'` keeps the hot index tiny (F20). Heartbeat upsert: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE is atomic insert-or-update and can reference EXCLUDED (F21). now()/CURRENT_TIMESTAMP is transaction start time; clock_timestamp() is wall-clock (F22). timestamptz is stored as UTC; bare `timestamp` is "without time zone" and silently drops zone info — always use timestamptz (F23).

3) HEARTBEAT / ROSTER PATTERNS (design reference, not a dependency)
- Kubernetes: two heartbeat forms (Node .status every 5 min by default; lightweight Lease renewed every 10 s by default; unreachable timeout 40 s; retry backoff 200 ms→7 s cap; controller checks every 5 s; 5 min more before eviction) (F24). A heartbeat is literally an update of Lease.spec.renewTime and the control plane judges availability from that timestamp (F25) — i.e. the "roster row + last_seen column" pattern, sanctioned at planet scale.

4) FAIR-SHARE WHEN CONTENDED, NO QUOTAS (max-min)
- Hadoop Fair Scheduler defines the behavior: "all apps get, on average, an equal share of resources over time… When there is a single app running, that app uses the entire cluster… resources that free up are assigned to the new apps", weights optional (F26). cgroup v2 formalizes "weights" (work-conserving, only active children participate, cpu.weight default 100, range 1–10000) vs "limits" (cpu.max, may be over-committed) (F27). DRF (Ghodsi et al., NSDI'11) notes round-robin, proportional sharing and weighted fair queueing all implement (weighted) max-min fairness and generalizes it to multi-resource (F28). Kubernetes APF uses per-flow fair queuing keyed by requesting user so one flood cannot starve others (F29). Net: a per-member round-robin (or DRR) at claim time = max-min fair, no quotas, full use when uncontended.

5) IDENTITY FROM TAILSCALE FOR THE API
- Tailscale Serve injects Tailscale-User-Login / -Name / -Profile-Pic into proxied HTTP, strips spoofed copies inbound, only for tailnet traffic (never Funnel), not for tagged devices, and the KB's best practice is that the backend listens on localhost only (F30).
- `tailscale whois ip[:port] [--json]` resolves Machine + User (email) + Capabilities (F31); the LocalAPI endpoint is GET /localapi/v0/whois?addr=IP[:port] → {Node, UserProfile, CapMap}, 404 on no match, gated by PermitRead (F32). On Linux tailscaled.sock is 0666 and any local unix-socket client gets read permission (F33), so a Python service can call it without root.
- BUT the hub runs userspace networking: tailscaled acts as a SOCKS5/HTTP proxy (F34) and netstack forwards inbound TCP to the node's Tailscale IP by dialing 127.0.0.1:<port> with a standard dialer (F35) — the backend's TCP peer address is loopback, so whois-on-IP cannot identify the caller there. Serve headers are therefore the identity mechanism on the hub. Serve-under-userspace is implied by the Docker image (TS_USERSPACE on by default + TS_SERVE_CONFIG) (F34) but is not stated for the bare-metal hub → spike (F36, unverified).

6) LOG POLICY (METADATA ONLY)
- Postgres defaults are already metadata-safe: log_statement=none, log_min_duration_statement=-1 (but when enabled, log_parameter_max_length=-1 logs bind params IN FULL), log_connections='' and log_disconnections=off (F37). Pin these explicitly so a future "debug" flip is a deliberate ADR-level act.
- llama-server: `--log-prompts-dir` is debug-only and disabled by default; `/slots` endpoint is ON by default (per-slot state incl. sampling params) → run `--no-slots`; `--metrics` (aggregate Prometheus) is off by default and is the metadata-friendly choice (F38).

7) LICENSES/TAGS VERIFIED: Docker Compose v5.5.0 Apache-2.0 (F41); psycopg 3.3.4 LGPL-3.0 (F42); tailscale v1.102.3 BSD-3-Clause (F43); FastAPI 0.141.1 MIT, uvicorn 0.52.4 BSD-3 as candidates (F44).

facts.statement: Compose Deploy Spec: `resources` has `limits` ("The platform must prevent the container to allocate more") and `reservations` ("The platform must guarantee the container can allocate at least the configured amount"); `cpus` = number of cores, `memory` = byte-value string, `pids` = integer; documented example uses limits cpus '0.50', memory 50M, pids 1 and reservations cpus '0.25', memory 20M. The page does not itself state whether non-Swarm Compose honors them.

docker compose v5.5.0 honors deploy.resources in non-Swarm mode: pkg/compose/create.go getDeployResources() maps service-level MemLimit/MemReservation/CPUShares/CPUS(NanoCPUs)/PidsLimit onto container.Resources, then setLimits() maps deploy.resources.limits.memory→Memory, limits.cpus→NanoCPUs, limits.pids→PidsLimit, and setReservations() maps reservations.memory→MemoryReservation and reservations.devices→DeviceRequests; code comment: "Cpu reservation is a swarm option and PIDs is only a limit" (reservations.cpus is ignored).

Compose service attributes: `cpus` "define the number of (potentially virtual) CPUs to allocate to service containers. This is a fractional number. 0.000 means no limit" and "When both are set, cpus must be consistent with the cpus attribute in the Deploy Specification"; `mem_limit` "configures a limit on the amount of memory a container can allocate" and must be consistent with deploy limits.memory; `mem_reservation` = memory reservation; `cpu_shares` = "relative CPU weight versus other containers"; `pids_limit` (-1 unlimited); `shm_size` configures /dev/shm size.

Compose `healthcheck` fields: test (string or list, e.g. ["CMD", ...]), interval, timeout, retries, start_period, start_interval (durations); example interval 1m30s / timeout 10s / retries 3 / start_period 40s / start_interval 5s. `depends_on` long syntax supports `condition: service_healthy` ("Compose guarantees dependency services marked with service_healthy are 'healthy' before starting a dependent service"), `service_started`, and `restart: true` (restart dependent after dependency updates); `restart` policies: no, always, on-failure[:max-retries], unless-stopped.

Compose `volumes`: short syntax VOLUME:CONTAINER_PATH[:ACCESS_MODE]; long syntax fields type (volume|bind|tmpfs|image|npipe|cluster), source (host path for bind), target, read_only, bind.propagation, bind.create_host_path ("Creates a directory at the source path on host if there is nothing present. Defaults to true"), bind.selinux; relative host paths resolve from the Compose file's parent directory and are only supported for local container runtimes.

Compose project names isolate environments; precedence (highest first): -p flag, COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME env, top-level `name:` attribute, base name of the project directory, base name of cwd; names must be lowercase letters/digits/dashes/underscores starting with a letter or digit. Top-level `version` is obsolete ("only informative and you'll receive a warning message that it is obsolete if used"); Compose always validates with the most recent schema.

postgres official image: POSTGRES_PASSWORD "is required for you to use the PostgreSQL image. It must not be empty or undefined"; for PostgreSQL 18+ PGDATA is version-specific ("For 18 it is /var/lib/postgresql/18/docker") and the declared VOLUME moved to /var/lib/postgresql — "Mounts and volumes should be targeted at the updated location"; for 17 and below "Mount the data volume at /var/lib/postgresql/data and not at /var/lib/postgresql because mounts at the latter path WILL NOT PERSIST database data when the container is re-created". Docker-specific env vars only take effect when the data directory is empty.

postgres official image: "the default /dev/shm size for containers is 64MB. If the shared memory is exhausted you will encounter ERROR: could not resize shared memory segment … No space left on device. You will want to pass --shm-size=256MB for example to docker run, or alternatively in docker compose"; the README's own compose example sets `shm_size: 128mb` (or a tmpfs mount at /dev/shm for swarm).

postgres official image: *.sql, *.sql.gz, *.sh under /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d run after initdb, in sorted name order, as the postgres user; "scripts in /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d are only run if you start the container with a data directory that is empty; any pre-existing database will be left untouched"; if a script fails and the orchestrator restarts the container with the already-initialized data dir, it will not continue with your scripts.

Current postgres official image tags include 18.6, 18, latest, 18.6-trixie, 18-trixie; 18.6-bookworm; 18.6-alpine3.24 / 18-alpine / alpine; 17.11, 17, 17.11-trixie, 17.11-bookworm, 17.11-alpine; plus 19beta3 variants.

PostgreSQL versioning policy: a major version is supported for 5 years after initial release. PG 18 first release 2025-09-25, final release 2030-11-14 (current minor 18.6); PG 17: 2024-09-26 → 2029-11-08 (17.11); PG 16: 2023-09-14 → 2028-11-09 (16.15).

pg_isready "returns 0 to the shell if the server is accepting connections normally, 1 if the server is rejecting connections (for example during startup), 2 if there was no response to the connection attempt, and 3 if no attempt was made"; -d dbname / -h host / -U username; "It is not necessary to supply correct user name, password, or database name values to obtain the server status; however, if incorrect values are provided, the server will log a failed connection attempt."

postgres official image supports arbitrary --user: "postgres doesn't care what UID it runs as (as long as the owner of PGDATA matches), but initdb does care (and needs the user to exist in /etc/passwd)"; documented workarounds include bind-mounting /etc/passwd read-only (--user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v /etc/passwd:/etc/passwd:ro) or pre-chowning the volume to the UID.

Docker resource constraints: --memory minimum allowed value is 6m; --cpus caps CPU (e.g. --cpus="1.5" on a 2-CPU host = at most one and a half CPUs); --cpu-shares default 1024 is a relative weight that "is only enforced when CPU cycles are constrained" (a soft limit); "When you use these settings, Docker modifies the settings for the container's cgroup on the host machine."

SELECT locking clause: "With SKIP LOCKED, any selected rows that cannot be immediately locked are skipped. Skipping locked rows provides an inconsistent view of the data, so this is not suitable for general purpose work, but can be used to avoid lock contention with multiple consumers accessing a queue-like table." Grammar: FOR lock_strength [OF from_reference…] [NOWAIT | SKIP LOCKED], lock_strength ∈ UPDATE | NO KEY UPDATE | SHARE | KEY SHARE; NOWAIT errors instead of waiting.
SELECT locking clause with LIMIT: "If a LIMIT is used, locking stops once enough rows have been returned to satisfy the limit (but note that rows skipped over by OFFSET will get locked)."
SKIP LOCKED was added in PostgreSQL 9.5: release note "Add SELECT option SKIP LOCKED to skip locked rows (Thomas Munro). This does not throw an error for locked rows like NOWAIT does."

NOTIFY: payload "In the default configuration it must be shorter than 8000 bytes. (If binary data or large amounts of information need to be communicated, it's best to put it in a database table and send the key of the record.)"; "if a NOTIFY is executed inside a transaction, the notify events are not delivered until and unless the transaction is committed"; recommended technique is to put the NOTIFY in a statement trigger on the table so notification happens automatically.

Advisory locks are application-defined locks the system does not enforce; session-level locks persist until released or session end and ignore transaction semantics, transaction-level locks auto-release at transaction end. pg_try_advisory_lock/pg_try_advisory_xact_lock return true/false without waiting; keys are one 64-bit or two 32-bit values. Warning: with ORDER BY/LIMIT, `SELECT pg_advisory_lock(id) FROM foo WHERE id > 12345 LIMIT 100; -- danger!` because LIMIT is not guaranteed to apply before the lock function runs.

Partial index: "an index built over a subset of a table; the subset is defined by a conditional expression (called the predicate)"; Example 11.2 indexes only unbilled orders (`CREATE INDEX orders_unbilled_index ON orders (order_nr) WHERE billed is not true;`) because they are a small fraction yet the most-accessed rows — the canonical pattern for indexing only queued jobs.

INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE "guarantees an atomic INSERT or UPDATE outcome … even under high concurrency. This is also known as UPSERT"; for DO UPDATE a conflict_target must be provided; SET/WHERE can reference the existing row by table name and the proposed row via the special `excluded` table (e.g. `ON CONFLICT (did) DO UPDATE SET dname = EXCLUDED.dname`).

CURRENT_TIMESTAMP / now() / transaction_timestamp() "return the start time of the current transaction, their values do not change during the transaction"; statement_timestamp() returns the start of the current statement; "clock_timestamp() returns the actual current time, and therefore its value changes even within a single SQL statement."

"All timezone-aware dates and times are stored internally in UTC" (timestamp with time zone / timestamptz, a PostgreSQL abbreviation); bare `timestamp` is `timestamp without time zone` per the SQL standard, and for that type "PostgreSQL will silently ignore any time zone indication"; docs recommend date/time types containing both date and time when using time zones.

Kubernetes node heartbeats: two forms — updates to Node .status and Lease objects in kube-node-lease (Leases are lightweight, reducing load in large clusters). Defaults: kubelet updates .status on change or every 5 minutes ("much longer than the 40 second default timeout for unreachable nodes"); kubelet creates/updates its Lease every 10 seconds, retrying on failure with exponential backoff from 200 ms capped at 7 s; the node controller checks each node every 5 seconds (--node-monitor-period), sets Ready=Unknown when unreachable, and by default waits 5 minutes after Unknown before the first eviction.

Kubernetes Lease API: "every kubelet heartbeat is an update request to this Lease object, updating the spec.renewTime field for the Lease. The Kubernetes control plane uses the time stamp of this field to determine the availability of this Node."

Hadoop YARN Fair Scheduler: "Fair scheduling is a method of assigning resources to applications such that all apps get, on average, an equal share of resources over time… When there is a single app running, that app uses the entire cluster. When other apps are submitted, resources that free up are assigned to the new apps, so that each app eventually gets roughly the same amount of resources"; "this lets short apps finish in reasonable time while not starving long-lived apps"; priorities act as weights; optional guaranteed minimum shares, with excess split among other running apps.

Linux cgroup v2 resource-distribution models: Weights — "A parent's resource is distributed by adding up the weights of all active children and giving each the fraction matching the ratio of its weight against the sum", work-conserving ("only children which can make use of the resource at the moment participate"), range [1, 10000], default 100; Limits — "A child can only consume up to the configured amount of the resource. Limits can be over-committed". cpu.weight default "100"; cpu.max default "max 100000" ($MAX $PERIOD).

Dominant Resource Fairness (Ghodsi, Zaharia, Hindman, Konwinski, Shenker, Stoica; NSDI 2011): "a large number of algorithms have been proposed to implement (weighted) max-min fairness with various degrees of accuracy, such as round-robin, proportional resource sharing, and weighted fair queueing"; DRF is "a generalization of max-min fairness to multiple resource types" that "seeks to maximize the minimum dominant share across all users", is sharing-incentivizing, strategy-proof, envy-free and Pareto efficient, and "In the single resource case, DRF reduces to max-min fairness for that resource."

Kubernetes API Priority and Fairness: "Within a priority level, a fair-queuing algorithm prevents requests from different flows from starving each other"; each request is assigned to a flow by FlowSchema plus a flow distinguisher ("either the requesting user, the target resource's namespace, or nothing") and "the system attempts to give approximately equal weight to requests in different flows of the same priority level"; shuffle sharding insulates low-intensity flows from high-intensity ones.

Tailscale Serve identity headers: Tailscale-User-Login ("the requester's login name (for example, alice@example.com)"), Tailscale-User-Name (display name), Tailscale-User-Profile-Pic; "If Serve finds the following headers on an incoming request, it will remove them for security reasons, to avoid header spoofing"; headers are included only for tailnet traffic via Serve (Funnel traffic does not include them), "are not populated for traffic originating from tagged devices", ARE populated for external users who accepted a device share; "When you use the identity headers to authenticate to a backend service, it's best practice to only have the service listen on localhost." Example: `tailscale serve 3000` proxies to http://127.0.0.1:3000; flags --bg, --http=<port>, --https=<port> (default), --tcp=<port>, --set-path, --yes; HTTPS uses an automatically provisioned TLS certificate.
facts.version: KB as of 2026-08-22; CLI flags at https://tailscale.com/kb/1242/tailscale-serve

facts.statement: Tailscale CLI `tailscale whois ip[:port]` — "Get the machine and user associated with a Tailscale IP"; `--json` outputs JSON and must precede the address; output sections Machine (Name = machine name, ID, Addresses, AllowedIPs, Tags for tagged devices), User (Name = "the email address for the owner of the device", ID), Capabilities.

Tailscale LocalAPI: client/local.Client.WhoIs (comment: "API maturity: this is considered a stable API") issues GET /localapi/v0/whois?addr=<ip[:port]> and decodes apitype.WhoIsResponse{Node *tailcfg.Node, UserProfile *tailcfg.UserProfile, CapMap}; the handler (ipn/localapi serveWhoIsWithBackend) requires PermitRead (else 403 "whois access denied"), accepts addr as IP or IP:port (or nodekey:…), and returns 404 "no match for IP:port" when unknown.

On Linux tailscaled's unix socket is created world-accessible (safesocket socketPermissionsForOS returns 0666 when PlatformUsesPeerCreds, which is true for linux/darwin/freebsd/solaris/illumos; otherwise 0600) and ipnserver actor.Permissions grants read=true to any unix-socket client (`return true, !a.ci.IsReadonlyConn(operatorUID, …)`), so read-only LocalAPI calls such as whois/status work without root; write requires root or the configured operator user.

Userspace networking: "tailscaled functions as a SOCKS5 or HTTP proxy which other processes in the container can connect through", enabled by passing `--tun=userspace-networking` to tailscaled before `tailscale up`; the official Docker image has TS_USERSPACE "Enabled by default. This is equivalent to tailscaled --tun=userspace-networking", TS_SERVE_CONFIG "Accepts a JSON file to programmatically configure Tailscale Serve and Tailscale Funnel", TS_SOCKET "Defaults to /var/run/tailscale/tailscaled.sock".
facts.version: KB as of 2026-08-22; Docker params at https://tailscale.com/docs/features/containers/docker/docker-params

facts.statement: In userspace mode tailscaled's netstack handles inbound traffic to the node's own Tailscale IPs (ProcessLocalIPs) and, for TCP to a Tailscale IP/port it does not itself serve, rewrites the dial target to the loopback address (`case isTailscaleIP: dialIP = ipv4Loopback`) and forwardTCP dials 127.0.0.1:<port> with a standard net.Dialer — i.e. the local backend receives a connection originated from the host's loopback, not from the peer's tailnet IP, so IP-based whois cannot identify the caller on a userspace-mode host.

Tailscale Serve (and therefore its identity headers) works while tailscaled runs with --tun=userspace-networking on a bare-metal Linux host (the hub). Implied by the official container image defaulting to userspace mode while exposing TS_SERVE_CONFIG, but not stated for non-container hosts in any KB page found.

PostgreSQL logging defaults: log_statement valid values none|ddl|mod|all, "The default is none"; log_min_duration_statement "-1 (the default) disables logging statement durations"; log_parameter_max_length "-1 (the default) allows bind parameters to be logged in full" (when statement logging is on); log_parameter_max_length_on_error "Zero (the default) disables including bind parameters in error messages"; log_connections default '' (disabled); log_disconnections default off; log_line_prefix default '%m [%p] '.

llama-server flags: `--log-prompts-dir PATH` "Log prompts to directory … only used for debugging, default: disabled"; `--slots, --no-slots` "expose slots monitoring endpoint (default: enabled)" (GET /slots returns per-slot processing state incl. sampling parameters); `--metrics` Prometheus endpoint "(default: disabled)"; `--log-disable`, `--log-file FNAME`, `--log-verbosity N` (default 3 = info).

recommendations: Postgres compose project: its own directory with top-level `name: corvid-db` (no `version:`), image pinned to a full tag (`postgres:18.6-trixie`, or `18.6-alpine` if size matters), bind mount `/srv/corvid/pg:/var/lib/postgresql` (18+ location; NOT /var/lib/postgresql/data), `shm_size: 256mb`, `restart: unless-stopped`, POSTGRES_PASSWORD via env file kept out of git. Cite R06-F6, F7, F8, F10.

Resource caps for the DB container: use `deploy.resources.limits: {cpus: '1.0', memory: 1g, pids: 200}` plus `deploy.resources.reservations.memory` — verified to be honored by docker compose v5.5.0 (R06-F2); never set deploy `reservations.cpus` (swarm-only). Keep `mem_limit`/`cpus` out to avoid the must-be-consistent rule (R06-F3). Tune the cap after measuring; a GTX-970-era hub should protect llama-server's RAM.

Healthcheck: `test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U $POSTGRES_USER -d $POSTGRES_DB"]`, interval 10s, timeout 5s, retries 5, start_period 30s; coordinator uses `depends_on: db: {condition: service_healthy}` if in the same project, or its own readiness loop if in a separate project. Pass real -U/-d so health probes don't spam failed-auth log lines (R06-F4, F12).

Schema migrations as /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/*.sql only for the very first boot; everything after via `db/` migrations applied by the coordinator (initdb.d never re-runs and a failed script leaves a half-initialized dir) (R06-F9).

Network exposure: do NOT publish 5432 at all if the coordinator shares the Docker network; if it must be published, bind to the hub's tailnet IP only (`100.x.y.z:5432:5432`), never 0.0.0.0 — matches CLAUDE.md §5.6.

Queue claim query (one statement, no advisory locks): `UPDATE job SET state='running', claimed_by=$node, claimed_at=clock_timestamp(), lease_until=clock_timestamp()+interval '2 minutes' WHERE id = (SELECT id FROM job WHERE state='queued' AND (run_after IS NULL OR run_after<=now()) ORDER BY priority DESC, created_at FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1) RETURNING *;` with partial index `CREATE INDEX job_queued_idx ON job (priority DESC, created_at) WHERE state='queued';` (R06-F15, F16, F20). Avoid OFFSET in claim queries (F16).

Wake-up without busy-polling: statement trigger `AFTER INSERT ON job … NOTIFY job_queued` with empty/key-only payload; workers LISTEN and also poll every ~5 s as a backstop (payload <8000 B, delivered only on commit) (R06-F18).

Lease/heartbeat for running jobs: `lease_until timestamptz` renewed by the executing agent; a reaper loop re-queues rows whose lease expired (`state='running' AND lease_until < now()`), bumping `attempt`. Use clock_timestamp() or client-side timestamps inside long transactions since now() is frozen at transaction start (R06-F22).

Roster schema: `node(node_id text PK, owner_login text, os text, arch text, caps jsonb, last_seen timestamptz, agent_version text, …)` written via `INSERT … ON CONFLICT (node_id) DO UPDATE SET last_seen=EXCLUDED.last_seen, caps=EXCLUDED.caps` (R06-F21); heartbeat every 10 s, node considered 'unreachable' after 40 s without a heartbeat, derived at read time (`CASE WHEN last_seen > now()-interval '40 seconds'`), never stored — mirrors Kubernetes Lease defaults (R06-F24, F25). Keep a separate append-only `heartbeat_log`/`job_run` table for the thank-you board, not the live row.
All time columns `timestamptz`, never bare `timestamp` (R06-F23).

Fair share with no quotas: at claim time pick the next job from the member with the fewest currently-running jobs (tie → oldest), i.e. per-member round-robin = max-min fairness; one member alone gets the whole pool, and a flood from one member cannot starve others (R06-F26, F28, F29). Put the same rule in front of llama-server (per-member FIFO lanes, round-robin dispatch into `--parallel` slots). Inside a host, express the co-op's share as weights (`cpu_shares`/cgroup cpu.weight) and reserve hard limits (`cpus`/cpu.max, `mem_limit`) for the OWNER's politeness caps (R06-F14, F27) — weights share, limits cap.

Identity for the API on the hub: coordinator listens on 127.0.0.1 only; expose it with `tailscale serve --bg <port>`; trust `Tailscale-User-Login` as the caller identity (Serve strips spoofed copies; only tailnet traffic gets headers); reject requests without the header (R06-F30). Do not rely on whois-by-source-IP on solarplexus: userspace netstack hands the backend a loopback connection (R06-F35). Keep `tailscale whois` / LocalAPI `/localapi/v0/whois` for kernel-mode nodes and for the agent's own CLI (R06-F31–F33).
Member devices must NOT be tagged (tags suppress identity headers); agents authenticate as the owner's login via the same headers, plus a `node_id` they generate locally (R06-F30).

Log policy: set `log_statement=none`, `log_min_duration_statement=-1`, `log_connections=''`, `log_disconnections=off` explicitly in the compose `command:` so defaults can't drift (R06-F37). Store only metadata in Postgres (who, which node, model name, token counts, durations, exit status); never prompt/completion text or job stdout. llama-server: `--no-slots`, never `--log-prompts-dir`, `--metrics` allowed (aggregate) (R06-F38). Write this as the docs/ 'what we log' page members read.

Credit rows to add to CLAUDE.md §4 in the same commit as the code: PostgreSQL (PostgreSQL License), postgres Docker Official Image (MIT Dockerfiles), Docker Compose (Apache-2.0), psycopg 3 (LGPL-3.0 — dynamic import from Python is fine), and note Tailscale Serve/whois usage under the existing Tailscale row; idea-credits for Hadoop Fair Scheduler, DRF, and Kubernetes leases.
Pin Postgres 18 (supported to 2030-11) unless the hub's Docker/kernel is old; plan `pg_upgrade --link` using the new /var/lib/postgresql layout (R06-F7, F11).
open_questions: Does `tailscale serve` (with identity headers) work on solarplexus while tailscaled runs in --tun=userspace-networking? Implied by the container image defaults (R06-F36) but unverified on bare metal — needs a 10-minute spike before the API design is frozen.

Same compose project or two? Putting coordinator + Postgres in one project gives `depends_on: service_healthy` for free; separate projects (as asked) need a named external network or a tailnet-bound port. Decide in the coordinator ADR.
Postgres major: 18 vs 17 on the hub — does the hub's Docker version/kernel support the 18 image cleanly, and who owns the bind-mount dir (uid 999 vs arbitrary --user)?

Agent identity: member-login headers (no tags) vs tagged machines with a shared secret — tags remove identity headers (R06-F30); what should the roster key on when one member owns several machines (node_id + owner_login?).

Fair-share granularity for inference: per request at the coordinator vs per token inside llama-server slots; does llama-server's own slot queue already behave acceptably at 6 users (measure before building).
Retention for the metadata-only logs: how long do job_run / heartbeat_log rows live, and is the contribution board fed from them or from a rollup table?
Do we want LISTEN/NOTIFY at all in v1, or is 5-second polling by ≤20 agents simply fine? (Probably fine; NOTIFY is an optimization.)
Ready-made Python queue libs on SKIP LOCKED exist; hand-rolled is ~30 lines. Confirm §7 non-goal reading: hand-roll here is acceptable because no scheduler is being invented.

Where does `tailscale whois` matter then? Kernel-mode nodes (laptops) can use source-IP whois for their local agent UI; confirm whether any API is served from a kernel-mode node or everything fronts through the hub.

verdicts.reason: Fetched https://docs.docker.com/reference/compose-file/deploy/ and the primary spec file https://raw.githubusercontent.com/compose-spec/compose-spec/bd6ccc6/deploy.md (also current main; bd6ccc6 dated 2026-07-21). Both confirm: resources has `limits` and `reservations`; reservations text is verbatim "The platform must guarantee the container can allocate at least the configured amount."; `cpus` = "as number of cores", `memory` = "a string expressing a byte value", `pids` = "set as an integer"; the example uses limits cpus '0.50', memory 50M, pids 1 and reservations cpus '0.25', memory 20M. Neither page body mentions Swarm or whether non-Swarm Compose honors/ignores these (only the note "Deploy is an optional part of the Compose Specification"); the only "swarm" strings on docs.docker.com are sidebar nav links to docker swarm CLI pages. Minor wording note, not a refutation: the `limits` quote "The platform must prevent the container to allocate more" matches compose-spec bd6ccc6/main exactly, whereas docs.docker.com's rendering is copyedited to "The platform must prevent the container from allocating more resources." Same meaning; claim stands for the stated version.

Fetched raw pkg/compose/create.go at tag v5.5.0 (github blob URL returns 200; raw file 1575 lines). Every element of the claim is verbatim in the source: getDeployResources() (line 707) is called from the container create path (line 364) and builds container.Resources with Memory: int64(s.MemLimit), MemoryReservation: int64(s.MemReservation), CPUShares: s.CPUShares, NanoCPUs: int64(s.CPUS * 1e9), and PidsLimit = &s.PidsLimit when non-zero (lines 715-734); when s.Deploy != nil it calls setLimits and setReservations (lines 738-741). setLimits (line 821) maps limits.MemoryBytes→Memory, limits.NanoCPUs*1e9→NanoCPUs, limits.Pids (>0)→PidsLimit. setReservations (line 800) maps reservations.MemoryBytes→MemoryReservation and reservations.Devices→DeviceRequests, and contains the exact comment "// Cpu reservation is a swarm option and PIDs is only a limit" (line 804); reservations.NanoCPUs is never read, so reservations.cpus is indeed ignored. GitHub releases API confirms v5.5.0 published_at 2026-08-17T10:01:05Z. Source is primary (official docker/compose repo at the pinned tag). Minor immaterial nits only: the Go struct field names are MemoryBytes/NanoCPUs/Pids (the claim uses the YAML keys memory/cpus/pids), and the pids limit guard is `> 0` rather than `!= 0`.

Fetched both the cited page (docs.docker.com/reference/compose-file/services/) and the underlying primary text (compose-spec/compose-spec 05-services.md at bd6ccc6, which is the current HEAD of main as of 2026-08-22; commit dated 2026-07-21). Every quoted fragment matches verbatim: cpus — "define the number of (potentially virtual) CPUs to allocate to service containers. This is a fractional number. `0.000` means no limit." and "When both are set, `cpus` must be consistent with the `cpus` attribute in the Deploy Specification"; mem_limit — "configures a limit on the amount of memory a container can allocate" and "When both are set, `mem_limit` must be consistent with the `limits.memory` attribute in the Deploy Specification"; mem_reservation — "configures a reservation on the amount of memory a container can allocate" (consistent with `reservations.memory`); cpu_shares — "defines, as integer value, a service container's relative CPU weight versus other containers"; pids_limit — "tunes a container's PIDs limit. Set to -1 for unlimited PIDs."; shm_size — "configures the size of the shared memory (`/dev/shm` partition on Linux) allowed by the service container." The Docker docs page is the official rendering of the Compose Specification and the pinned spec commit agrees; the claim is accurate and current for the stated version.

Fetched https://docs.docker.com/reference/compose-file/services/ (raw HTML, 2026-08-22) and verified every element verbatim. healthcheck: "test ... can be either a string or a list. If it's a list, the first item must be either NONE, CMD or CMD-SHELL"; example block is exactly test: ["CMD","curl","-f","http://localhost"], interval: 1m30s, timeout: 10s, retries: 3, start_period: 40s, start_interval: 5s; "interval, timeout, start_period, and start_interval are specified as durations" (retries is an integer count, which the claim's own example "retries 3" reflects — the trailing "(durations)" parenthetical is slightly loose but not wrong as exemplified). depends_on long syntax: conditions service_started, service_healthy ("Specifies that a dependency is expected to be 'healthy' (as indicated by healthcheck) before starting a dependent service"), plus the exact sentence "Compose guarantees dependency services marked with service_healthy are 'healthy' before starting a dependent service"; restart: "When set to true Compose restarts this service after it updates the dependency service" (Compose 2.17.0+). restart policies listed exactly as no / always / on-failure[:max-retries] / unless-stopped. Source is the primary Compose Spec reference on docs.docker.com and is current. Minor omissions (service_completed_successfully, required, start_interval requiring Compose 2.20.2) do not contradict the claim as stated.

Fetched https://docs.docker.com/reference/compose-file/services/ (HTTP 200, 2026-08-22) and extracted the `volumes` attribute section. Every element of the claim is supported verbatim or near-verbatim: short syntax "(VOLUME:CONTAINER_PATH), or an access mode (VOLUME:CONTAINER_PATH:ACCESS_MODE)"; long syntax "type: The mount type. Either volume, bind, tmpfs, image, npipe, or cluster"; "source: ... a path on the host for a bind mount ..."; "target"; "read_only"; "bind: ... propagation ... create_host_path: Creates a directory at the source path on host if there is nothing present. Defaults to true. ... selinux: The SELinux re-labeling option z (shared) or Z (private)"; and the note "Relative host paths are only supported by Compose that deploy to a local container runtime. This is because the relative path is resolved from the Compose file's parent directory which is only applicable in the local case." The page is the official docs.docker.com rendering of the Compose Specification (primary for the stated version) and is current (it references Compose 2.35.0 features). The claim omits other long-syntax sub-options (volume.nocopy/subpath, tmpfs.size/mode, image.subpath, consistency) and the short-syntax z/Z access modes, but it does not assert exhaustiveness, so nothing is contradicted.

Fetched both cited pages (raw HTML via curl plus WebFetch) on 2026-08-22. docs.docker.com/compose/how-tos/project-name/ states verbatim: "Compose uses a project name to isolate environments from each other"; precedence "from highest to lowest" is: the -p command line flag; the COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME environment variable; the top-level name: attribute in your Compose file; the base name of the project directory containing your Compose file; the base name of the current directory if no Compose file is specified; and "Project names must contain only lowercase letters, decimal digits, dashes, and underscores, and must begin with a lowercase letter or decimal digit." docs.docker.com/reference/compose-file/version-and-name/ states verbatim: the top-level version property "is only informative and you'll receive a warning message that it is obsolete if used. Compose always uses the most recent schema to validate the Compose file, regardless of the version field." Every element of the claim matches current official Docker documentation (primary source). Minor note only: the claim's "starting with a letter or digit" omits the word "lowercase," but since names are restricted to lowercase letters anyway this is not a material discrepancy.

verdicts.corrected_statement: The postgres official image supports running as a "(mostly) arbitrary user" via --user (docker-library/postgres#253; Alpine since #1018). Caveat: "postgres doesn't care what UID it runs as (as long as the owner of PGDATA matches), but initdb *does* care (and needs the user to exist in /etc/passwd)". The docs list three workarounds: (1) let the image use nss_wrapper to fake /etc/passwd (docker-library/postgres#448; Debian variants install libnss-wrapper and the entrypoint applies it automatically when the UID is not in /etc/passwd); (2) bind-mount /etc/passwd read-only from the host: --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v /etc/passwd:/etc/passwd:ro; (3) initialize the data directory separately from the final runtime with a chown in between -- run once as the default postgres user to initdb, stop, `chown -R UID:GID` the initialized volume, then run with --user UID:GID.

# R07 — Status page & identity

- **Depth:** full
- **Written:** 2026-08-22 by research agent (Fable) · **Verified:** 2026-08-22 (adversarial pass: pending)
- **Feeds:** Phase 2 spec (status page v0 at `:8092`, identity dependency of the coordinator API), ADR-0003 (Caddy front door), ADR-0002 (tags vs identity), S-05 (serve headers), R06 (heartbeat interval → node-down threshold)

## Purpose

Decide (a) Grafana vs a simple server-rendered page for the Phase 2 "live map of the co-op"; (b) how a member's Tailscale identity reaches CORVID web apps behind Caddy on the hub — and what changes when the hub's tailscaled runs in userspace mode, as solarplexus does today; (c) Caddy basics (`reverse_proxy`, `handle_path`, `bind`, `forward_auth`, `log`, config location) and licences; (d) what the live map must show per ADR-0001 and the Phase 2 acceptance numbers.

## Headline findings (the plan writer should read these first)

1. **Grafana is AGPL-3.0-only at v13.2.0** (with Apache-2.0 sub-packages); Grafana Labs' own Enterprise image is *proprietary* though "free". OSS Grafana has every panel the map needs (Stat, Gauge, Table, State timeline, Status history, Node graph, Canvas) and a built-in PostgreSQL data source — but it brings a second identity system (`[auth.proxy]`/anonymous), phone-home defaults (`reporting_enabled`, `check_for_updates` both true), binds `0.0.0.0` by default, and cannot guarantee "thanks, never ranks" (any table can be sorted). **Recommendation: status page v0 = a small server-rendered page** (FastAPI + Jinja2, optional htmx polling) reading Postgres; Grafana is a Phase 4 option for history/thank-you board if wanted.
2. **Identity, two mechanisms, both verified at tailscale v1.102.3 source:** `tailscale serve` injects `Tailscale-User-Login`, `Tailscale-User-Name`, `Tailscale-User-Profile-Pic` into proxied requests and *deletes* any incoming header of the same name (anti-spoof); headers are **not set for traffic from tagged nodes** and not set for Funnel. `tailscale whois ip[:port]` (CLI or LocalAPI `/localapi/v0/whois?addr=`) resolves a connecting address to node + user; on Linux any local user can call it (read-only LocalAPI over the 0666 unix socket `/var/run/tailscale/tailscaled.sock`).
3. **Userspace mode changes the wiring (matters today on solarplexus):** an inbound tailnet TCP connection to the node's own 100.x IP is rewritten by tailscaled's netstack to a dial of `127.0.0.1:<port>` on the host, and tailscaled registers that loopback `ip:srcport` → peer mapping so `whois 127.0.0.1:<srcport>` still resolves the peer. Consequences: services must listen on loopback (binding the tailnet IP is impossible — there is no `tailscale0`), they see `127.0.0.1` as the client, and whois must be called with **ip:port** (exactly what `tailscale nginx-auth` and Caddy's documented `forward_auth` Tailscale example pass via `Remote-Addr`/`Remote-Port`). In kernel mode (planned for solarplexus, finding 10) the app sees the real 100.x source and may bind the tailnet IP.
4. **Caddy is Apache-2.0 at v2.11.4.** `reverse_proxy` passes `Host` through and sets `X-Forwarded-For/Proto/Host` (ignoring incoming ones unless `trusted_proxies`); `header_up -Name` deletes a request header; `handle_path /x/*` = `handle` + `uri strip_prefix`; `bind <ip>` pins the listener; `forward_auth` grants on 2xx and `copy_headers A>B` renames identity headers for the app — Caddy's docs ship a Tailscale example for exactly this; `*.ts.net` certs come from local tailscaled (needs the tailnet HTTPS feature and `TS_PERMIT_CERT_UID=caddy`). Access logs redact Cookie/Authorization by default. Linux package: `/etc/caddy/Caddyfile`, `systemctl reload caddy`, admin API `localhost:2019` (the hub already listens on 2019 — R00-F7). `import conf.d/*` lets CORVID drop in its own route file.
5. **ADR-0002's `tag:member`** on machines members *also browse from* would strip serve identity headers and make whois return tags instead of a user. Tag only servers; keep members' consuming devices user-owned.
6. **HTTPS on the tailnet publishes `solarplexus.tail2990fc.ts.net`-style names to public CT logs** (Tailscale's own warning). `tailscale serve` has a `--http=<port>` flag (serve only, not funnel) and the HTTPS-feature prompt is only triggered for the HTTPS serve type (source), so plain-HTTP serve with identity headers is plausible — **S-05 must confirm at runtime**.

facts.statement: Grafana Labs' licensing page: 'On April 20, 2021, Grafana Labs announced that going forward, our core open source projects will be moving from the Apache License v2.0 to AGPLv3.' Grafana, Loki and Tempo are AGPLv3; those who modify and offer it as a service and do not want AGPL obligations 'can contact us to secure a commercial license'; a non-AGPL, proprietary-licensed Enterprise binary is available free, with paid licence keys unlocking enterprise features.

Grafana docs: 'Grafana Enterprise is a commercial edition of Grafana that includes additional features not found in the open source version.' Enterprise-only features listed: role-based access control, data source permissions, data source query/resource caching, reporting and PDF export, custom branding, usage insights, recorded queries, Vault integration, auditing, request security, settings updates at runtime, team sync, enhanced LDAP, SAML, protected roles, premium data source plugins (40+). None of these is needed for a friends-scale status page.

Grafana Docker docs: images are `grafana/grafana` (Open Source) and `grafana/grafana-enterprise`; 'The recommended and default edition of Grafana is Grafana Enterprise. It is free and includes all the features of the OSS edition.' Caution: 'Starting with Grafana release 12.4.0, the grafana/grafana-oss Docker Hub repository will no longer be updated… use the grafana/grafana Docker Hub repository.' Default port 3000; persistent data at /var/lib/grafana; any config key can be set via env `GF_<SectionName>_<KeyName>`.
facts.version: docs 'latest' as of 2026-08-22 (note applies from Grafana 12.4.0)

facts.statement: Grafana 'ships with the PostgreSQL data source out of the box' (PostgreSQL 9.0 and newer). Configure page warning: 'the database user you specify should have only SELECT permissions on the relevant schemas and tables. Grafana does not validate the safety of queries, so users could run potentially harmful SQL (for example, DROP TABLE). Create a dedicated PostgreSQL user with restricted permissions.' TLS modes: disable / require / verify-ca / verify-full.

Grafana OSS visualizations relevant to a node map, none marked enterprise-only or beta on the index page: State timeline ('for state changes over time'), Status history ('for periodic state over time'), Stat ('for big stats and optional sparkline'), Gauge ('how far a single metric is from a threshold'), Table, Geomap, Node graph ('for directed graphs or networks'), Canvas ('explicitly place elements within static and dynamic layouts').

Grafana thresholds: 'A threshold is a value or limit you set for a metric that's reflected visually when it's met or exceeded'; modes Absolute ('defined by a number') or Percentage ('relative to minimum or maximum'); defaults Base=green, 80=red, Mode=Absolute; supported by Bar chart, Bar gauge, Candlestick, Canvas, Gauge, Geomap, Histogram, Stat, State timeline, Status history, Table, Time series, Trend — i.e. ADR-0001's 'distance to next product threshold' maps directly onto Stat/Gauge/Bar gauge thresholds.

Grafana config defaults that a tailnet-only, no-logging deployment must override: [dashboards] min_refresh_interval default 5 seconds ('prevents users from setting the dashboard refresh interval to a lower value'); [server] http_addr empty 'is equivalent to setting the value to 0.0.0.0, which means the Grafana service binds to all interfaces' (set it to the tailnet IP or 127.0.0.1 per CLAUDE.md §5.6); http_port default 3000; [analytics] reporting_enabled default true ('Grafana sends anonymous usage statistics to stats.grafana.org'); check_for_updates default true; [auth] disable_login_form default false; [security] cookie_secure default false.

Grafana anonymous access: [auth.anonymous] keys enabled, org_name ('Organization name that should be used for unauthenticated users'), org_role (Viewer by default; 'other valid values are Editor and Admin'), hide_version, device_limit ('Limits the number of anonymous devices in your instance'). In Grafana Enterprise 'anonymous access is licensed as active users' (1 user per 3 devices) — irrelevant for the OSS build.

Grafana auth proxy: [auth.proxy] enabled=true, header_name = X-WEBAUTH-USER, header_property = username|email, auto_sign_up = true (creates users on first sight), sync_ttl = 15, whitelist = (list of proxy IPs; 'This can be used to prevent users spoofing the X-WEBAUTH-USER header'), headers = Name:X-WEBAUTH-NAME Email:X-WEBAUTH-EMAIL, enable_login_token = false. This is how a Tailscale identity header (mapped by Caddy header_up) becomes a Grafana login with zero passwords.

Grafana provisioning: data sources and dashboards are provisioned from YAML under the provisioning directory (conf/provisioning, or /etc/grafana/provisioning on deb/rpm); 'each configuration file contains a list of data sources, under the datasources key'; dashboard providers point at a folder of JSON dashboards; updateIntervalSeconds ≤10 makes Grafana watch the filesystem; allowUiUpdates controls whether UI edits persist (provisioned files win on reload). Enables dashboards-as-code in the CORVID repo.
Caddy's LICENSE at tag v2.11.4 is the Apache License, Version 2.0; v2.11.4 was published 2026-06-03.

Caddy reverse_proxy: syntax `reverse_proxy [<matcher>] [<upstreams...>] { … }`; by default passes incoming headers including Host unmodified but sets/augments X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Proto, X-Forwarded-Host; 'For these X-Forwarded-* headers, by default, the proxy will ignore their values from incoming requests, to prevent spoofing' (trust via the `servers > trusted_proxies` global option); `header_up [+|-]<field> [<value|regexp> [<replacement>]]` / `header_down` modify proxied headers (`header_up -Some-Header` deletes); upstream forms include localhost:4000, http://localhost:4000, h2c://127.0.0.1, unix//var/php.sock; flush_interval controls streaming.

Caddy handle_path 'Works the same as the handle directive, but implicitly uses uri strip_prefix to strip the matched path prefix'; `handle_path /api/* { reverse_proxy localhost:9000 }` forwards with /api removed. Therefore ADR-0003's `/status` → `:8092` should use `handle_path /status/*` only if the status app is mounted at root, and `handle /status/*` if the app knows its own prefix.

Caddy forward_auth 'proxies a clone of the request to an authentication gateway'; 'If the upstream responds with a 2xx status code, then access is granted', otherwise the upstream's response is returned; `copy_headers` lists 'HTTP header fields to copy from the response to the original request' with `Before>After` renaming; it is sugar over reverse_proxy. Caddy's docs include a Tailscale example: `forward_auth unix//run/tailscale.nginx-auth.sock { uri /auth; header_up Remote-Addr {remote_host}; header_up Remote-Port {remote_port}; header_up Original-URI {uri}; copy_headers { Tailscale-User>X-Webauth-User Tailscale-Name>X-Webauth-Name Tailscale-Login>X-Webauth-Login Tailscale-Tailnet>X-Webauth-Tailnet Tailscale-Profile-Picture>X-Webauth-Profile-Picture } }`.

Caddy bind 'Overrides the interface to which the server's socket should bind'; `bind <hosts...>` (addresses, no port; e.g. `bind 10.0.0.1`, `bind 127.0.0.1 [::1]`); by default 'the listener binds to the empty (wildcard) interface'; 'Virtual hosts are not shared across different listeners'. This is the directive that satisfies CLAUDE.md §5.6 for Caddy (bind the tailnet IP in kernel mode; 127.0.0.1 in userspace mode — see R07-F26).

Caddy log directive 'Enables and configures HTTP request logging (also known as access logs)'; 'By default, headers with potentially sensitive information (Cookie, Set-Cookie, Authorization and Proxy-Authorization) will be logged as REDACTED' (disable via the log_credentials global option). The page documents no option to log request bodies.

Caddy automatic HTTPS for Tailscale: 'Domains ending in .ts.net will not be managed by Caddy. Instead, Caddy will automatically attempt to get these certificates at handshake-time from the locally-running Tailscale instance'; requires 'HTTPS is enabled in your Tailscale account' and Caddy running as root or tailscaled configured to let the caddy user fetch certs. Tailscale KB (validated 2026-01-05): 'Starting with the beta release of Caddy 2.5'; set `TS_PERMIT_CERT_UID=caddy` in /etc/default/tailscaled; a site block named `machine-name.domain-alias.ts.net` 'automatically enables HTTPS'.
facts.version: KB validated 2026-01-05; Caddy docs https://caddyserver.com/docs/automatic-https as of 2026-08-22

facts.statement: Tailscale HTTPS certificates KB (validated 2025-12-10): MagicDNS is a prerequisite; `tailscale cert` requests a Let's Encrypt certificate (90-day expiry, renewal is the user's job unless Caddy integrates); certificate names become part of public Certificate Transparency logs — 'Do not enable the HTTPS feature if any of your machine names contain sensitive information' (names are <machine>.<tailnet>.ts.net); frequent requests can hit Let's Encrypt rate limits ('waiting 34 hours').

Caddy Linux service: the systemd unit reads /etc/caddy/Caddyfile, runs as user/group caddy, config is applied with `sudo systemctl reload caddy`, which talks to the admin API at localhost:2019. The `import` directive 'includes a snippet or file' and accepts globs (`import sites-enabled/*`), works anywhere including inside site blocks — so CORVID can own a drop-in route file instead of editing the hub's existing Caddyfile.

Tailscale Serve KB (validated 2026-01-20): Serve adds `Tailscale-User-Login`, `Tailscale-User-Name`, `Tailscale-User-Profile-Pic` to proxied requests; 'These identity headers are not populated for traffic originating from tagged devices'; headers apply to tailnet traffic, not Funnel; 'Tailscale Serve requires you to enable HTTPS certificates in your tailnet.' The page does not mention a plain-HTTP (`--http`) mode.

tailscale v1.102.3 source, ipn/ipnlocal/serve.go `addTailscaleIdentityHeaders` (lines ~1078-1107): first DELETES any incoming `Tailscale-User-Login`, `Tailscale-User-Name`, `Tailscale-User-Profile-Pic`, `Tailscale-Funnel-Request`, `Tailscale-Headers-Info` ('Clear any incoming values squatting in the headers'); for Funnel sets `Tailscale-Funnel-Request: ?1` and returns; calls `b.WhoIs("tcp", srcAddr)`; returns without headers if the source is not a tailnet peer or `node.IsTagged()` ('Not setting identity headers for tagged nodes'); otherwise sets Login/Name (RFC 2047 Q-encoded if non-ASCII) and Profile-Pic plus `Tailscale-Headers-Info: https://tailscale.com/s/serve-headers`. `addProxyForwardedHeaders` sets X-Forwarded-Host, X-Forwarded-Proto (https only when TLS) and X-Forwarded-For = peer's tailnet IP. Both run in the ReverseProxy Rewrite hook for every serve web handler (line ~959-981), not only TLS ones.
facts.version: tailscale v1.102.3 (published 2026-08-20); hub runs 1.98.4 — re-check at upgrade

facts.statement: tailscale v1.102.3 CLI (cmd/tailscale/cli/serve_v2.go ~line 239-251): `tailscale serve` accepts `--bg`, `--set-path`, `--https=<port>` ('default mode'), and — for `serve` only, not `funnel` — `--http=<port>` ('Expose an HTTP server at the specified port'), plus `--tcp`, `--tls-terminated-tcp`, `--yes`. The interactive 'enable HTTPS certificates' flow (`enableFeatureInteractive(... CapabilityHTTPS)`) is invoked only when the serve type is HTTPS (lines ~461-473). Runtime confirmation that identity headers appear on a `--http` listener is S-05's job.

`tailscale whois [--json] [--proto tcp|udp] ip[:port]` 'shows the machine and user associated with a Tailscale IP (v4 or v6)' (cmd/tailscale/cli/whois.go; KB 1080 validated 2026-07-30: 'Get the machine and user associated with a Tailscale IP'). Output: Machine Name/ID/Addresses and, for untagged nodes, User Name (LoginName) and ID; for tagged nodes it prints Tags instead of a User. JSON form is apitype.WhoIsResponse {Node, UserProfile, CapMap}.

LocalAPI whois (ipn/localapi/localapi.go v1.102.3): route `whois` → `GET /localapi/v0/whois?addr=<ip | ip:port | nodekey>[&proto=tcp|udp]` over the tailscaled unix socket; requires a valid Host header ("local-tailscaled.sock" or empty; loopback only with password) and no Referer/Origin; needs PermitRead. ipn/ipnserver/server.go `actor.Permissions`: for a unix-socket connection `read = true` for every local client (write only for root/operator); safesocket: socket mode 0666 on peer-credential platforms (Linux); default path /var/run/tailscale/tailscaled.sock (paths.go). So an unprivileged coordinator process on Linux can call whois without sudo.
facts.version: tailscale v1.102.3; also ipn/ipnserver/server.go, safesocket/safesocket.go + unixsocket.go, paths/paths.go at the same tag

facts.statement: Userspace-networking inbound path (wgengine/netstack/netstack.go v1.102.3, acceptTCP/forwardTCP): for an inbound TCP connection whose destination is this node's own Tailscale IP, `case isTailscaleIP: dialIP = ipv4Loopback` — tailscaled dials `127.0.0.1:<port>` on the host with a standard net.Dialer and copies bytes; if the dial fails it logs 'could not connect to local backend server' and RSTs. After dialing it calls `ns.pm.RegisterIPPortIdentity("tcp", backendLocalIPPort, clientRemoteIP)` so the loopback (IP:ephemeral-port) of that forwarded connection maps to the peer. `LocalBackend.WhoIs` (ipn/ipnlocal/local.go) first looks the IP up as a node; if not found and a port is given it asks `ProxyMapper().WhoIsIPPort(proto, ipp)`. Consequences on a userspace-mode hub: listeners must be on 127.0.0.1 (or wildcard), the app sees 127.0.0.1 as client, and whois must be called with ip:port (client source port), as `tailscale nginx-auth` / Caddy's forward_auth example do via Remote-Addr + Remote-Port. Serve handlers are dispatched from the same netstack path (`ns.lb.TCPHandlerForDst`).
facts.version: tailscale v1.102.3 (netstack.go acceptTCP ~L1530-1738, forwardTCP ~L1743-1800; local.go WhoIs ~L1698-1738). solarplexus runs 1.98.4 in userspace mode (R00-F2)

facts.statement: Tailscale's userspace-networking KB (validated 2025-11-12) documents only the outbound side (`--tun=userspace-networking`; SOCKS5/HTTP proxy via ALL_PROXY/HTTP_PROXY); it says nothing about inbound connections or Serve. tailscale/caddy-tailscale (Apache-2.0; repo description 'A highly experimental exploration of integrating Tailscale and Caddy'; status badge experimental; no release tags; last push 2026-01-06) embeds a tsnet node in Caddy and offers a listener, proxy transport, and an auth provider. Its README says 'you don't necessarily need this plugin to use Caddy with Tailscale. With Tailscale installed on a machine, Caddy can already bind to the Tailscale network interface, proxy requests to other Tailnet nodes, get automatic certificates, and authenticate Tailscale users' (linking Caddy's forward_auth Tailscale example). Requires a custom xcaddy build. Not recommended for CORVID.
facts.version: main branch, last push 2026-01-06 (no tags); LICENSE at main

facts.statement: `tailscale nginx-auth` (cmd/nginx-auth in the tailscale repo, BSD-3-Clause, status experimental) answers an auth sub-request over a unix socket (/run/tailscale.nginx-auth.sock, systemd socket activation) given `Remote-Addr` and `Remote-Port` headers, and returns `Tailscale-User` (user@host form), `Tailscale-Login`, `Tailscale-Name`, `Tailscale-Profile-Picture`, `Tailscale-Tailnet` for the proxy to copy into X-Webauth-* headers. It is the reference design for 'whois-as-forward_auth'; whether Ubuntu packages it (tailscale-nginx-auth) was not verified.

facts.statement: Beszel v0.18.8 (MIT, 2026-08-17) is 'a lightweight server monitoring platform' with a PocketBase hub + per-host agent; metrics include CPU, memory, disk, disk I/O, network, load, temperature, fan, 'GPU usage / power draw - Nvidia, AMD, and Intel', battery, Docker/Podman containers, S.M.A.R.T.; multi-user with OAuth/OIDC and password auth that can be disabled; agent connects outbound to the hub (HUB_URL + TOKEN + KEY); hub default port 8090 (collides with ADR-0003's inference port if co-hosted). facts.statement: Gatus v5.36.0 (Apache-2.0, 2026-05-19) is 'a developer-oriented health dashboard' monitoring HTTP/ICMP/TCP/DNS with conditions (status, response time, body, cert expiry) and alerting; 'External Endpoints' 'are not monitored by Gatus, but they are instead pushed programmatically' ('You can create your own agent that lives in a private network and pushes the status'); storage.type memory|sqlite|postgres. A plausible zero-code service-status page for llama-server/coordinator health checks, but it has no notion of capacity/utilisation/threshold panels.
Uptime Kuma 2.5.3 (MIT, 2026-08-22) is 'an easy-to-use self-hosted monitoring tool' (Node.js) — uptime/status-page class, not a metrics dashboard.

Perses v0.54.0 (Apache-2.0; CNCF sandbox; the Grafana-like 'dashboard as code' alternative) 'currently supports Prometheus metrics, Tempo traces, Loki for logs, Pyroscope for profiling' — no SQL/PostgreSQL data source, so it cannot read the CORVID roster directly.

Metabase v0.63.14: 'Outside of the top-level "enterprise" directory, source code in a given file is licensed under the AGPL'; the enterprise directory is under the Metabase Commercial License; hub.docker.com/metabase/metabase binaries are AGPL. A BI-over-Postgres option in the founder's stack, but like Grafana it brings its own login and is a second, heavier UI.

htmx LICENSE at v2.0.10 (latest 2.x tag; v4 is pre-release) is Zero-Clause BSD (0BSD) — an acceptable, tiny dependency if the server-rendered status page wants partial-page polling without a JS build step.

ADR-0001 (Accepted 2026-08-22) consequences: 'The dashboard shows pool capacity, utilisation, and how close the next product threshold is; contributions appear only as thanks'; no per-member quotas, counts or ranks; data hard-partitioned per member; identity comes from the mesh on every request; default posture no prompt/content logging anywhere.

Phase 2 acceptance (package design spec §7 + plan Task 28): all three build nodes live on the map with capabilities; node-down visible within N = 3 × the heartbeat interval chosen in R06 (plan sketches a 15 s heartbeat → N = 45 s); capability report carries only what the owner opted in (`offers`); status page v0 is 'a server-rendered page at :8092 or Grafana' with panels: node liveness map, pool capacity/utilisation, distance to next threshold, thank-you list — never counts/ranks; hub services are compose-bounded infrastructure; page shows a stale badge when Postgres is down; no prompt/content text in any log.

ADR-0003 (Proposed) and R00-F7: solarplexus ports 8090–8093 are free; ports 80 and 443 are not in the hub's listening list (free for Caddy/Serve); Caddy already runs on the hub on a custom port with path routes and its admin API on 2019; whether it is the Debian package (/etc/caddy/Caddyfile) or a container is not recorded in R00 — an open question for the Phase 2 plan.

recommendations: Status page v0 = a server-rendered page, not Grafana: FastAPI + Jinja2 (deps already chosen by R06 for the coordinator) serving `/status` at :8092, re-rendered every 5–15 s (meta refresh or htmx 0BSD polling). Rationale: ADR-0001's four panels are bespoke (threshold distance, thanks-without-numbers), the page must never offer a sortable per-member table, and Grafana adds AGPL, a second identity system, `0.0.0.0` and phone-home defaults (R07-F8) to a 16 GB hub shared with Plex/Immich. Keep Grafana as a Phase 4 option for time-series history; if adopted: image `grafana/grafana` (OSS, AGPL — not the proprietary enterprise image), GF_SERVER_HTTP_ADDR=127.0.0.1 (or tailnet IP), GF_ANALYTICS_REPORTING_ENABLED=false, GF_ANALYTICS_CHECK_FOR_UPDATES=false, GF_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_ENABLED=true org_role Viewer, GF_AUTH_DISABLE_LOGIN_FORM=true, optional [auth.proxy] fed by Caddy header_up from the identity header with whitelist=127.0.0.1, a SELECT-only Postgres role, dashboards provisioned as JSON from `deploy/grafana/`, and a §4 row (AGPL-3.0-only, Grafana Labs) in the same commit.

Live-map data contract (for R06's schema and the page): per node — name, owner display name, last_heartbeat_at, age = now() − last_heartbeat_at, state = live (age < 1×interval) / stale (< 3×) / down (≥ 3×), and only the opted-in capabilities (offers, cpu cores, ram_gb, gpu name + vram_mb, battery/idle flags) under the owner's slider caps. Pool capacity = Σ over live nodes of offered (capped) RAM/VRAM/cores; utilisation = currently assigned/used by CORVID work; thresholds = a small `product_threshold` table (product, metric, needed) so 'distance to next threshold' is `needed − current` rendered as a progress bar; thanks = alphabetical list of contributor names with no numbers, no order by amount, no per-member usage. No geo map of houses (privacy); the 'map' is logical. Page shows a 'stale data' badge when the last successful DB read is older than 2× the refresh.

Identity plumbing — decide by hub Tailscale mode and keep backends loopback-only: all CORVID backends (8090–8093) bind 127.0.0.1 on the hub; Caddy is the only tailnet-facing listener (`bind <tailnet IP>` in kernel mode; `bind 127.0.0.1` while solarplexus is in userspace mode, where tailscaled forwards inbound 100.x:80 → 127.0.0.1:80 — R07-F26). Preferred identity mechanism: a tiny CORVID `whoami` forward_auth endpoint (Python, ~30 lines) that runs `tailscale whois --json {remote_host}:{remote_port}` (or the LocalAPI whois over the unix socket) and returns Tailscale-User/Login/Name headers, wired exactly like Caddy's documented Tailscale forward_auth example (R07-F15, R07-F29). It works in both tailscaled modes, needs no HTTPS feature (no CT-log disclosure, R07-F19), and depends on nothing experimental. Alternative A: `tailscale serve --bg --http=80 http://127.0.0.1:<caddy>` (Serve injects headers and strips squatters, R07-F22/F23) — adopt only if S-05 shows headers on --http; Alternative B: Serve on https:443 (requires enabling HTTPS certs; accept CT-log exposure of `solarplexus.<tailnet>.ts.net`). In every variant Caddy must `header_up -Tailscale-User-Login` (and siblings) on the route *before* forward_auth/serve re-adds them, so a member cannot self-assert identity; and ADR-0002's ACL should expose only Caddy's port(s) to members, never 8090–8093.

ADR-0002 amendment: `tag:member` must not be applied to devices a member browses from — tagged nodes get no serve identity headers and whois returns tags, not a user (R07-F21/F22/F24). Tag hubs only; members' laptops/phones stay user-owned. If a member's contributing desktop is also their browsing device, leave it untagged and express the ACL in terms of users/autogroup:member instead.

Caddy integration on the hub: CORVID ships `deploy/caddy/corvid.caddy` (site block or snippet with `handle_path`/`handle` routes for /, /chat, /v1, /api, /status plus the forward_auth block) and the Phase 2 plan installs it via an `import` line in the existing Caddyfile (R07-F20), then `systemctl reload caddy` (or `docker exec caddy caddy reload` if the hub's Caddy is a container — open question). Use `handle /status/*` if the status app is mounted at /status, `handle_path` only for apps that expect to be at root (R07-F14). Leave the existing media-stack routes untouched. Access logs: default redaction is fine (R07-F17); never enable `log_credentials`; no request bodies are logged by Caddy.

S-05 scope (tighten the card): on ahnoway (kernel mode) and, once Phase 0 steps land, on solarplexus (userspace mode): (1) `tailscale serve --bg --http=8099 http://127.0.0.1:<echo>` — do identity headers appear? (2) `tailscale serve --bg --https=443 …` — same, and note whether the tailnet HTTPS prompt fires; (3) connect directly to 100.x:<echo> on the userspace hub and record the source IP/port the echo server sees; (4) `tailscale whois --json 127.0.0.1:<that port>` while the connection is open — does it resolve the peer? (5) repeat (3)/(4) after solarplexus is switched to kernel mode. Record exact header names and values (Login may be an email or `user@github`).

Lightweight alternatives — what they are good for: Gatus (Apache-2.0) as an optional zero-code *service* health page (HTTP checks of /v1/models, /api/health; external endpoints pushed by agents) if the founder wants uptime history without writing it; Beszel (MIT) only as a design reference for per-host metrics incl. NVIDIA/AMD/Intel GPU (its hub port 8090 collides with ADR-0003 if co-hosted); Perses does not read SQL (skip); Uptime Kuma is uptime-only (skip); Metabase is a heavier AGPL BI UI (skip for v1). None replaces the ADR-0001 panels.

Log policy carried over from R06: the status page and whoami endpoint log only metadata (timestamp, path, status, latency, node id) — never identity header values in the access log beyond what Caddy logs by default, never query strings containing member names, never bodies.

Will solarplexus be switched from userspace to kernel mode before Phase 2 (status finding 10)? It decides bind strategy (tailnet IP vs 127.0.0.1) and whether whois needs ip:port.

Is the tailnet HTTPS-certificates feature acceptable given CT-log publication of `<machine>.tail2990fc.ts.net` names (R07-F19)? If not, Serve-over-HTTPS and Caddy automatic *.ts.net certs are off the table and the front door stays plain HTTP on the mesh.

If Grafana is adopted later: measure its RAM/CPU on the 16 GB hub next to Plex/Immich before committing; confirm the OSS image tag to pin (v13.2.0 today).
Member device tagging in ADR-0002's ACL baseline vs identity headers — needs a decision before the first member's device is tagged.

Fetched https://grafana.com/licensing/ live (HTTP 200, 2026-08-22); it is Grafana Labs' own page, i.e. primary. It contains verbatim: "On April 20, 2021, Grafana Labs announced that going forward, our core open source projects will be moving from the Apache License v2.0 to AGPLv3." and "Our core projects (Grafana, Grafana Loki, and Grafana Tempo) have moved to AGPL." (versions Grafana 8.0, Loki 2.3, Tempo 1.0). It states that customers who modify the AGPL version and distribute or offer it as a service over a network and do not want AGPL obligations "can contact us to secure a commercial license to meet these needs." It describes the Enterprise download as "a free-to-use, proprietary-licensed, compiled binary that matches the features of the AGPL version, and can be upgraded to take advantage of all the commercial features in Grafana Enterprise ... with the purchase of a license key." Fetched the cited page (docs 'latest', 2026-08-22). Everything in the claim is supported EXCEPT the parenthetical "(40+)". Verbatim checks: the definition sentence matches exactly; the "Enterprise features" section lists role-based access control, data source permissions, data source query and resource caching, reporting (PDF report, scheduled email), export dashboard as PDF, custom branding, usage insights, recorded queries, Vault integration, auditing, request security, settings updates at runtime; the "Authentication" section lists team sync, enhanced LDAP integration, SAML authentication, protected roles. But the "Enterprise data sources" section says only "you also get access to premium data sources, including:" and then names exactly 39 data sources — the page nowhere states "40+" (no digit string "40" appears in the page text). Cross-check against the primary plugin catalog (https://grafana.com/api/plugins, status=enterprise) shows 38 enterprise data source plugins + 3 enterprise app plugins = 41 enterprise plugins, so "40+ data source plugins" is not supported there either. Minor, but the claim as stated attributes a number to the docs page that the page does not contain. The judgment clause ("none needed for a friends-scale status page") is an inference, not checkable against the source, and is not contradicted by it (the page also notes many Enterprise features are in paid Grafana Cloud, i.e. "Enterprise-only" correctly means not-in-OSS).

Cited page fetched 2026-08-22 (HTML and the .md variant). Most of the claim is supported verbatim: "Each configuration file contains a list of data sources, under the `datasources` key, to add or update during startup"; dashboard YAML in provisioning/dashboards holds a `providers` list with `type: file` and `options.path` ("path to dashboard files on disk"); "More than 10 seconds: Grafana polls the path at that interval. 10 seconds or less: Grafana watches the filesystem for changes"; and `allowUiUpdates: true` persists UI edits to the DB while "If you save a provisioned dashboard in the UI and then later update the provisioning source, Grafana always overwrites the database dashboard with the one from the provisioning file." However, the claim as stated is NOT supported in two places: (1) the parenthetical "(conf/provisioning, or /etc/grafana/provisioning on deb/rpm)" appears nowhere on the cited page. The page's only path statements are about grafana.ini ("<WORKING DIRECTORY>/conf/defaults.ini" / "conf/custom.ini"; "The Deb and RPM packages install the configuration file at /etc/grafana/grafana.ini") — the dossier misattributed the config-file location note to the provisioning directory. The linked configure-grafana page ([paths] provisioning) describes the setting without stating a default. The actual defaults are only in the Grafana repo: conf/defaults.ini sets `provisioning = conf/provisioning`, and the deb/rpm packaging sets `PROVISIONING_CFG_DIR=/etc/grafana/provisioning` (packaging/deb/default/grafana-server, packaging/rpm/sysconfig/grafana-server), passed to the unit as cfg:default.paths.provisioning. So the paths are factually right but uncited. (2) "provisioned files win on reload" is looser than the source: the doc says files overwrite the DB copy when the provisioning source is later updated (and with updateIntervalSeconds >10 detection is polling, <=10 filesystem watch, with a caveat that watch events may not propagate through Docker bind mounts/network filesystems); it does not say a mere reload/restart discards UI edits when the file is unchanged. Refuted on strict "source supports claim as stated" grounds; substance is salvageable with corrected attribution and wording.
verdicts.corrected_statement: Grafana provisioning (docs 'latest', fetched 2026-08-22): data sources and dashboards are provisioned from YAML files placed under the provisioning directory's provisioning/datasources and provisioning/dashboards subfolders. The provisioning root is the [paths] `provisioning` setting; its default is `conf/provisioning` (grafana repo conf/defaults.ini) and the deb/rpm packages point it at `/etc/grafana/provisioning` via PROVISIONING_CFG_DIR in packaging/deb/default/grafana-server and packaging/rpm/sysconfig/grafana-server — these defaults are NOT stated on the administration/provisioning page, which only gives grafana.ini's location (conf/defaults.ini, conf/custom.ini, /etc/grafana/grafana.ini on deb/rpm). Per the provisioning page: "Each configuration file contains a list of data sources, under the `datasources` key, to add or update during startup"; dashboard config files contain a list of `providers` (type: file) whose `options.path` points at a folder of JSON dashboards; `updateIntervalSeconds` >10 means Grafana polls the path at that interval, <=10 means Grafana watches the filesystem (note: watch events may not propagate through Docker bind mounts or some network filesystems — set >10 to force polling); `allowUiUpdates: true` lets UI edits be saved to Grafana's DB, but if the provisioning source is later updated Grafana always overwrites the DB dashboard with the file (ignoring the JSON `version`); `allowUiUpdates: false` blocks saving ("Cannot save provisioned dashboard"). This enables dashboards-as-code in the CORVID repo.
