R03 and R04 do not mention it, yet R04's Phase 1 candidates are Q4_K_M/Q8_0 GGUFs split over RPC — a plan writer needs the ggml-org/llama.cpp issue number and whether it is resolved (or an explicit note that a spike, e.g. S-02/S-03, covers it empirically).

exo v1.0.71 cross-house viability is not established: README says devices 'automatically discover each other' via libp2p (EXO_LIBP2P_NAMESPACE) but not whether discovery crosses subnets/VPNs (Tailscale has no mDNS/UDP broadcast) or whether peers can be listed manually — does exo 1.x work over a tailnet at all? Matrix should also record: model formats (HuggingFace Hub / MLX only — GGUF?), Apple Silicon required (Intel Macs excluded by MLX), minimum RAM, and that Linux install is source-only (uv + Node 18+ + Rust nightly; no pip/app) while macOS is EXO-latest.dmg on Tahoe 26.2+.

Ollama F31 concludes the GTX 970 on driver 535 is outside Ollama's support, but gpu.mdx at v0.32.15 also says Vulkan is 'enabled by default when the backend is installed' on Windows/Linux — does Ollama's Vulkan backend run Maxwell/Pascal NVIDIA GPUs on pre-550 drivers (which would reverse the member-guide statement)? Ollama's Windows minimum OS version is also not recorded.

prima.cpp: README does not state which upstream llama.cpp commit/version it forked from or last synced with, and lists supported families only as Llama, Qwen/QwQ and DeepSeek GGUF (Q4K/Q6K/Q80/IQ1) — are R04's Phase 1 candidates (Qwen3.8-27B, Gemma 4 31B, Muse-Glimmer-30B) loadable at all? Also its ring assumes one LAN ('physically fully connected because they all connect to the same Wi-Fi', ports 9000/10000) — untested over tailnet IPs. Watch-list only; needed only if anyone runs it.

research.dossier:
DOSSIER R10 — Hub integration points + Phase 3–5 outlines (researched 2026-08-22, primary sources only; pages fetched with curl and read in full, GitHub raw files at pinned tags).

== 1. Tdarr (distributed transcoding) — node model and licence ==
Architecture: Tdarr_Server is the central process all Nodes connect to; Tdarr_Node runs on the same or other devices and pulls tasks from the Server; nodes exist for Windows, Linux (x64/arm64) and macOS, plus Docker images ghcr.io/haveagitgat/tdarr (server, optional internal node) and ghcr.io/haveagitgat/tdarr_node. Nodes connect OUTBOUND to the server on serverPort (default 8266) and open no inbound port (nodeIP/nodePort obsolete since 2.00.17) — so a friend's node reaches solarplexus over the tailnet with zero inbound exposure. Node config is env vars (override JSON): serverURL (recommended, e.g. http://solarplexus:8266), nodeName, nodeType, priority, apiKey, pathTranslators (JSON only). Two node types: "mapped" (default; node and server must see the SAME media + transcode-cache paths via shares, reconciled with pathTranslators) and "unmapped" (node works from its own cache and uploads/downloads files automatically — but WITHOUT Tdarr Pro it is limited to 10 MB video / 0.1 MB other files, i.e. useless; Pro removes the cap). Unmapped mode also exposes library/cache files via Tdarr's network API, so auth=true + apiKey is advised. NVENC in the node container = --gpus=all + NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES=all.
Licence: Tdarr is NOT open source. LICENSE.md is an EULA with tiers Personal Free / Personal Subscription / Business Subscription; it prohibits redistribution, reverse engineering and "any unauthorized use" without permission, is governed by UK law and can be modified "with or without notice". GitHub reports licence "Other/NOASSERTION". The plugin repo (Tdarr_Plugins) is GPL-3.0. Latest binaries per storage.tdarr.io/versions.json: 2.86.01 (docs' updater links point at 2.81.01). Tdarr Pro pricing could not be verified from a static primary page (tdarr.io is a JS app) — left unverified.
Meaning for §4: CORVID may *integrate with* a member-installed Tdarr (credit row: "Tdarr — proprietary EULA, Personal Free tier; not redistributed by CORVID") but must never bundle or redistribute it, and the real Phase-3 transcode path across houses is either (a) mapped Tdarr nodes over tailnet SMB/NFS shares from solarplexus, or (b) CORVID's own ffmpeg-in-a-capped-container jobs, which avoids the proprietary dependency and the Pro paywall entirely. Recommend (b) as the Phase-3 default and Tdarr as an optional hub integration.

== 2. Immich remote machine learning ==
Immich v3.1.0 (2026-07-29, AGPL-3.0). The immich-machine-learning container can run on a different host; the server sends image previews to it over HTTP; the ML container "does not persist this data", and — the docs' own danger note — "as an internal service, the machine learning container has no security measures whatsoever". Compose: image ghcr.io/immich-app/immich-machine-learning:${IMMICH_VERSION:-release}[-cuda], volume model-cache:/cache, port 3003; then Admin → Machine Learning Settings → Add URL http://ip:3003. Smart Search + Face Detection go remote; Facial Recognition stays server+DB. Multiple URLs are tried sequentially (no load balancing); adding a URL keeps local fallback, replacing it means jobs fail (and must be retried) when the remote is down. Both hosts should run the same IMMICH_VERSION. CUDA backend: compute capability ≥ 5.2, official driver ≥ 545 (CUDA 12.3), NVIDIA Container Toolkit on Linux (not needed under WSL2); Linux and Windows/WSL2 servers only; hwaccel.ml.yml cuda = deploy.resources.reservations.devices {driver nvidia, count 1, capabilities [gpu]}. Multi-GPU via MACHINE_LEARNING_DEVICE_IDS + MACHINE_LEARNING_WORKERS, each GPU must hold all models.
Fleet impact: solarplexus (driver 535 / CUDA 12.2, GTX 970 CC 5.2) meets the CC floor but NOT the ≥545 driver floor — it cannot host the -cuda ML image without a driver upgrade; the RTX 2070 Super laptop (CC 7.5) and RTX 3050 node (CC 8.6, CUDA 13.1) can. Bind 3003 to the tailnet IP only (no auth exists), and pin versions.

== 3. Docker resource caps for batch jobs ==
Containers are unconstrained by default. Hard caps: --memory (min 6m) with --memory-swap set EQUAL to it to deny swap (unset = container may use as much swap again as memory; -1 = unlimited), --memory-reservation is soft; do not use --oom-kill-disable without -m. CPU: --cpus="1.5" ≡ --cpu-period=100000 --cpu-quota=150000; --cpuset-cpus pins cores; --cpu-shares is soft. Check `docker info` for "WARNING: No swap limit support". GPU: --gpus all | device=0 | device=<UUID> | '"device=0,2"' requires the NVIDIA driver + NVIDIA Container Toolkit (configure with `sudo nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=docker && sudo systemctl restart docker`); "NVIDIA GPUs can only be accessed by systems running a single engine"; capabilities via --gpus 'all,capabilities=utility'. Host protection flags from the docker run reference: --read-only (root fs RO), --tmpfs, --pids-limit, --cap-drop, --security-opt no-new-privileges (su/sudo stop working). Docker Engine by default "drops all capabilities except those needed, an allowlist instead of a denylist approach"; best practice is to remove all capabilities except those explicitly required. Docker Engine (moby) is Apache-2.0; Docker Desktop is free for personal use / small business (<250 employees AND <$10M revenue) under the Docker Subscription Service Agreement. NVIDIA Container Toolkit v1.20.0 is Apache-2.0; its tested-platform table lists Ubuntu 22.04/24.04/26.04, Debian 11, RHEL 8/9/10, Amazon Linux, SUSE — Arch is not listed, though "Releases can work on more platforms than indicated".
Proposed job template (all enforced by the agent locally): docker run --rm --cpus=<cap> --memory=<cap> --memory-swap=<same> --pids-limit=<n> --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --mount type=bind,src=<scratch>,dst=/work --cap-drop ALL --security-opt no-new-privileges [--gpus device=<idx>] <image>.

== 4. WSL2 + Docker + CUDA on Windows ==
NVIDIA CUDA on WSL User Guide (v13.3, updated 2026-06-25): install ONLY the Windows NVIDIA driver — "Do not install any Linux display driver in WSL"; the Windows CUDA driver is stubbed into WSL2 as libcuda.so; if a toolkit is needed install the WSL-Ubuntu package / cuda-toolkit-12-x metapackage only, never cuda / cuda-12-x / cuda-drivers. GPU acceleration is for Pascal and later in WDDM mode (Maxwell "not officially supported"); WSL kernel ≥ 4.19.121 (5.10.16.3+ recommended); `wsl.exe --install` then `wsl.exe --update`. Docker in WSL2 is supported (NVIDIA Container Toolkit ≥ v2.6.0 / libnvidia-container 1.5.1+; CLI and Docker Desktop) with the limitation that only `--gpus all` works (no per-index GPU filtering) and NVML queries such as GPU utilization are unsupported. Docker Desktop GPU support exists only with the WSL2 backend (GPU-PV), validated with `docker run --rm -it --gpus=all nvcr.io/nvidia/k8s/cuda-sample:nbody nbody -gpu -benchmark`. Immich's openvino-wsl/cuda notes confirm WSL2 hosts are supported for the ML container.

== 5. gVisor as the upgrade path ==
gVisor is a Go userspace application kernel; runsc is an OCI runtime that plugs into Docker: `sudo runsc install` (or apt repo, which auto-configures Docker), `sudo systemctl restart docker`, `docker run --runtime=runsc …`. Needs Docker ≥ 17.09, Linux ≥ 5.6, x86_64/ARM64. Default platform is systrap (no KVM needed; KVM is bare-metal-only advice; ptrace deprecated). GPU support via --nvproxy works with Docker's --gpus flag; officially supported GPUs are T4, A100/A10G, L4, H100, with consumer cards on the same microarchitectures "likely" to work (RTX 3090/4090 named); driver support is a STRICT version match (`runsc nvproxy list-supported-drivers`; --nvproxy-allow-unsupported-driver for known-but-unqualified versions; unknown versions always fail). At release-20260817.0 the supported list includes 535.129.03/183.06/247.01/261.03/274.02/288.01/309.01, 550.90.12, 570.x, 580.x, 590.48.01, 610/615/620.x. Default driver capabilities allowed are compute+utility only; only /dev/nvidiactl, /dev/nvidia-uvm, /dev/nvidia# are exposed. gVisor's own caveat: "NVIDIA driver updates must be part of any security plan with or without gVisor". Apache-2.0. Note the 2026-07 packaging change (runsc + gvisor-bin/ sidecars; auto-download ends Sept 2026) — install via apt. Verdict: a credible Phase-4/5 upgrade for Linux/WSL2 batch nodes once less-trusted workloads appear; not needed for v1 (friends-trust), and GPU-in-gVisor on consumer Turing/Maxwell is a spike, not a plan.

== 6. Folding@home team basics ==
The v8 client is open source: fah-client-bastet (backend, GPL-3.0, latest tag v8.5.6) and fah-web-client-bastet (web UI, GPL-3.0); Windows/macOS installers are signed, Linux packages are not (download only from foldingathome.org). Teams pool points under a team number; team 0 = none; members join by entering the number in Web Control (Account Settings with an F@h Account, or per-machine Machine Settings without). Creating a team is done in Web Control → Settings → Teams and REQUIRES a Folding@home Account (free; email + passphrase); you are assigned a team number to share. A passkey (requested at apps.foldingathome.org with username+email, emailed, never shown) ties WUs to a donor and is required for the Quick Return Bonus; it is private and distinct from the account passphrase. Headless Linux: write <account-token> and <machine-name> into /etc/fah-client/config.xml, `sudo systemctl restart fah-client`, then rotate the token. Politeness built in: "Only When Idle" scheduling, CPU-count slider, per-GPU checkboxes, idle (lowest) process priority. Rules: run only on machines you own or have explicit permission for; bundling the client into another installer without the user's knowledge/consent violates the EULA — so CORVID's agent must NOT silently install F@h; it can only link members to the official installer and the team number. Stats update hourly; a new team appears immediately; use daily_team_summary.txt rather than scraping. The live team leaderboard host (stats.foldingathome.org) was unreachable from this research host — unverified.

== Phase 3–5 outline implications ==
Phase 3 (batch jobs): ship the capped-container template above; first workload = ffmpeg transcode via the CORVID queue (open, credit-clean) with Tdarr as an optional member-run integration; Windows nodes via Docker Desktop (free tier) on WSL2 with --gpus all only. Phase 4 (politeness/dashboard): F@h team CORVID as the "leftovers" default, opt-in per member, using F@h's own idle/priority controls; Immich remote-ML as the photo-brain worker on the 2070 Super/3050 nodes, tailnet-bound. Phase 5 (converge): evaluate gVisor runsc for batch nodes (ADR), and decide Tdarr-vs-native-ffmpeg and hub driver upgrade (≥545 unlocks Immich CUDA on solarplexus; check gVisor nvproxy list before/after).

facts.statement: Tdarr is a two-component click-to-run web app: Tdarr_Server is the 'Central process which all Nodes connect with' and Tdarr_Node is 'Processes running on same/other devices which collect tasks from the Server'; nodes are available for Windows, Linux (including arm/arm64) and macOS.

Tdarr Nodes connect outbound to the Server on serverPort and do not open an inbound node port; the legacy nodeIP/nodePort variables have not been needed since 2.00.17, so published node-port mappings (8267/8268) can be removed.

Node configuration: environment variables override JSON config; node vars include nodeName, serverURL (recommended, e.g. http://192.168.1.100:8266; serverIP/serverPort are deprecated in favour of serverURL), nodeType, unmappedNodeCache, priority (-1 none, 0 highest), apiKey, startPaused, pollInterval; pathTranslators can only be set via JSON (or base64 env).

Tdarr has two node types. 'Mapped' (standard) requires the node to be on the same file system as the server or have mapped shares with path translators so source and cache folders on server and node point to the same location. 'Unmapped' (new in 2.27.01 with Tdarr Pro) works independently of the server's file system with automatic download/upload, but without Tdarr Pro is limited to video files up to 10MB and other files up to 0.1MB; Pro removes these limits.

When 'Allow unmapped Nodes' is enabled, files in Tdarr's library source and cache folders become accessible through Tdarr's network API; the docs advise enabling authentication. Unmapped nodes are configured with nodeType=unmapped and unmappedNodeCache=/cache (a dedicated directory, auto-cleaned).

Tdarr authentication: set server auth=true (authSecretKey auto-generated), set username/password in the web UI, create an API key under Tools -> API Keys and set apiKey on each Node; for automation seededApiKey must start with 'tapi_' and be at least 14 characters.

Tdarr is not open source: the repository's LICENSE.md is an 'END USER LICENSE AGREEMENT (EULA) FOR TDARR' with three tiers (Personal Free; Personal Subscription; Business Subscription & Trial); it states 'Redistribution, reverse engineering, or any unauthorized use of the Software is prohibited without explicit permission from Tdarr', is governed by the laws of the United Kingdom, and 'Tdarr reserves the right to modify this EULA at any time, with or without notice'. GitHub's licence detection reports 'Other' (SPDX NOASSERTION).
The Tdarr plugin repository (HaveAGitGat/Tdarr_Plugins) is licensed GPL-3.0, separate from the proprietary Tdarr binaries.

The official Tdarr version manifest lists 2.86.01 as the newest release with Tdarr_Server and Tdarr_Node zips for win32_x64, linux_x64, linux_arm64, darwin_x64 and darwin_arm64; the docs' Tdarr_Updater download links currently point at 2.81.01.

Tdarr Docker images are ghcr.io/haveagitgat/tdarr (Server plus optional internal Node via internalNode=true) and ghcr.io/haveagitgat/tdarr_node; NVENC in containers uses --gpus=all with NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES=all and NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=all (add --runtime=nvidia only if docker info lists an nvidia runtime), and Server and Node must share the same media (/media) and transcode cache (/temp) paths.

Tdarr Pro subscription price and exact feature list could not be verified from a static primary page (tdarr.io home/download pages are JavaScript apps; no pricing page in the docs sitemap). The EULA confirms paid 'Personal Subscription' and 'Business Subscription' tiers exist.

Immich lets you host the machine-learning container on a more powerful remote system; the server container sends requests containing the image preview to the remote ML container, which 'does not persist this data or associate it with a particular user'. Smart Search and Face Detection use the remote ML; Facial Recognition does not (server + database only).
facts.version: docs last updated 2026-07-27; same text in docs/docs/guides/remote-machine-learning.md at tag v3.1.0

facts.statement: Immich's own danger note: 'Image previews are sent to the remote machine learning container... as an internal service, the machine learning container has no security measures whatsoever. Please be mindful of where it's deployed and who can access it.'

Remote ML compose: service immich-machine-learning, image ghcr.io/immich-app/immich-machine-learning:${IMMICH_VERSION:-release} (append -cuda/-rocm/-openvino/-armnn/-rknn for acceleration, optionally extends hwaccel.ml.yml), volume model-cache:/cache, ports 3003:3003, restart: always; then in Admin > Machine Learning Settings click 'Add URL' and enter http://ip:port. 'Version mismatches between both hosts may cause bugs and instability' — update both together.

Multiple ML URLs are tried sequentially — 'there is no attempt to distribute load across multiple containers'; adding a URL (rather than replacing) keeps the local ML container as fallback, while replacing it means Smart Search/Face Detection jobs fail when the remote is unavailable and must be retried via the 'Missing' button in Job Status.

Immich CUDA ML backend prerequisites: GPU compute capability 5.2 or greater; official NVIDIA driver installed and >= 545 (must support CUDA 12.3); on Linux (except WSL2) NVIDIA Container Toolkit is required. Only Linux and Windows (through WSL2) servers are supported; 'CUDA is the most reliable' backend. hwaccel.ml.yml 'cuda' service = deploy.resources.reservations.devices: [{driver: nvidia, count: 1, capabilities: [gpu]}].

Immich is licensed under the GNU AGPL v3 (LICENSE file at tag v3.1.0; site footer 'available as open source under the terms of the GNU AGPL v3 License'); latest GitHub release is v3.1.0 published 2026-07-29.

Immich multi-GPU: set MACHINE_LEARNING_DEVICE_IDS to a comma-separated list and MACHINE_LEARNING_WORKERS to the number of devices; each GPU must be able to load all models — 'It is not possible to distribute a single model to multiple GPUs'.

Docker memory caps: by default a container has no resource constraints; -m/--memory sets a hard maximum (minimum 6m); --memory-swap is total memory+swap — if set equal to --memory the container gets no swap, if unset the container may use as much swap again as --memory, -1 = unlimited swap; --memory-reservation is a soft limit below --memory; Docker advises not to set --oom-kill-disable unless -m is also set.

Docker CPU caps: --cpus="1.5" guarantees at most 1.5 CPUs and is equivalent to --cpu-period=100000 --cpu-quota=150000; --cpuset-cpus restricts to specific cores (e.g. 0-3 or 1,3); --cpu-shares (default 1024) is a soft weight only enforced under contention.
Some resource-constraint features need kernel support; `docker info` prints e.g. 'WARNING: No swap limit support' when a capability is disabled in the kernel.

Docker GPU access requires the NVIDIA driver plus NVIDIA Container Toolkit; use --gpus all, --gpus device=0, --gpus device=<UUID>, or --gpus '"device=0,2"' (quoted because of the comma); driver capabilities can be narrowed, e.g. --gpus 'all,capabilities=utility'; 'NVIDIA GPUs can only be accessed by systems running a single engine'.

docker run hardening flags: --read-only ('Mount the container's root filesystem as read only'), --tmpfs (mount a tmpfs, e.g. --tmpfs /run:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=65536k), --pids-limit ('Tune container pids limit'), --cap-drop ('Drop Linux capabilities'), and --security-opt no-new-privileges (processes cannot gain privileges; su/sudo no longer work).

Docker Engine security: 'By default Docker drops all capabilities except those needed, an allowlist instead of a denylist approach'; 'The best practice for users would be to remove all capabilities except those explicitly required for their processes.' The daemon itself requires root unless Rootless mode is used.
Docker Engine (moby/moby) is licensed Apache-2.0.

Docker Desktop is licensed under the Docker Subscription Service Agreement and is free for small businesses (fewer than 250 employees AND less than $10 million annual revenue), personal use, education and non-commercial open source projects; paid subscription required for professional use in larger organizations, government entities and commercial use beyond the free tier. Docker Engine/Moby licensing is unchanged.

CUDA on WSL2: install only the Windows NVIDIA driver — 'This is the only driver you need to install. Do not install any Linux display driver in WSL'; the Windows CUDA driver is stubbed inside WSL2 as libcuda.so; if a toolkit is needed use the WSL-Ubuntu package and 'Install the cuda-toolkit-12-x metapackage only' — do NOT choose the cuda, cuda-12-x or cuda-drivers meta-packages.
facts.version: CUDA on WSL 13.3 documentation, last updated 2026-06-25

facts.statement: WSL2 GPU acceleration is available on Pascal and later GeForce/Quadro GPUs in WDDM mode; 'Maxwell GPUs are not officially supported in WSL 2, but it may still work'; WSL kernel must be at least 4.19.121+ (5.10.16.3+ recommended); setup is `wsl.exe --install` then `wsl.exe --update`; R495+ Windows drivers include WSL2 CUDA support.

Docker in WSL2 is 'Supported' with NVIDIA Container Toolkit minimum v2.6.0 / libnvidia-container 1.5.1+, 'CLI and Docker Desktop Supported'; known limitations: with the NVIDIA Container Toolkit for Docker 19.03 only `--gpus all` is supported (no per-index GPU filtering on multi-GPU systems), NVML/nvidia-smi does not support all queries (e.g. GPU utilization), and Unified Memory full managed-memory support is unavailable.

Docker Desktop GPU support is only available on Windows with the WSL2 backend (NVIDIA GPU Paravirtualization); prerequisites: NVIDIA GPU, up-to-date Windows 10/11, WSL2-GPU-PV-capable NVIDIA driver, latest WSL2 kernel (`wsl --update`), WSL2 backend enabled; validate with `docker run --rm -it --gpus=all nvcr.io/nvidia/k8s/cuda-sample:nbody nbody -gpu -benchmark`.

NVIDIA Container Toolkit: after installing, configure Docker with `sudo nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=docker` then `sudo systemctl restart docker` (rootless variant writes $HOME/.config/docker/daemon.json). Tested platforms table lists Ubuntu 22.04/24.04/26.04, Debian 11, RHEL 8.x/9.x/10.x, Amazon Linux 2/2023, OpenSUSE/SLES 15.x — Arch is not listed, but 'Releases can work on more platforms than indicated in the table above'. Latest release v1.20.0; licence Apache-2.0.

gVisor is an application kernel written in Go that runs in userspace and ships the OCI runtime `runsc`, which integrates with Docker; the Sentry intercepts application syscalls and does not pass them through to the host kernel, and a per-container Gofer mediates file-system access. Compatibility caveat: gVisor 'does not presently implement every system call, /proc file, or /sys file'.

gVisor with Docker: requires Docker 17.09.0+; install with `sudo runsc install` (adds a 'runsc' runtime to /etc/docker/daemon.json) then `sudo systemctl restart docker`, run with `docker run --runtime=runsc ...`; many docker options (e.g. --cpus, -v, -p) work with runsc. The apt repository install (storage.googleapis.com/gvisor/releases) auto-configures Docker; gVisor supports x86_64 and ARM64 and requires Linux 5.6+.

gVisor platforms: `systrap` is the default (it replaced `ptrace` as default in mid-2023; ptrace is no longer supported); KVM platform needs /dev/kvm access (user in kvm group) and is recommended on bare metal only; platform chosen via runsc --platform in daemon.json runtimeArgs.

gVisor GPU support (nvproxy): enable with runsc flag --nvproxy; Docker's --gpus flag works directly with --runtime=runsc; officially supported GPUs are T4 (Turing), A100/A10G (Ampere), L4 (Ada), H100 (Hopper) — 'other NVIDIA GPUs based on the same microarchitectures... will likely work as well', naming RTX 3090 and RTX 4090; driver support is a strict version match (`runsc nvproxy list-supported-drivers`; --nvproxy-allow-unsupported-driver for known-but-unqualified versions; unknown versions always fail); by default only compute and utility driver capabilities are allowed; only /dev/nvidiactl, /dev/nvidia-uvm and /dev/nvidia# are exposed; all nvproxy functionality is supported on systrap and ptrace (cudaMallocManaged flaky on KVM).

gVisor is Apache-2.0 (LICENSE at tag release-20260817.0, the latest release tag). Since 2026-07 releases moved from two binaries to runsc + containerd-shim-runsc-v1 + a gvisor-bin/ sidecar directory; runsc's best-effort auto-download of missing sidecars 'will be dropped at the end of September 2026' — the apt repo is the recommended install path.

gVisor's GPU security caveat: 'while gVisor will protect the host from the sandboxed application, NVIDIA driver updates must be part of any security plan with or without gVisor'; nvproxy is a passthrough that forwards ioctl(2) calls to the host NVIDIA driver with minimal intervention.

The Folding@home v8 client is open source: fah-client-bastet (the headless folding service; GPL-3.0 at tag v8.5.6, the latest tag) and fah-web-client-bastet (local web UI; GPL-3.0); the MD engines are GROMACS and OpenMM. Current public release packages are fah-client 8.5.6 for windows-10-64bit, macos-12-universal, debian-10-64bit and debian-stable-arm64 (the debian-stable-64bit directory lists 8.1.18).

F@h teams: 'A team pools the points of everyone folding under one team number'; team is optional (0 = none), one team at a time; join by entering the team number as 'Team' in Web Control (Account Settings with a Folding@home Account, or each machine's Machine Settings without one). Creating a team: Web Control → Settings → Teams → New Team (name, optional URL/logo) — 'you'll need to be signed in to a Folding@home Account first' (free) — and 'You'll be assigned a team number to share with anyone you want to recruit'.

F@h passkey: a unique token tying work units to a donor; request at apps.foldingathome.org (username + email; the passkey is emailed, not displayed); Quick Return Bonus requires a passkey plus >=10 returned bonus-eligible WUs and >=80% return rate; keep it private and use the same passkey on every machine; a passkey is not the account passphrase. Username 'anonymous' is allowed.

Headless Linux F@h: write <account-token v="..."/> and <machine-name v="..."/> into /etc/fah-client/config.xml, `sudo systemctl restart fah-client`, then rotate the token in Account Settings ('Only the most recent account token can add new machines'). The Debian package runs as the fah-client systemd service; logs in /var/log/fah-client, data in /var/lib/fah-client.

F@h politeness controls: per-machine Scheduling includes 'Only When Idle — fold only when nobody is using the keyboard or mouse' and 'Keep Awake'; a CPUs slider sets how many cores may be used; each supported GPU has its own enable/disable checkbox; the client runs 'at idle (lowest) priority'. Rules: 'Run Folding@home only on computers you own or for which you have the owner's explicit permission'; bundling the client into another software package without the user's knowledge violates the EULA; Windows/macOS installers are signed, Linux packages are not.

F@h stats: 'Stats are updated hourly, on the hour'; a username appears after the first returned WU while 'A brand-new team appears right away'; raw data is in daily_team_summary.txt / daily_user_summary.txt at apps.foldingathome.org and crawling live stats pages gets an IP permanently banned. Hardware characteristics are reported to the assignment server; IP address/hostname/geo are never published.

The live team leaderboard at stats.foldingathome.org/teams could not be fetched from the research host (TCP connect failure) and via the WebFetch tool; its content (per-team fields, join UI) is therefore unverified.

recommendations: Phase 3 default transcode path: CORVID's own ffmpeg-in-a-capped-container job (open, credit-clean) rather than Tdarr; treat Tdarr as an optional, member-installed hub integration. Tdarr's EULA forbids redistribution, so CORVID must never bundle Tdarr binaries/images or wrap its installer; link to official downloads only and record it in §4 as 'proprietary EULA, Personal Free tier, not redistributed'.

If Tdarr is used: run Tdarr_Server on solarplexus bound to the tailnet IP (serverIP/serverBindIP), set auth=true and per-node apiKey, and use MAPPED nodes over tailnet-only SMB/NFS shares with pathTranslators — unmapped nodes are capped at 10 MB files without Tdarr Pro and expose library/cache via the network API.

Immich photo brain: run ghcr.io/immich-app/immich-machine-learning:${IMMICH_VERSION}-cuda on the RTX 2070 Super laptop or RTX 3050 node (both meet CC>=5.2 and driver>=545); solarplexus (driver 535 / CUDA 12.2) cannot host the CUDA image until upgraded to >=545 (GTX 970 CC 5.2 would then qualify). Bind port 3003 to the tailnet interface only (the ML service has no auth), pin both hosts to the same IMMICH_VERSION (currently v3.1.0), and add the remote URL (keep local fallback) rather than replacing it; one remote URL only since Immich does no load balancing.

Batch-job container template (enforced locally by the agent, §5.3/§5.5): docker run --rm --cpus=<owner cap> --memory=<cap> --memory-swap=<same value> --pids-limit=<n> --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --mount type=bind,src=<scratch>,dst=/work --cap-drop ALL --security-opt no-new-privileges [--gpus device=<idx>] <image>; add a CI/agent preflight that checks `docker info` for 'WARNING: No swap limit support' and that the NVIDIA Container Toolkit is configured (nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=docker).

Windows member guide (WSL2 path): install only the Windows NVIDIA driver (never a Linux driver in WSL), `wsl --install` + `wsl --update`, Docker Desktop (free for personal use) with the WSL2 backend; expect `--gpus all` only (no per-GPU indexing) and no NVML utilization queries; require Pascal-or-newer GPUs (Maxwell unsupported in WSL2). Validate with the nbody cuda-sample container.
Arch/EndeavourOS laptop: NVIDIA Container Toolkit is not in NVIDIA's tested-platform table — verify with a spike before relying on --gpus there; Ubuntu hub and Debian-family nodes are covered.

gVisor: adopt as the documented Phase-4/5 upgrade path for Linux/WSL2 batch nodes (install via apt repo; --runtime=runsc; systrap default needs no KVM). Do not enable by default in v1 (friends-trust model). GPU-in-gVisor is a spike: nvproxy requires a strict driver-version match (check `runsc nvproxy list-supported-drivers` against each node's exact driver) and officially supports datacenter GPUs only; consumer Turing/Ampere 'likely' work, Maxwell (GTX 970) is not on any supported microarchitecture.

Folding@home: founder creates 'team CORVID' once in Web Control (needs one free F@h Account), publishes the team number in the member guide; each member installs the official client themselves (the agent must NOT silently install or bundle F@h — rules/EULA forbid it), picks their own username/passkey (passkey stays private), and uses F@h's built-in 'Only When Idle' + CPU slider + per-GPU toggles, which already satisfy §5. Linux/headless members use /etc/fah-client/config.xml with an account token; Windows/macOS installers are signed, Linux packages are not (download from foldingathome.org only). Thank-you board can pull daily_team_summary.txt, never scrape live stats.

ADR for Phase 5: decide (a) Tdarr integration vs native ffmpeg jobs, (b) hub driver upgrade to >=545 (unlocks Immich CUDA on solarplexus; re-check gVisor nvproxy list after), (c) gVisor enablement criteria (when a workload is less than fully trusted).

§4 credit rows to add on adoption: Immich (AGPL-3.0), Docker Engine (Apache-2.0), Docker Desktop (Docker Subscription Service Agreement, free personal tier — Windows members), NVIDIA Container Toolkit (Apache-2.0), gVisor (Apache-2.0), Folding@home client (GPL-3.0); Tdarr only as a non-redistributed proprietary integration, Tdarr_Plugins (GPL-3.0) only if CORVID writes plugins.
open_questions: Exact NVIDIA driver build on solarplexus (535.x.y) and on the RTX 3050 node (CUDA 13.1 implies a 590+ driver) — needed for gVisor nvproxy's strict version match and to confirm whether a hub upgrade to >=545 (Immich CUDA) is acceptable alongside llama.cpp RPC.

Does gVisor nvproxy actually run CUDA workloads on GTX 970 (Maxwell) or RTX 2070 Super (Turing consumer)? Only datacenter GPUs are officially supported.
Why does the Folding@home debian-stable-64bit package directory list 8.1.18 while other platforms are at 8.5.6 — is there a newer apt repo path members should use?
